PREFACE 

"Our Continental Neighbors" is the third is the third book in the series published under the gen eral title Our World and Ourselves. It follows "Our Home State and Continent,' 

with which it is closely articulated. It covers the study of all the inhabited continents except North America. "Our Continental Neighbors" is a definitive title. The peoples of each continent are studied in their living environment. The treatment of the different regions and peoples has been expanded or restricted on the basis of their relative importance in our modern world. 

South America and Europe are the two continents that are, on the whole, closest to us physically, socially, commercially, and politically. Our interest in South America is memorialized historically in the Monroe 

Doctrine. Our South American neighbors have long looked upon the United States as the leading champion of their political rights. 

The Pan-American Union is an expression of this growing sense of common interests in this new world of our day. Geographically, too, the countries of this continent to the southeast of us afford, either through contrast as in Brazil, or through likeness as in Argentina, an interesting study to pupils already familiar with our own country. Our extensive and increasing trade with South American countries, their need of our products, and their actual and potential buying power lend unusual interest to their study by our boys and girls. In every way South 

America is one of our closest, most interesting, and most important continental neighbors.

News of importance from Europe figures even more prominently in our daily newspapers than news from South America. 

Since the World War, the dependence of Europe upon our country, and the interest of our country in the countries of Europe, have become more and more evident. 

Europe is our original ancestral home. Its institutions, languages, laws, and customs have been transplanted across the Atlantic, where they are to be found today in more or less modified form. Our best foreign markets are in Europe, and from European countries we buy a large part of our imports. 

American tourists are to be found at all seasons of the year in every European country. 

For all of these reasons it is generally agreed that Europe and the leading countries of Europe must take a commanding place in any study of foreign nations and peoples. 

Asia, likewise, demands our careful attention. That we have serious and increasing political interest in the peoples of that continent cannot be ignored or denied. Our commercial transactions with China, Japan, and

India give to parts of Asia an economic importance that even the breadth of the Pacific cannot minimize. Perhaps, too, no other continent affords the pupil such varied contrasts with his own, as does Asia. 

Africa and Australia, likewise, together with the important neighboring islands, are given accounts adequate to their importance. 

Thus the entire cycle of our continental neighbors is covered. When a pupil has familiarized himself with the interesting materials of this volume, in addition to what he learned about North America the year before, he has a world view and understanding into which he can fit his further study. 

He will know of the peoples of the world; of their geographical environments, their manner of living, their products, and the way in which the lives and work of distant peoples

vi 

PREFACE 

in all corners of the world affect his own. 

Moreover, he will know in what ways climate and physiography have helped to influence the lives of peoples in all parts of the world. 

Because of the decisive influence of relief and climate on the lives and fortunes of mankind, the text has been provided with a map equipment unequaled in any other textbook of its kind. That the pupils may always have before them the chief physical features of any region that is being studied, there is provided a physical map as well as a political map of each continent, and the colored maps of smaller regions are of the physical-political type. They are conveniently placed for reference throughout the text. In addition, an unusually large number of black and white maps have been included, each of which has been so made as to present clearly a chosen fact or group of facts. There are maps of each continent showing the various parts that have individual character, either physiographic or climatic. Besides an average annual rainfall map of the world, there are given two semiannual rainfall maps of each continent instead of the one annual rainfall map included in most textbooks. Among the other maps are those showing the distribution of population, important crops, mineral products, and other matters of importance in the several continents. All of these maps have been kept as simple as they must be to be used intelligently by young students. 

Great care has been taken in the choice of the illustrations, both as to size and as to placement, so that they can be easily studied. 

Each one was chosen because it helps to interpret the text - not merely because it is a beautiful picture. However, taken as a whole, they constitute an unusually attractive as well as a valuable body of illustrative material. 

The teaching material is one of the special features of the book. This material is of far greater value than the formal map and review questions of an earlier day, and the lifeless summaries that frequently tempt children to take a short cut in their study. The interesting exercises here provided furnish abundant review material and emphasize the more important geographic relationships and principles. They have considerable variety in form, and thus avoid the monotony often found in checks and review exercises.

Above all, they lead the learner to arrive at many conclusions for himself.

ALBERT PERRY BRIGHAM CHARLES T. MCFARLANE

SOUTH AMERICA 

We think and speak of the United States as our country," and of the continent of North America, of which it forms so large a part, as "our continent." Most of the people of the United States were born within its borders, but the ancestors of nearly all of them came from beyond the seas. Some few of our people have but lately come from other lands. In this book you are to study the lands and people of the other continents, and you will learn about the countries from which your ancestors came. Let us begin with South America, the nearest neighbor of our own continent.

The continent of South America is joined to North America by the Isthmus of Panama. 

The two continents were discovered and explored in the closing years of the fifteenth century and the early years of the sixteenth century and were then spoken of as the "New World." This name is still much used by the people of the older countries of Europe. 

In learning about the continents and oceans it is best, at first, to make use of a globe. 

This is because the forms of the land and ocean areas are shown accurately on a globe, as are also their true positions in relation to one another. In studying a globe you will find that the continent of South America is not directly south of North America, but southeast of it. You can get an idea of how far east the continent of South America lies, by making use of the meridian of 80° west longitude. Find this meridian on your schoolroom globe. Trace it southward from the North Pole, across the eastern part of Canada and the United States, into the 

Atlantic Ocean, across Cuba, the Caribbean

Sea, and the Isthmus of Panama, and on southward to the South Pole. You see that most of North America is west of this meridian, while nearly all of South America is east of it. Remember, too, that all of North

America is in the Northern Hemisphere and most of South America is in the Southern Hemisphere. On the globe trace the Equator from east to west across the continent of 

South America. 

In 

North and South America Compared. some ways the continents of North and South 

America are much alike. You would not call them "twin continents," perhaps, but they are enough alike so you may think of them as "sister continents." Each is shaped somewhat like a triangle (V). In each, the shortest side of the triangle is on the north, the longest side is on the west, and the sharpest angle is toward the south. 1

SOUTH AMERICA 

The most extensive highlands in both continents are near the Pacific Ocean. Their mountain systems are among the greatest on earth; they are high and long and broad, and inclose high plateaus. There are also mountain and plateau areas in the eastern part of each continent, as well as lowlands along their eastern coasts, and interior lowlands between their two chief regions of highland.

There are similarities in the drainage of the two continents, also. In each there are great rivers that flow from the interior of the continent into the oceans, or seas, to the north, the east, and the southeast. 

In many other ways the two continents are very different from each other. Along the coast of South America there are no great indentations such as are found in the northern continent in Hudson Bay and the Gulf of Mexico. The broad part of South America is in the tropics, where the lowlands are always hot and where, over large areas, there are heavy rains and dense forests. But the broad part of North America is in the Temperate and Frigid zones. 

Map Study. 1. You have learned that the parts of a physical map which are colored green represent lowlands. Observe how large a part of 

South America is made up of lowlands. Notice that these lowlands are drained by three great river systems, all flowing into the Atlantic 

Ocean. Name the three great rivers. Which one of them has a delta, like the Mississippi 

River in our own country? 

2. The parts of the land shown in a brown or a lighter color represent highland regions. Find the very high mountain system along the entire 

Pacific coast. What is its name? Point out the lower highland region in eastern South 

America. What is its name? Find a smaller highland region in the interior of northern South 

America. What is its name? 

3. Find the Equator and the Tropic of Capricorn. The locations of these lines tell you that the greater portion of South America is in the Torrid Zone. By turning to the map of North 

America (page 375) you can see that nearly all of Canada and all of the main part of our own country are in the North Temperate Zone. Only two of the larger countries in South America lie mainly in the South Temperate Zone - Argentina and Chile. Point them out on the map (facing page 1). 

4. Notice that with the exception of a narrow southern extension all of Brazil, the largest country in South America, is in the Torrid Zone. 

However, the elevation of the Brazilian Highlands does much to make more temperate the climate of a large section of Brazil. Why is this so? 

5. Two great seaports on the Atlantic coast are Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires. Point out their location on the map. An important seaport on the Pacific coast is Valparaiso. Point out its location.

Making a Sketch Map of South America. 

Look at the map of South America until you have the shape of its outline so well in mind that you can draw it from memory. It will not be so hard to do this as it was to make your sketch map of North America, because the coast line of South America is much more regular. There are no deep indentations like the Gulf of Mexico or 

Hudson Bay, with resulting peninsulas like 

Labrador or Florida. Do not try to draw your first outline from memory. Keep looking at the map. Use a pencil so that you can erase the lines easily if your map does not look right. 

Do not try at first to show all the little ins and outs. Make smooth lines. Remember that your aim is to represent correctly the general shape of the continent to get right proportions in length and breadth of the different parts. 

Start at the most eastern point near Cape St. Roque and follow the coast line toward the southwest until you reach the southern tip at

Cape Horn. Then go on up the western coast to the Isthmus of Panama. Be careful to show the bulge toward the west as you pass the middle of this western coast line. Then go on across the northern and northeastern coasts until you reach the point where you started.

Now go back over your map and locate the mouths of the three great river systems of South America the Orinoco, the Amazon, and the Plata. 

Plata. Later on you can draw in the main rivers, the boundaries of the different countries, and mark the location of the important cities.

BRAZIL 

Turn to the map facing page 1 and find 

Brazil. You will see that it is the largest country in South America. It includes nearly half of the continent within its boundaries, and is somewhat larger than our own country.

Although the southern point of Brazil is in nearly 34° south latitude, most of the country lies within the Torrid Zone, since it is broadest in the north. Brazil includes the part of the continent that juts eastward into the Atlantic Ocean, a fact that had much to do with its discovery and early history. 

It was Vasco da Gama, a Portuguese navigator, who first sailed from Europe around the southern end of Africa to India. That was in 1498. After his return to Portugal, another expedition was sent out to India, under command of Pedro Alvarez de Cabral.

Warned by da Gama of calms near the west coast of Africa, Cabral sailed so far west to escape them that he saw the coast of the land we now call Brazil. This land was promptly claimed for Portugal and was later settled by the Portuguese. It was for a long time under their control but later became an independent country. You are now to learn how it has added to the world's resources and wealth. 

A Trip to Brazil. - Brazil has a seacoast more than 3600 miles in length. Every one of the South American countries except 

Ecuador and Chile borders Brazil. Count the bordering countries on the map facing page 1. How many are there? 

Would you like to take a trip to Brazil, sailing from New York? As most of Brazil is in the Torrid Zone, you would probably want to be there during the cooler months of its year. Remember that countries south of the Equator are having their summer when we are having our winter, and their winter when we are having our summer. Therefore you would sail from New York in the summer. 

Suppose you go first to Rio de Janeiro, which is the largest city of Brazil. It is also the capital of the country, although Brazil has set aside a large tract of land in the interior, where a new capital sometime may be built. 

Your steamer will head toward the southeast, for it must keep to the east of the easternmost point of South America. Each day the ship's "run" for the preceding twenty-four hours will be marked on a map which every one can see. A few days out from New York, your ship crosses the Tropic of Cancer and enters the Torrid Zone. The weather becomes very hot, but beyond the Equator it begins to get cooler again.

SOUTH AMERICA 

E. M. Newman,  

A. 

Southern parts of Rio de Janeiro as seen from the top of the Sugar Loaf, looking west. At the right you see a small part of the great harbor. At the left are seen two beaches on the coast of the ocean. 

About 600 miles south of the Equator, your ship rounds the easterly part of South America. Its course is changed to the southwest, following the general direction of the coast of the continent. It is nearly twelve days after leaving New York when your ship at last turns toward the coast of the continent and sails into the harbor of Rio de 

Janeiro or "Rio," as it is often called. 

The Great Harbor. The harbor of Rio de Janeiro is not only the best on the coast of South America; it is one of the best in the world. Its position on the Atlantic is almost midway between the northern and southern points of the continent. To reach it you have traveled about 5500 miles. From 

London or Liverpool in England the distance is only a very little longer.

Even by that route the distance between 

San Francisco and Rio is nearly 9000 miles.

Before the construction of the canal what route would a ship have taken between these two ports? 

As your ship nears the shore at Rio, you will notice, beyond a very narrow coastal plain, what appear to be high mountains close around the city and rising to a jagged and irregular crest line behind it. The harbor entrance, about a mile wide, opens into a great bay. The entrance is deep enough for the largest ships in the world. On the west of the entrance, a mass of granite shaped like a blunt cone, and called the Sugar Loaf, reaches a height of over 1200 feet. The bay has a width of eleven miles and extends northward between inclosing highlands for more than sixteen miles. It is deep enough so the 

Ships from the west coast of the United

States use the Panama Canal route to Rio. | largest ships can move freely about in it.

- Rio de Janeiro and vicinity. Can you find the parts of the city that are seen in 6 A?

It is large enough so that all the naval vessels of the world could anchor within it at one time (A). On its southwestern shore is Rio de Janeiro.

The City. Rio de Janeiro was first built on a low alluvial plain. Sea walls and harbor works since constructed have changed the old irregular coast line into straight lines and graceful curves. Shallow bodies of water inclosed by the sea walls have been filled in. Beautiful boulevards have been built along the water front. They are shaded by magnificent trees, and made lovely with beds of gorgeous flowers. The harbor has many docks, piers, and wharves. 

There are warehouses, grain elevators, and all the modern equipment for loading and unloading ships.

Rio has a population of about 

1,500,000 people and is larger than any other city of South America except Buenos Aires. It is more than one fifth as large as New York, nearly 'half as large as Chicago, smaller than 

Philadelphia or Detroit, but two and a half times as large as Buffalo. 

Prosperous and Progressive. That Rio is both prosperous and progressive is indicated in part by its very size. It is shown also by the beauty of its streets and of its buildings, both public and private; by the extent of its foreign and domestic commerce; and by the amount and variety of its manufactures.

There is a canal two miles in length running through the heart of the city. On each side of it there is a street bordered by double rows of royal palms. There are numerous other broad streets and avenues also, bordered by trees of one kind or another (B). When the weather is fair, many people may be seen sitting at little tables along the edge of the sidewalks in front of the more popular cafés.

There they enjoy drinking coffee and watching those who pass by.

Through the wholesale traders of Rio, both foreign and domestic goods are distributed to smaller places along the Brazilian coast and to inland settlements. Inland towns are reached by railroad lines that lead up the valleys of the mountains to the great plateau beyond.

Seen from the sea or from the harbor of Rio de Janeiro, the imposing heights that border this central part of the Brazilian coast appear to be a great range of mountains. 

But after climbing to the level of the highland beyond it, you discover that it is really the seaward-facing escarpment of a great plateau. 

This highland region bears many names in its various parts, and its area is more than half that of all Brazil. Its surface is rolling and varies in elevation from about 800 to 3000 feet above sea level. It is crossed by a number of mountain ridges having a general northeast-southwest direction.

Even though it lies almost wholly within the tropics, its elevation so reduces its temperature that it is a pleasant land in which white people can live and work in comfort.

The Rainfall Maps. The maps on this page show the rainfall in South America as it is divided between the warmer and cooler parts of the year. Notice that in most parts of the continent the rainfall in one half year is very different in amount from that in the other half year. In some places it is more. 

In other places it is less. The time in the year when the rain comes, and its amount, make a great difference in the crops that are raised in different parts of the continent, and in the right seasons in which to raise them.

These maps do not show how the rainfall varies in amount from year to year; so you must not expect too much from them. Indeed, in using any map, be sure that you know what it is intended to show.

The falls and rapids of the Brazilian Highlands, if fully used, could develop an enormous amount of electrical power. Up to the present, only a small part of the available energy has been used.

Industrial Regions of the Brazilian High lands. - What are the industries carried on in this great highland area? The mineral wealth of Brazil is found chiefly in the eastern part. Agriculture is most successful in the eastern and southeastern parts, but, with irrigation, it is possible also in the northeast. 

In the south there are large forests, and in the west there are grasslands much like those of the Great Plains of our own country. 

Mineral Resources. Both gold and diamonds are found in Brazil, but the annual production of each is small, much less than it was years ago. There are large deposits of manganese, a metal used in the manufacture of steel. It is exported to the United States and other steel-making countries. There are some deposits of a low-grade bituminous coal, but only a small amount is mined. Four or five times as much coal of a high grade is imported from the United States and Great

Britain. There are enormous deposits of a very high-grade iron ore, but as Brazil has no good coking coal, not much is mined. It is a reserve supply upon which the steel-making centers of the world may sometime call. 

Agriculture. Except for parts of the coastal plain, the agricultural areas in the eastern and southeastern Brazilian Highlands are the most densely settled sections of the country. Even in these sections only a small part of the land has been brought under cultivation. In the grasslands farther west, only a small fraction of the area is used for pasture, and the population is sparse. The most valuable of all the crops raised in 

Brazil is coffee. 

From Rio de Janeiro to Santos and São 

Paulo. To get to the coffee-growing country from Rio, let us take a steamer to the port of Santos. This city is about 230 miles to the west and a little south of Rio. It is built on flat lands bordering a tidal stream that has been deepened and along which docks and wharves have been built for the use of the many steamers that come to this port. though much coffee is exported through Rio, Santos has become the greatest coffee port in the world. It was at one time a very unhealthful city, but doctors and engineers working together have now made it a safe place in which to live.

Coffee-growing regions of America. In which country is the largest of these regions? railroad is a very interesting and unusual one. 

It is a double-track route built in a series of steep inclines, each one of which has a power station. The trains are pulled up or lowered on these inclines by wire cables.

On the plateau about 50 miles northwest of Santos is the city of São Paulo, the chief city of the coffee-growing region. It has a population of about 900,000 and is the railroad center of this part of Brazil. It is only a little more than 300 miles by rail from Rio, and other lines lead out through the great coffee plantations. 

Coffee Plantations. In Brazil coffee grows best on the well-drained, rolling uplands near the Tropic of Capricorn, having an elevation of from 1000 to 3000 feet above sea level (A). The land has a fine, rich, red soil formed in part from decaying volcanic rock. The most successful plantations are the very large ones. So much expensive machinery is needed in growing coffee and Cultivating coffee trees. The trees stand close together in the rows, and are pruned to keep them from growing very high. preparing it for the market that men with small farms and only a little money cannot succeed in the industry.

Some of the larger plantations cover hundreds of square miles and have millions of trees. The coffee trees are planted in long rows along the slopes and across the tops of the rolling hill lands, because the hill slopes and tops have less frost than the valleys. 

On these plantations many laborers are. needed to cultivate the trees (B), to plant new ones, to help in picking the fruit, and to prepare the coffee for export. These laborers and their families live in villages that have been built in pleasant places on the plantations. On each of the very large plantations there may be two or three of these villages. 

During the harvest season other laborers are brought in, as they are in the wheat fields of our own country.

ripe, the fruit of the coffee tree looks like clusters of dark red cherries. Usually each one of these has two seeds, or "beans." To get them out, the fruit is crushed in a machine that tears and loosens the pulp without

From this machine the whole mass goes to another, where the beans are separated from most of the pulp. They are then scrubbed to remove any small particles of pulp that may still cling to them. 

After the beans have been cleaned, they must be dried.

The coffee crop is usually harvested during the dry season-June to September - and at that time the beans can almost always be dried out of doors in the sun. This is done by spreading them on drying platforms (A). 

The drying is carefully watched and the beans are raked from time to time so that they will all dry equally. If heavy dews are expected or rain threatens, they are raked into piles and covered to keep them from getting wet. 

Sometimes, when wet weather prevents outof-door drying on the platforms, drying machines are used. The beans are covered with a tough outer skin and a delicate inner one called the silver skin. Both of these coverings are removed from the dried beans by machines. 

When the coffee is ready to be shipped, it is put up in bags of 132 pounds each. The annual production of Brazil averages more than 13,000,000 of these bags. From most of the plantations the coffee is sent to São Paulo, and from that city to Santos or to Rio de Janeiro for export. The roasting and grinding of the coffee is done in the country where it is to be used, and usually only a short time before it is used.

Corn is grown in many parts of the eastern highland area, but especially in the east and south (32 B). The annual value of this crop is about two fifths that of coffee.

A Question to Discuss. - Coffee is roasted and ground in the countries where it is to be used, and as near the time of its use as possible. 

Why would it not be just as well to have these things done in Brazil before the coffee is shipped? velopment of cotton growing and an increase in the growing of tobacco and sugar cane were partly due to the World War, when ships were not available to import these products. 

The increase in the production of these and other crops is due, also, to the need the coffee growers feel for other crops to raise. In some years more coffee is produced than can be sold profitably, and the plantation owners therefore do not want to depend upon that crop alone. 

Tobacco is grown in the highlands and especially in the region between the coastal mountains and the São Francisco River.

BRAZIL 

15 08 Beans are raised in the central and southern parts of the highlands, and thousands of bushels are exported. Manioc or cassava, from which tapioca is made, is also grown. 

Yet all of these crops taken together use only a small part of the highland area that is available for agriculture. If you could fly over these lands in an airplane, you would see millions of acres where there are no roads, no villages, and few if any inhabitants. It is a fertile but empty land waiting for the settlers that will some day come. 

Live Stock. In the western part of these great eastern highlands of Brazil, there are vast areas of grasslands. In the southern part of the country, also, there are grasslands which are parts of a rolling plateau much like our own Great Plains. Many millions of cattle are being raised on these pasture lands. But so vast are these grassy areas that many times as many millions could be raised there as no doubt they will be, sometime in the future. The Brazilian government is encouraging the cattlemen to improve their stock by importing fine animals from other countries.

Horses, mules, and donkeys are raised for use on the farms and plantations, for there are not many roads on which trucks and pleasure cars can be used with comfort. 

Sheep are raised for their flesh and wool, goats for their hides, and hogs for their meat. 

Modern slaughtering and meat-packing plants have been built in São Paulo and in Rio de Janeiro, and a large export trade in meat and hides has been built up. There are also plants where jerked beef is prepared for sale in the hotter parts of the country where fresh meat would spoil quickly. Jerked beef is lean beef that has been salted and dried.

On the hill slopes there are forests of both evergreens and hardwoods. Some pine is cut for export and some rosewood is sent to the United States. Sawmills have been erected and lumbering is becoming a more and more important industry. 

Maté, or Paraguay tea, a drink much used in South America, is made from the dried and pulverized leaves of a small tree that grows in southern Brazil and in adjoining countries.

A. Cacao trees with full-grown pods. 

The Coastal Plain. - - You have already learned that there is a narrow coastal plain along much of the eastern coast of Brazil. It It is not of uniform width. In some places it disappears altogether, where mountains reach the coast and slope steeply down to the sea. In other places it is wide enough to include some rather large but shallow lakes. 

Parts of it are salt marsh or swamp land. 

Other parts are high enough above sea level and well enough drained to furnish excellent farm land. Among the products of the coastal plain are cotton, sugar, lumber, and cacao "beans," from which chocolate is made. 

Cacao. The cacao tree grows best in a region of high but even temperature, where the rainfall is heavy and well distributed through the year. An average temperature of 75° to 80° and a rainfall of from 50 to 150 inches are required for its most successful growth. The trees grow in shaded places, in a deep, rich, well-drained soil. The cacao pods are the size of a large cucumber and hang from the trunk and larger branches of the tree (A). The ripe pods, when gathered, are opened and the beans and the pulpy mass surrounding them are scooped out. The pulp is allowed to ferment and in so doing becomes hot. The heating improves the quality of the beans, and the pulp turns into a liquid that is allowed to run off, as it has no value. 

The beans are usually dried on brick or cement platforms, and are then bagged and shipped to chocolate-manufacturing countries. The United States uses about two fifths of the world's crop of cacao. Brazil ranks second among the producing nations; it is outranked only by one of the countries of tropical Africa.

Cities of the Highlands and Coastal Plains. 

You have visited three of the largest cities of 

Brazil. These are: (1) the beautiful capital city of Rio de Janeiro; (2) Santos, the coffee port, and (3) São Paulo, the city in the highlands northwest of Santos. 

Of these three cities, Santos is chiefly concerned with coffee and the coffee trade, and has but few and small manufactures. Here coffee is handled, sorted, graded, stored, and shipped. Everywhere you see coffee and smell its delightful aroma, for in addition to the large quantity prepared for shipment some is roasted for local use.

In Rio, there are large textile mills. These make use of cotton from Brazilian fields and wool from Brazilian sheep ranches, as well as of some imported wool and silk. Cattle and sheep from the grazing regions furnish the

A. - Part of São Paulo, Brazil. The tall smokestacks show you where some of the factories are located. raw materials for Rio's slaughtering and meat-packing plants, and for its tanneries and shoe factories. Its sugar refineries use the sugar from cane grown on the northern coastlands and on highland plantations. 

Lumber from the forests is made into furniture and other articles, and its flour mills import much wheat but also use wheat grown in southern Brazil.

São Paulo (A) is a very modern city.. It has fine public and private buildings; broad, well-paved streets; excellent street railways; and large manufacturing industries. Waterfalls not far away generate electricity that is used for lighting, and for the operation of street railways and factories. Indeed, so much electricity is used that São Paulo is often called the "electrical city." São Paulo has large manufacturing industries. These include a number of shoe factories, many tobacco factories, a large cement plant, and paper mills. All of them use raw materials of the country, although much more wood pulp is imported than is taken from home forests.

Turn to the map on page 8. Follow the coast north from Rio, until you find the city of Bahia (called by Brazilians São Salvador).

It is built at the entrance of a large bay, at the foot and on the western slope of a peninsula that rises steeply from the shore. This bay is shaped somewhat like the one on which the city of Rio is located, and it forms a large and beautiful harbor.

The older part of Bahia along the water front has narrow, crooked streets, but modern wharves and docks have been built, and steamers are loaded and unloaded by machinery. Many of the old buildings are roofed with tiles, and bright tiles have been built into their walls. The modern city is on the higher slopes and is reached by elevators and steep, winding roads. The streets are wider, and the houses and other buildings are larger and much like those in our cities. 

Bahia is the port of large tobacco and cacao regions. There are many factories in which cigars and cigarettes are made for local use and for export. Other exports of Bahia are cacao, hides, tobacco, coffee, and sugar.

SOUTH AMERICA 

Turn again to the map on page 8. On the coast of Brazil, north of Bahia, find the city of Pernambuco (Brazilian name, Recife).

It is built on low land around a lagoon formed by two small rivers, and on an island between the rivers. Its several parts are connected by a number of bridges. As it is so near the 

Equator, its average temperature is high and the rainfall is heavy. These conditions and the nearness of swamp lands on the south made it, for a long time, a very unhealthful place in which to live. Efforts to improve conditions have been successful, and sickness is much less common than in former years. 

In spite of its disadvantages, Pernambuco is one of the important ports of Brazil. It is much nearer to the ports of the United States and Europe than are the other seacoast cities you have been studying. It is the outlet of a sugar-raising and cotton-raising region, and its exports include sugar, cotton, hides and skins, and lumber.

The Amazon Basin. Much of northern 

Brazil is drained by the Amazon River system. This river rises in a small lake on the eastern slope of the Andes Mountains, and flows eastward to the Atlantic Ocean. Measured along its winding course, it is about 

3500 miles long. Only the Mississippi 

Missouri River is longer, and no river in the world has a greater volume of water. 

The size of the Amazon drainage basin is enormous. It is three fourths as large as the 

United States and includes more than half of Brazil and parts of several other countries. 

What countries are these (map facing page 1)?

Although the headwaters of the Amazon and of its tributaries reach back into the highlands, much of the Amazon basin is less than 1000 feet above sea level, and large areas are only a few feet above the normal level of the river. The seaward slope of the land bordering the Amazon is so gentle that for the last 2000 miles of its course there are times when the river drops only an inch in each five miles. Yet its volume is so great that its muddy waters can be traced in the ocean more than a hundred miles from its mouth. 

It is the lowlands of this Amazon basin, and their resources, industries, and people, that you are now to study. The map on page 8 will help you to fix in mind the location of the places about which you read.

19 The steamer on which you travel will use this channel because of its greater safety. 

All the other outlets of the Amazon are more or less blocked by sand bars and swift currents, and by floating trees and island-like masses of shrubs, grasses, and earth. 

About 80 miles up the Rio Pará from the ocean, you reach the well-built and attractive city of Pará (or Belém) on the east bank of the river. Pará reached its greatest size and importance some years ago when the Amazon basin was producing most of the world's rubber. At that time it was the chief outlet for all the products that came down the river, and the place from which supplies were distributed. In recent years the production of rubber in Brazil has decreased, and as a result the commerce of Pará also has decreased. More than 90 per cent of the world's rubber supply now comes from rubber plantations in Asiatic countries. 

Even if you make only a short stay in Pará, you will find it both hot and rainy. It is built on low land only a short distance south of the Equator, and its average yearly rainfall is about 100 inches. In hot countries people usually rest during the middle of the day, when it is hottest, and in Pará it is in the early afternoon that the heaviest rainfall also may be expected. You should therefore do your shopping, make your calls, and visit theaters, parks, and museums in the late afternoon and evening when it is cooler and the rain for the day is over. 

The steamer on which you made your journey to Pará could, with perfect safety, go many hundreds of miles up the Amazon. 

But it will probably be best to change to one of the smaller river steamers for the trip. 

A short time after leaving Pará, you will pass the mouth of a large river coming in from the south. It is the Tocantins. Find it on the map. 

At last your steamer enters the main stream of the Amazon. Like many other large rivers, the Amazon varies considerably in A.

Boat on the Amazon River. Notice the thick forest.

In width from point to point in its course. some parts it is only a mile wide and you can see the dense forests, called silvas, on each of its banks. Near the ocean where it begins to spread out, it has a width of as much as 50 or 60 miles and from the center of the stream no land can be seen.

During the rainy seasons when flood waters pour into the Amazon from its headwaters and its many tributaries, it may rise in places as much as fifty feet or more. Both the main stream and the tributaries within the rainy belt overflow their banks and spread out over the bordering lowlands. The Amazon becomes a great lake whose width is sometimes as much as 200 miles. During these flood periods, the people who live on the lower lands along the river are forced to move to higher lands or to live in boats until the flood goes down. The forest trees and the interlacing vines that bind them together rise out of the water as a wall of living green (A).

The Amazon Forests. In hot, rainy regions such as that of the Amazon, the forest areas, called rain forests, are very dense. 

They are entirely unlike those in our own country or other temperate regions where many trees of one kind are found growing close together over large areas. In the rain forests there are as many as forty or fifty kinds of trees and those of the same kind are widely scattered. Cutting trees for lumber is therefore less easy and more expensive than in the forests of temperate lands. 

To add to the lumberman's difficulties, all forms of vegetation grow with the greatest luxuriance. There are no open spaces carpeted with dead leaves, where patches of sunlight fall in ever-changing patterns, such as we find in our own forests. In the great tropical forest of the Amazon, almost every inch of soil is occupied by some plant. It is a real jungle. The trees stand close together. 

Great vines, rooted in the soil, wind their way upward around the trunks of the trees, slowly choking them to death. They swing from branch to branch and from tree to tree. 

Shrubs and other growths block the spaces between the tree trunks. Those who must The largest of the forest trees are tall, but they are by no means so gigantic as the big trees of California. Most of the trees of the rain forest are of moderate size. Included among them are such hardwoods as mahogany, rosewood, ebony, and Spanish cedar, and others whose wood will take as fine a polish as any of these.

Among the trees of this vast forest, a forest that is said to be the largest in the world, are many whose wood, or bark, or sap, or fruit, or seeds yield products valuable to mankind.

Products of the Amazon Forest. - The name Brazil was given to the country because a red dyewood known by that name was found in the forest. Brazil-nut trees also are found there in great numbers. You have probably eaten the delicious white meat of Brazil nuts. They are three-sided, and fifteen or twenty of them are found closely packed in the round, hard shells that grow on the trees. They are gathered in great quantities by Indians who live in the forest, and are sold to traders to be shipped to other countries.

Cacao trees (page 16) are found growing wild, especially along the lower course of the Amazon. There are other trees from which a vegetable wax is obtained. There are plants that yield long, strong fibers. Some of these fibers are as fine as silk. Today they are used by the natives in making hammocks and some other articles, but sometime they may come into the markets of the world.

A. Tap and cup on a rubber tree. Some of the Brazilian rubber trees grow very large. 

Of all the trees of the Amazon forest, the ones that have so far been of greatest value are those from which rubber is obtained, of which there are several varieties. They are found in flooded lowlands, and because those along the rivers are most easily reached it is from such regions that most of the Brazilian rubber comes. 

How Rubber Is Obtained. Much of the land where rubber trees grow is owned by large companies. Native Indian rubbergatherers are hired to collect rubber and prepare it for market. As soon as the season of floods is over, the rubber-gatherers go into the forest. Each one is told where to camp, and he puts up a simple shelter with open sides and a roof of palm leaves, where he and his family live during the rubber-gathering season.

As the rubber trees are some distance from each other, each man locates about a hundred B. 

United States Rubber Co. 

Rubber-gatherer on his rounds. Here he is crossing a small stream on a very simple foot bridge. trees and cuts a path from tree to tree. This path is so arranged that it starts and ends near his camp. Next the trees are tapped, by making a gash or gashes in the bark. There is a milky-white fluid, called latex, circulating through the inner bark, and it is from this that crude rubber is made. Under each cut a cup is fastened to catch the latex (A). The latex, however, does not flow for long, and a new cut is usually made each day. This is generally done by taking a thin shaving from the surface of the cut that was made the day before.

Early each morning the rubber-gatherer starts on a round of his trees, tapping them and fastening on the cups. When he returns to camp he gets his breakfast, for he eats when he can and has no fixed hours for his meals. He rests awhile and then goes around with a pail to gather the latex from the cups on the trees (B).

SOUTH AMERICA 

United States Rubber Co. 

A. Making rubber by smoking the latex. Compare the size of the ham just started with those in the next picture. 

When he gets back he builds a fire, using oily nuts that make a great deal of smoke. 

He pours a little of the latex on a stick, or paddle, and turns it around and around in the smoke (A). Soon the latex hardens and takes on a brownish color. More and more latex is added and smoked until it has all been hardened in this way. That gathered on following days is treated the same way until a large ball of this crude rubber has been formed. Such balls are called hams.

At the end of the season boats are sent from camp to camp, to gather the rubber hams to be shipped down the river. Not all rubbergatherers work for large companies. Some work for themselves alone, but the methods are about the same.

Rio Negro (Spanish for "Black River") on account of its dark-colored water. Find it on your map. Not far up this river, on some high land that borders it, is the city of 

Manáos. Your steamer will take you to this river port, and there your journey ends. You could sail on up the Amazon many miles into Peru, to the west of Brazil; for the river has neither falls nor rapids to interrupt steamer traffic for 2700 miles from its mouth.

The city of Manáos is not so large as Pará. 

It is a city of the forest and a center of the rubber trade (B). It was the profits on rubber that built its fine buildings and laid out its wide streets and beautiful parks. At present the rubber industry is not prosperous, and Manáos is not the important city that it was some years ago. But it may sometime become a shipping center for other forest products. 

Animal Life in the Forest. Before leav ing these forests of the Amazon, let us learn a little about the animal life. In the great river itself and in its tributaries there are large alligators and hundreds of varieties of fish. In the jungle there are pumas and

BRAZIL 

23 A. Jaguar or American leopard. This animal is larger and heavier than the leopard of Asia and Africa. jaguars, fierce cat-like animals of great strength. There are monkeys, large and small, that chatter at each other as they swing among the branches. There are snakes, the largest of which is the boa constrictor that wraps itself about its prey and crushes it. 

There is the sloth that hangs back downward from the branches, and there is the foul vampire bat. As a touch of beauty, there are rare birds of brilliant and beautifully colored plumage.

The Savannas. - Read again on pages 1920 about the northward and southward movement of the belt of equatorial calms or doldrums. On the northern and southern margins of the region over which the doldrums move, the rainy seasons are short and the dry seasons are long. During the rainy season grass grows quickly on extensive plains called savannas. In the dry season, the grass withers and dies. When the grass is fresh and green the savannas make wonderful pastures. But the dry seasons are so long, the heat is so great, insects are so annoying to cattle, and there are so many cattle diseases, that the savannas, called campos in Brazil, are not yet much used for cattle ranges. Grasslands in other parts of Brazil and in other South American countries are much more favorably located for cattle and sheep raising. 

Comparing the Mississippi and the Amazon. Although the Amazon is not so long as the Mississippi-Missouri, it is much longer than the Mississippi alone. Because of the greater rainfall in its basin the Amazon has a far larger volume of water; and it is, on the average, much wider and deeper than the great river of our continent. So vast is the volume of water carried by the Amazon that the Brazilians call it Rio Mar- meaning 

River Sea.

It is only by dredging that a depth of 9 feet is maintained in the Mississippi River as far north as Cairo. Expensive work was necessary also in order to get that same depth on the Ohio River to Pittsburgh. As a result of dredging and other costly work, ocean steamers can reach New Orleans, about 110 miles from the Gulf of Mexico. The Amazon averages more than 100 feet in depth for a distance greater than the total length of the Mississippi. Ocean steamers can reach 

Iquitos, 2300 miles from its mouth. Smaller steamers can go still farther up the main stream and from 500 to 1000 miles on all the larger tributaries.

There are times when lands bordering the 

Mississippi are flooded. To prevent such floods, levees have been built along the river at a cost of many millions of dollars. Without the levees there would be annual floods, much of the valuable farm land could not be used, and the Mississippi basin, which now has a population of nearly 50,000,000, would be far less densely peopled. The Amazon and many of its tributaries have annual floods when their waters spread out over vast areas. No attempt is made to control them. 

The whole basin, nearly twice the size of the Mississippi basin, has a population of less than 3,000,000, and no industries of sufficient value to make a control of floods necessary. 

On maps, pages 2 and 4, find the Guiana Highlands, and see which part of that area is drained to the Amazon. These highlands have an east-west direction, and when the

doldrums are farther south the northeast trade winds blow across them. The northern and eastern part of the highlands have heavy rains, but the southern slopes and the lower lands just to the south have much less.

The People of Brazil. There are about 

43,000,000 people living in Brazil. That is a small number for so large a country. How does it compare with the number living in our own country? If the population of Brazil were spread out evenly over the whole country, there would be only twelve people in each square mile. The map on this page shows how the people really are distributed. Notice the large part of Brazil where the average number of people is less than two for each square mile. Notice also the denser population in the southeastern part of the country, and in the coastal regions near great cities.

When the settlement of Brazil was first undertaken by Europeans, they found Indians occupying parts of the country. Most of the early white settlers were from Portugal, but some were from Spain. Later, Negro slaves were imported from Africa.

Some good roads have been built in and near the larger cities, and the use of trucks and automobiles is increasing.

Many Brazilians of today trace their | But in large parts of the country horses and descent from the early Portuguese and 

Spanish settlers. About 2,000,000 immigrants, including Germans, Italians, and Japanese, have settled in the most promising agricultural regions of Brazil in recent years.

Many Brazilians, called mestizos, are descended from marriages between Portuguese or Spanish and the Indians. They are proud of their ancestry and are a very important element of the population. Other Brazilians, of all shades of color from almost black to light yellow, are descended from marriages of Negroes to Indians or to white persons.

Government, wealth, and the control of industry are largely in the hands of the whites and the mestizos. The Indians are, for the greater part, poor and ignorant. Most of them and their number is unknown live in the unexplored regions of interior

Brazil. Many of them are savages who have never seen a white man. a white man. Even in recent years, some explorers who have visited interior Brazil have never been heard of again. 

Most of the Negroes live in the coastal lowlands around Bahia and Pernambuco (A) and to the north and south of these cities. 

Transportation. The railroads of Brazil (maps, pages 8 and 28) are few and short. 

Most of them lead inland from coast cities.

In the whole vast basin of the Amazon there is but one short road. This was built, at great cost, around the falls of the Madeira oxen furnish the best means of transportation. Both in railroads and in highways our own country is far better equipped than Brazil, making it much easier to transport people or freight from place to place. 

Brazil, however, has 40,000 miles of waterways, more than any other country in the world. Thousands of miles of these waterways are wide and deep enough for ocean steamers. Many more thousands of miles are safe for river steamers of moderate size.

Trade between the United States and 

Brazil. For many years Brazil traded chiefly with the countries of Europe. Today much of its trade is with the United States. This change was natural. Its The people of the United States now use more coffee, rubber, cacao, and hides and skins than are used by the people of any other country. Brazil ranks first in the production of coffee and second in cacao. animal industries furnish an enormous number of hides and skins, and although its rubber production has greatly decreased, fine 

Pará rubber is still the world's best.

In exchange for what we get from Brazil, we send foodstuffs, textiles, coal, gasoline, machinery and tools, automobiles and trucks, and building steel.

SOUTH AMERICA 

Brazil is largely in the Torrid Zone. Our country is in the Temperate Zone. Naturally the two countries will always have products to exchange, and trade between them should increase. Brazil has enormous empty spaces suitable for agriculture and grazing. It has great wealth of iron ore, but little coal. The value of its forests cannot be told, because there is now no way by which those in the Amazon Valley can be cut at a profit. Yet with an increasing population, the empty lands will be occupied. 

Some day the iron ore will be needed. Some Some of it may be sent to steel-manufacturing countries, and coal brought back as a return cargo. The same sort of exchange is made between the Lake Superior iron region and the Pennsylvania coal regions. The world's need of timber may sometime become so great that a way will be found to use even the forest trees of the Amazon basin. When these changes come, let us hope that both our own country and Brazil will be benefited by them.

Go now from Brazil to the more southern part of South America, east of the Andes

Mountains (map, page 28). There you will find three countries - Paraguay, Uruguay, and Argentina. 

Which of the three is the largest? Argentina is about a third as large as Brazil and more than four times as large as Texas (Tables 1 and 6, pages 376, 377). The size of Paraguay may not be given accurately, as that country and Bolivia disagree as to the boundary between them. If the disputed territory is divided equally between them, Paraguay will have an area one tenth that of Argentina, or two and one half times that of New York. Uruguay is about one and a half times as large as New York. It is the smallest of the South American republics. 

This group of countries lies between 21° and 55° south latitude, and mostly in the South Temperate Zone - except that a small part of Argentina and a large part of Paraguay are north of the Tropic of Capricorn in the Torrid Zone.

Five Natural Regions. -This group of countries may be divided into five natural regions whose boundaries are based largely upon differences in climate (map, page 4).

The Pampas. The Pampas region is a nearly level, almost treeless area about one fourth the size of Argentina. Its eastern part is a region of fine and fertile soils. Farther west and nearer the mountains, the soil is somewhat coarser. You remember that our Great Plains increase gradually in elevation toward the Rocky Mountains. In the same way the Pampas rise gradually toward the Andes.

The average annual rainfall is nearly 40 inches along the Atlantic Ocean, but this decreases to less than 16 inches along the inland margin of the Pampas about 400 miles farther west (maps, page 10). There are few streams and none of them are large. The rain that falls sinks rapidly into the earth except when there is an especially heavy downpour. Then a thin sheet of water, like a very shallow lake, may spread over the surface, but it disappears in a short time. 

The whole of the Pampas region is used for grazing, dairying, or agriculture, and it raises a great surplus of food to be sent to other countries. Grazing is the oldest of these industries and the most profitable.

Animal Industries of the Pampas. - The early Spanish settlers brought their farm animals with them to this new country. The lands upon which they settled were unfenced, and some of their cattle, horses, and sheep wandered away on the Pampas. As snow seldom falls there, and the temperature never drops to zero, these wanderers were able to live without shelter. The native grasses furnished plenty of food, and within a few years there were great numbers of wild horses, cattle, and sheep roaming the plains. 

They were hunted like other wild animals. 

Horses caught alive were tamed for use or for sale. Wild cattle were killed for their hides, and sheep for their skins and wool. 

Later, a jerked beef industry and the manufacture of beef extracts developed. 

The breeding of fine horses and the better kinds of sheep (A) and cattle (30 A) began in the latter part of the nineteenth century. 

It was then that the owners of the great ranges or estancias began to fence their pastures. High-grade animals, for which very high prices were paid, were imported from 

Europe and the United States.

A. Cattle-raising regions of South America. 

At the same time the cattlemen began to plant alfalfa on former pasture lands to take the place of the native grasses. Alfalfa grows rapidly and makes an excellent pasture. From fields that are not pastured, it can be cut for hay several times during the growing season, or it can be put in a silo to be fed as green fodder. Alfalfa is used in 

Argentina to fatten cattle for market, as corn is used in the United States.

Beef cattle and sheep that are fat enough to be slaughtered are sold to great meatpacking plants, most of which are owned by the meat packers of the United States. Find the cities of Buenos Aires, La Plata, Rosario, and Santa Fé in Argentina; and Montevideo and Paysandú in Uruguay. There are packing plants in all of these places. Most of the beef is chilled and then sent in refrigerator ships to eastern United States and to countries in Europe. Some beef and nearly all the mutton are frozen and sent abroad in ships that keep the meat frozen during the voyage. At the end of the trip it is stored where it can be kept frozen until it is sold.

A. Cows and calves on an estancia in Argentina. 

The flavor of frozen beef is not so good as that of chilled beef, but freezing does not seem to injure the flavor of mutton. Transportation by water is so much cheaper than transportation by rail, that meat from Argentina or Uruguay can be sold in eastern United States for less than meat from the packing plants of central United States. 

Dairying is increasing in both Argentina and Uruguay, especially in those parts of the country reached by railroads; and both butter and cheese are exported. Other animal products that are sold include (1) much fine wool for clothing, (2) hides and skins to be made into leather, (3) fats for making tallow, soap, and candles, and (4) bones that are used for a variety of purposes.

Very few of the great land owners live on their estancias, which are left in charge of trusted managers. Under the managers, gauchos, or native cowboys, care for the cattle.

Crops are raised and alfalfa planted chiefly by tenant farmers, many of whom are Italians.

Italians. Contracts are made with these tenant farmers for a period of years. The farmer agrees to plow the pasture and to cultivate the soil to get rid of the native grasses. 

He also agrees to leave the land planted to alfalfa at the end of the contract period. 

He must then move to another location on the estancia - perhaps many miles away or to another estancia.

Most of the wealthy land owners are unwilling to divide their great estates into smaller fields for careful cultivation, being content with the income from the sale of the animals that are raised. They are equally unwilling to sell their land. Tenant farmers and immigrants find it almost impossible to buy farms. 

As tenants they will not build roads, or put up schoolhouses for their children, or good homes for themselves. They know that in a few years they must move to a new location

and leave behind whatever they have built. 

All this makes them discontented and unhappy. In In the United States things are very different. Farms average about 150 acres in size. 

Most of the farmers own their farms, live on them, and do much or all of the work, hiring additional help only as it is needed. many cases farms that are for sale are purchased by tenant farmers or immigrants.

In most of the northern regions there are churches, schools, stores, and railroads in near-by villages which can usually be reached over good roads.

How the Land of Argentina Can Be Used. - 

A study of the best use for the land of Argentina has been made. It shows that nearly one third can be used for crops, and a slightly larger amount for grazing. Nearly one fourth is covered with forest or can be used for orchards. Less than one tenth is waste. 

Of the land on which crops can be raised, only one fourth is now being cultivated.

Most of the cultivated farms are large, and the best of modern agricultural machinery, imported from the United States, is in use. 

The chief crops are alfalfa (page 29); cereals, especially wheat and corn; and flax.

The Corn Lands. When you were studying the corn belt of central United States, you learned that corn needs more moisture than wheat. Notice that the area of greatest corn production in Argentina (B) is east of the wheat belt (page 31), in a region of heavier rainfall (maps, page 10), as it is in our own country.

In the United States, a large part of the corn raised is used to fatten hogs and cattle. 

In Argentina, the raising of hogs has not yet developed into a great industry, and most of the cattle are fattened on alfalfa (page 29). 

As a result, most of the corn raised in Argentina is exported. 

Flaxseed. You probably know that flax is raised in Europe for its fiber, from which linen is made; and that much flax is raised in certain of our North Central States for its seed. This is becoming a great industry in 

Argentina also. Most of the crop is exported, a large part of it coming to the United States. 

The flaxseed is used in making linseed oil. 

Gran Chaco. North of the Pampas is the 

Gran Chaco, a region of forests and savannas or grasslands (map, page 4). It is in tropical and semitropical South America, and includes parts of Argentina and Paraguay. It also extends northward through Bolivia into western Brazil (map facing page 1). Compare the two maps carefully.

The savannas furnish pasture for large herds of native cattle. Their meat is not as good as that of the fine beef animals of the Pampas, but some of it is used as jerked beef and in the manufacture of beef extracts. 

The hides, however, are of good quality. 

They are dried and then sent to the coast for export to our own and other countries. 

In the forested region of the Gran Chaco, the most valuable trees are the quebracho, the Paraná pine, and the small maté tree. 

Quebracho. Quebracho is an extremely hard and very heavy wood. The name means "ax-breaker." The heart wood of this tree is rich in tannic acid used in tanning hides to make leather. Great quantities of this tannic acid are needed in all leathermaking countries. The leather industries of our own country depend largely on South America for hides and skins, and on Argentina for supplies of tannic acid. Our hemlock and oak forests no longer furnish enough bark to supply the tannic acid that we need. 

To extract the tannic acid from the wood of the quebracho tree, the logs are chipped into small pieces and boiled in water. The jelly-like extract that is obtained is packed in bags and hardened into cakes weighing about a hundred pounds each. The two countries taking the most of this extract are the United States and Germany. The wood of this tree is used also for railroad ties and fence posts because it does not decay quickly. 

Other Forests in the Plata Basin.- Much of the region that you are now studying is drained by the Paraguay, Paraná, and 

Uruguay river systems. Find them on the map, page 28. Their waters finally reach the broad bay that is named Plata River. 

Between the Paraguay and Paraná rivers there are other hardwood forests, but very little timber is being cut on account of the difficulty and expense of getting it to market.

In the region drained by the Paraná River there are large pine forests, and lumbering is increasing. The wood of the Paraná pine is easily worked and is excellent for many building uses. Some of it is exported. 

The maté groves are found in this and in adjoining regions. Read again about maté on page 15.

Cotton. In some parts of the Gran 

Chaco, cotton is now grown (14 A). The soil is fertile, there is enough rain and it comes at the right time, and there is a dry harvesting season. The industry is prosperous even though it is difficult and expensive to get the cotton to market. cotton to market. The yield is large, labor is cheap, and the boll weevil is not known. 

Much of the cotton grown is used in Argentina mills, but some is exported. 

The Sheep Lands of Patagonia. — The plateau and plains region of Patagonia is south of the Pampas and east of the Andes Mountains (map, page 4). In this part of 

South America the prevailing winds are from the northwest (page 9). They blow from the Pacific Ocean, bringing moisture that falls as rain or snow to the west of the Andes or on their western slopes. After these winds have crossed the mountains they have very little moisture left, and much of Patagonia has less than 10 inches of rainfall annually (maps, page 10). Some snow is blown through mountain valleys to melt on the eastern slopes and furnish moisture for a few short mountain streams. There is enough moisture, especially toward the south and in the southern islands, to permit a scanty growth of grass. Several million sheep are raised, some for their wool, others for mutton. 

This region is as dry as the sheep-raising regions in Australia and in North America.

As in all regions where only sheep can be raised, there are very few people for so large an area. Among the shepherds are Scotch, Welsh, and English. Some of them came to the mainland of South America from the 

Falkland Islands in the Atlantic Ocean, east of the southern part of South America.

These islands belong to Great Britain, and have long been used for raising sheep.

A Great and Beautiful City. On the miles from the open Atlantic, is the city of Buenos Aires. It is the capital of Argentina, the largest city in South America, the largest city south of the Equator, and the largest city in the world whose people speak the Spanish language. On the maps of three continents, notice that this city is in about the same latitude as Cape Town in 

South Africa and Sydney in Australia. 

Nearly four fifths of the trade of Argentina. with the rest of the world is carried on through the port of Buenos Aires and its outer port, La Plata. At almost any time of the year, ships from many parts of the world may be seen loading or unloading at the wharves or piers there.

A. The Christ of the Andes. This statue stands on the boundary between Argentina and Chile. 

All of the leading railroads of Argentina. center in Buenos Aires. Most of them are owned and operated by English companies. 

Two lines cross the Andes Mountains. One of these is the Transandine Railroad from Buenos Aires to Valparaiso in Chile. It is about 900 miles in length. In the high mountains it has been necessary to build many miles of snow sheds over the track, so that trains can run during the winter. 

At a high point in the Andes, just above the tunnel through which the railway passes, stands a famous monument. It is a statue of the Christ (A), put up as a pledge of peace between the two countries. 

Another railroad from Buenos Aires to the 

Pacific passes through Rosario and Tucumán to La Paz in Bolivia. From La Paz there are three lines to ports on the Pacific Ocean. 

Most of the other railroad lines of Argentina are much shorter and serve the wheat, corn, flax, and cattle regions, and the dairying districts. In the plains of Argentina there are no hills to be cut through or tunneled, and few streams to be bridged. So level is the land that one railroad has 175 miles of track without a curve. Several air lines carrying mail and passengers are in operation from Buenos Aires as a center. 

The chief manufacturing industries of the city are those that have developed naturally out of the resources of the country. They include huge meat-packing plants, flour mills, creameries and cheese factories, tanneries, and shoe factories.

SOUTH AMERICA The People of Argentina. -You learned that the population of Brazil includes many people of the white race but also many Indians, Negroes, and people of mixed blood. 

In Argentina, however, almost all the people are of the white race. Among them are many of Spanish or Italian descent, and some other 

European people.

In most of Argentina the climate is like that in other temperate parts of the world, where we find the greatest civilized countries of the present day. White people can work there in comfort and with energy.

Most of the European immigrants of recent years are industrious and thrifty. Some of them have been able to purchase land or to enter into business and have prospered. The government of Argentina now requires each immigrant to prove that he has good character and good health, and that he is willing to work. It is only people of this kind who are wanted in Argentina, even though many millions more can find homes there before it is as densely populated as our own country. 

Mineral Resources of Argentina. It is probable that Argentina will always be largely a farming and grazing country. However much the country may have in the way of mineral wealth, no great mineral deposits of high value have been discovered either in the Andes or elsewhere. Small quantities of gold, silver, copper, lead, and zinc have been found, and some mining of these metals is going on. Petroleum has been found in the northwestern part of the country and in southern Patagonia, but the chief producing area is near the coast about 900 miles south of Buenos Aires.

Deposits of low-grade coal and some lignite have been located, and iron-ore deposits are reported from several places in the northcentral part of the country. The development of manufacturing on a large scale depends to a large degree upon cheap coal and iron. The fact that in Argentina there means that the machinery and the coal for manufacturing plants must be imported. 

Manufacturing in Argentina is chiefly directed to the preparation of foodstuffs and other raw materials for export. Most manufactured goods for use in Argentina are imported from other countries (page 37).

Iguassú Falls, sometimes called the Victoria Falls, are on the Iguassú River between 

Argentina and Brazil, in the midst of an uninhabited forest. They have a width of two and a half miles and a drop of 210 feet. 

One part is divided into two drops of about 100 feet each (A). The Iguassú Falls have a greater width and a greater volume of water than our own Niagara Falls; and their total drop is 50 feet longer than that of Niagara.

A Land of One Industry. The single great industry of Uruguay is grazing. Great herds of cattle and enormous flocks of sheep are spread out over the rolling grasslands, which are not so nearly level as those of the Pampas in Argentina. These pastures of 

Uruguay are a southern continuation of the hill lands of southeastern Brazil.

The native grasses are so good, and the rainfall is so abundant and well distributed, that much less land has been planted to alfalfa in Uruguay than in Argentina. Agriculture has developed very slowly. The soils are fertile and the climate ideal for raising cereals, flaxseed, and fruits and vegetables, but the people of Uruguay prefer the freedom of life that the grazing industry gives.

SOUTH AMERICA 

Montevideo. Across the Plata River, northeast from Buenos Aires, is the city of Montevideo. It is the capital of Uruguay, and its largest city. Railroads spread out from it into the grazing country and bring the cattle and sheep to its meat-packing plants (A). All of these plants are owned by companies in the United States or England.

Montevideo is on a natural harbor that is much nearer the open Atlantic than is Buenos 

Aires. The ocean commerce of Uruguay passes through the port of Montevideo. The chief exports are animal products, only a small part of which come to our country. 

The imports are chiefly manufactured goods from the United States and Europe. Trade with our country is increasing.

A. The Strait of Magellan, 360 miles long, is fringed by mountains which are usually snow-covered. 

Along the coast the northern part is hot, the central part temperate, and the southern part cold. Within the different sections of the country there are deserts, fertile plains, and great forests. There are coast ranges and fringing islands, interior lowlands, and mountain peaks from whose towering slopes snow never melts. In the north, little or no rain falls. In the south, glaciers formed from snow fields in mountain valleys come down to the sea as they do in 

Alaska and British Columbia. Chile is a land of great contrasts.

From Buenos Aires to Valparaiso. 

trip from Buenos Aires, the great port of

Argentina, to Valparaiso, the chief port of Chile, can be made either by rail or by water. From Buenos Aires, the railroad runs west through corn and wheat fields and vast pasture lands that stretch out endlessly to distant horizons. It passes through Mendoza, surrounded by its irrigated vineyards, and climbs the eastern slopes of the Andes. 

Through tunnels it reaches the western slopes of the Andes, and drops down to the plains of Chile and the sea.

The ocean route may be around the islands at the southern end of the continent past 

Cape Horn, or through the Strait of Magellan.

This strait was named after a Portuguese navigator who was the first to discover this winding channel from the Atlantic to the

Pacific. He was in command of three ships, one of which was the first to sail around the earth, although Magellan himself was killed when his ships stopped at the Philippine 

Islands. Magellan's new route from the 

Atlantic to the Pacific grew more and more important as the New World was settled. 

Parts of the channel, however, are narrow, and shifting winds and changing currents make careful steering very necessary (A).

Coal. Chile is fortunate in having coal deposits of considerable size. They are probably the largest in South America. The chief deposits and the mines now operating are on the coast between Concepción and Valdivia, where the coal veins extend out under the sea. About 1,500,000 tons are mined annually, most of which is sold to 

Chilean railroads. The lack of good coal in most South American countries has retarded the development of manufacturing, even where raw materials are available.

Between the islands and the mainland there is an "inside passage." There are also narrow bays or fiords leading back into the mountains that rise steeply from the sea, as they do in 

British Columbia and the Panhandle of southern Alaska. 

The Central Valley. Spanish explorers sailing southward along the desert coast of western South America found a break in the coastal mountains. At this point they were happy to discover a green valley that led into the interior. They called it "Valley of Paradise." In Spanish this is Valparaiso. 

The name has been kept as that of the chief seaport of Chile, from which railroads and highways extend eastward to the Central

Valley. On the west, between this valley and the Pacific, are the coast ranges. On the east are the snow-covered Andes Mountains towering thousands of feet above the level of the valley and stretching on and on toward the north and the south. Toward the north the snow line rises on the side of the mountain because of increasing warmth. 

Toward the south it sinks nearer and nearer to sea level as the temperature decreases. 

One of the peaks in this part of the Andes is Mt. Aconcagua -the highest in the New 

World. Its top is about 23,000 feet above the level of the sea.

Dense evergreen and hardwood forests water for many mountain streams, some of cover the rain-soaked and mist-shrouded which as they reach the valley form beautiful western slopes of the mountains of southern lakes. A Land of Large Estates. In the early days of settlement in Chile, large grants of land were made to some men, and in this way great estates were created. Many of the largest holdings have been more or less split up through sales or their division among heirs. Even at the present time, however, nine tenths of the land in the Central Valley is held in estates of over 500 acres (A). The number of small farms is increasing, and this leads to a more careful cultivation of the land. In Chile, as in Argentina, many of the owners of the great estates live in the cities and leave the management of their land to others. 

Principal Products. Among the crops grown in the Central Valley, wheat ranks first. It is raised in all parts of the valley (map, page 31), and more than half of the land under cultivation in Chile is devoted to this crop. The demand for wheat bread is so great that less than one tenth of the crop is exported. Smaller amounts of barley, oats, corn, and rye are raised.

Parts of this valley are so well suited to the raising of fruits that it has been called the "California of South America." In the warmer northern part oranges, lemons, figs, and olives are raised. and olives are raised. In the more temperate region berries and such orchard fruits as apples, peaches, pears, plums, and cherries are grown. There are many vineyards (map, page 34) in the valley, especially in the northern irrigated portion. A large winemaking industry has developed, and some of the grapes are made into raisins. 

Nearly every variety of vegetable can be grown, and in regions where the cold season is very short two or three crops may be raised in a single growing season. The building of the Panama Canal greatly shortened the sea voyage between Chile and the cities of eastern and central United States.
