Among the nuts grown in Chile are almonds and walnuts. Large quantities of the walnuts are exported to the United States. 

Cattle, sheep, and hogs are raised in the Central Valley, but there are no great pasture lands such as are found in Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. As a result stock raising is of minor importance and has developed chiefly in connection with mixed farming. 

There are dairy farms near the cities. 

Two Important Cities. The two largest and most attractive cities of Chile are Santiago, the capital, and Valparaiso, the chief seaport. Santiago is in the Central about 1800 feet above sea level and has a climate so mild that flowers bloom in parks and gardens at all times of the year. Yet peaks of the Andes within sight of the city are capped with snow from year's end to year's end. There

There are fine public and private buildings, well-paved and well-lighted streets, excellent shops, and many rather small factories. The main north-south railroad of Chile passes through the city and it is connected by an electric railroad 117 miles. in length with Valparaiso to the northwest. 

Valparaiso is the largest seaport on the 

Pacific coast of South America. The harbor is not naturally so well protected as is that of Rio (page 6) or those of our own ports of 

New York and San Francisco. It has therefore been necessary to build breakwaters to protect shipping in the harbor from storms.

Principal mineral products of South America. 

Northern Chile and the Atacama Desert.

Northern Chile is in the region of the southeast trade winds (diagram, page 9), and is dry. The winds usually blow along the coast or down from the mountains, and from cool to warmer regions. They bring little or no rain to northern Chile. Winds that have crossed the continent from the Atlantic have lost their moisture on their journey and bring none to these western coasts. Some rain or snow falls on the cold upper parts of the Andes. Small streams tumble down the mountain sides but only one of these reaches the Pacific. The others dry up or are lost in the sands of the desert.

The Desert of Atacama, named after Indians who once lived in that region, includes a large part of northern Chile. It is one of the most desolate regions in the world. 

Some trees and grass grow along the banks of the small mountain streams or where they sink into the desert. Elsewhere, for miles and miles on end, no living thing can be seen. It is a cruel region in which to live and work, as day after day passes with a cloudless sky and a burning sun overhead, and hot sand under foot.

The Atacama Desert, however, and other desert areas farther north in Chile, are so rich in minerals that thousands of men are employed in the mines there, and many, many millions of dollars have been invested in the mining properties and machinery. Railroads have been built from mines and refining plants to seaports along the coast, and to connect with the main line to Santiago and Valparaiso. At the ports there are houses for the workers who help to load and unload steamers by using smaller boats. The larger ships must stay well out to sea to avoid being dashed on shore in time of storm. Water is brought to the camps from high up in the mountains, and food, machinery, and other supplies must be brought in by railroad or steamer. A large part of the meat supply, however, comes from Argentina. The cattle are driven across the Andes and slaughtered after they reach the mining settlements. 

Nitrate. The most valuable of the minerals found in this desert region is a salt called nitrate of soda, or "nitrate." It is found mixed as a kind of cement with rock material, and forming layers so hard that they must be broken up by dynamite. 

The nitrate areas are scattered through the desert from 19° to 27° south latitude.

Some of the layers may have as much as 40% of nitrate, but most of them have much less. Some layers are only a few inches thick; others may be several feet thick.

Some are found on the surface, others are buried to a depth of many feet beneath materials that contain no nitrate. 

Rock material containing a valuable amount of nitrate is crushed and then put into tanks of boiling water. The water

CHILE 

Courtesy Nitrate Corporation of Chile 

A. 

A nitrate plant where by boiling, concentrating, and crystallizing the raw materials are prepared for market. 

Point out the pipes, the tanks, and the large loading machine. dissolves the nitrate, allowing the heavier waste material to sink to the bottom of the tank. From the tank the water with its dissolved nitrate is run off into pans, where the water is evaporated, leaving a mass of white nitrate crystals. As soon as it is dry enough, the nitrate is packed into bags and stored, or sent to the ports for export. In refining nitrate some borax and some iodine, a drug used in medicine and surgery, are obtained. There are also old lake basins whose deposits contain borates from which borax is made.

Nitrate is used chiefly in the manufacture of fertilizers and explosives. Before the discovery of methods by which nitrogen can be taken from the air and used in the manufacture of nitrates, most of the world's supply came from Chile. Enormous amounts were exported yearly to the United States and European countries. Some of these countries are now manufacturing nitrate to meet a part of their needs, but Chile still exports large amounts, which vary from year to year. 

Iquique and Antofagasta are the chief ports for the shipment of nitrate, although several other smaller ports are used.

The government of Chile raises a part of the money to meet its expenses by taxes on exports. In years when much nitrate is exported, from one fourth to one half of the money needed has been raised by the tax on it. The government of our country, under the Constitution of the United States, has no power to tax exports. 

Years ago parts of northern Chile belonged to Bolivia and Peru. Bolivia had a seacoast and harbors, and Peru a longer coast line than it now has. Then came a war between those countries and Chile. Chile won, and its boundary has been established where it is shown on the map (page 28). The lands formerly belonging to Peru and Bolivia now yield much of Chile's supply of nitrate. 

The railroads of Bolivia connect with those of Chile to reach the sea, and, under a treaty between the two countries, Bolivian exports and imports are handled at the ports of Chile. This arrangement, however, is not quite satisfactory to Bolivia. It would prefer, as would any other nation, its own seacoast and harbors. In that way it could more freely carry on its trade with the rest of the world.

Other Minerals in Chile. There are several copper-producing regions in Chile. 

The largest of these is in the Desert of Atacama, about 160 miles northeast of the port of Antofagasta. It is a mountain of ore that is mined by blasting off the face of the mountain and using power shovels (A) to load the trains that take the ore to the smelters. It is a low-grade ore that could not be mined profitably until large-scale operations by modern methods (B) were put in use by the United States company that now owns the mine. There is another coppermining region in the Andes of central Chile. 

The output of these and other mines makes Chile second among the copper-producing countries of the world.

Two large bodies of high-grade iron ore are known in Chile. One is in Atacama but this is not now being worked. The other, not far from Coquimbo, is owned by a Pennsylvania steel company. An electric line has been built from the mines to the coast, where modern ore docks, like those on Lake Superior, have been constructed. The ore is sent to the United States for smelting, while Chile imports manufactures of iron and steel. 

For many years Chile was a large producer of silver, but in recent years the amount has greatly decreased. A small amount of gold is obtained in the refining of copper and silver ores, and some lead, zinc, manganese, and sulphur are obtained.

The People. The people of Chile are descended from Spanish and other European peoples, and from mixed marriages between these settlers and the Indians. They are progressive and industrious, and proud of their nickname of "Yankees of South America." For the most part, the Indians of 

Chile were a more sturdy, powerful, and independent people than those of countries farther north. In the edge of the forest between southern and central Chile are the remnants of a very proud Indian race called Araucanians (A), who maintained their independence until about fifty years ago.

THE WEST COAST DESERT 

You have learned that much of northern

Chile is a desert, rich in minerals, but having no forests or well-watered fields. Even the higher Andes there have so little rain or snow on their western slopes that only one of the mountain streams crosses the desert to the 

Pacific Ocean. The Atacama Desert of northern Chile is part of the West Coast

Desert region (map, page 4). 

If you could fly from Chile northward over the coastal region of Peru, you would find that it also is, for the greater part, a barren waste. Yet there would be one very noticeable difference. There are more streams coming out of the mountains, they extend farther into the desert, and more of them reach the ocean. Why is this so, and how has it influenced the distribution of people and the nature of their industries? 

Winds and Rainfall. The West Coast

The West Coast 

Desert is in the region of the southeast trade winds (page 9; see also the maps on page 10). Winds from the Atlantic Ocean 

cross the continent and are cooled as they are forced into higher altitudes, up the eastern slopes of mountains. On these eastern slopes the rainfall is very heavy, and on their higher parts there is snow. Winds blow through passes in the eastern ranges, and bring some rain and snow to the tops of the western Andes. At times, storms and heavy fogs sweep in from the Pacific and bring moisture to the western Andes of Peru. 

Irrigation. In your flight over the Peruvian coast lands, you would notice that the streams reaching the lower lands are used for irrigation. Water is taken from the rivers at some high point and spread over lower-lying fields through a network of irrigation ditches. Where this life-giving water is brought to the fields there is no more desert. Instead, there are fields of cotton, sugar cane, and rice, and orchards and gardens. Every river that comes out of the mountains is made to yield its precious water to the fields. There also you will see pleasant cities (A) or villages with homes and shops and market places.

Cities of the West Coast. 

On the map, page 50, find Lima, Callao, and Mollendo.

Lima is the capital, largest city, and chief business center of Peru (51 A). It is well back from the coast and is surrounded by irrigated fields from which much of its food supply comes. Its chief manufactures are cotton goods, woolen goods, and shoes. Lima is connected by railroad with the mining regions in the mountains, and with Callao (A), a near-by seaport that has the only good natural harbor on the 1400 miles of Peru's seacoast.

This long coast line of Peru is equal to the distance from Key West to New York on our

Atlantic coast, or from San Diego to Vancouver on our Pacific coast. To the wharves and docks of Callao come ships from many countries, bringing goods from all the world The Smaller Ports. In flying along the coast of Peru, you would see hill lands, sand dunes, bare rocks, and cliffs. Then you would catch sight of a curving coast line that partly incloses a bay. Its waters are sheltered enough from storms so that steamers lying off shore are more or less protected. 

A pier runs out into the water. Here boats can be loaded and unloaded, and boatmen transfer goods between the pier and steamers anchored in the deep water of the bay.

HIGHLANDS OF PERU AND BOLIVIA 

To understand what you will find in the highlands of Peru and Bolivia, you should know about the people who lived there before 

Spanish explorers came to the New World.

In those highlands, many thousands of feet above the level of the sea, there are the ruins of cities, temples, and palaces. Even so late as the latter part of 1932, some explorers stumbled by accident upon the ruins of a great city unknown before then. What is the story of the people who lived in these ancient cities? 

A Story of the Past. The shores of 

South America were discovered by Christopher Columbus, and by other explorers and adventurers from Spain and Portugal.

As a result these two countries gained control of almost the whole continent. They found, everywhere, native Indian people as other explorers found them in North America.

Some of the Indians were savages roaming wild in the forest where their descendants may be found today. Others had reached a high degree of civilization. They tilled the land and used the water of the mountain streams to irrigate their fields. They built wonderful stone buildings and good roads. 

They had an orderly government. 

The natives who had made the greatest progress in these arts of civilization belonged to the empire of the Incas. Their capital was Cusco, an an ancient city among the mountains of Peru. The lands that were controlled by the Incas are largely in Peru and Bolivia, but extend also into Ecuador on the north, and Chile on the south.

SOUTH AMERICA 

One of these is the region of mountains and plateaus. The other is a lowland east of the 

Andes, a part of the great interior lowland of the continent. Each of these countries has boundary disputes about the extent of its lowland area (map facing page 1).

It is in these two countries that the Andes - here often called "the roof of the Western World" reach their greatest width and nearly their greatest height. The average elevation of the eastern and western ranges of the Andes is almost twice that of our Rocky Mountains, and the great peaks of Illimani and Sorata (map, page 50) reach heights of more than 21,000 feet. Compare them with 

Mt. Whitney, the highest peak in the United 

States (14,500 feet), and Mt. Marcy, the

A. — Llamas in a residential street of La Paz, Bolivia. highest peak in New York (5344 feet). 

Notice that there are packs on the backs of some of them. 

The Incas, and the tribes ruled by them, mined much gold and silver, and used those precious metals in decorating their buildings and in making ornaments of various kinds. 

They were experts in agriculture. Along the coast they constructed irrigation works, and cultivated fields along the rivers, as you have learned is being done today. In the mountain valleys they made terraces on the steep slopes by building walls to hold the soil in place, and raised potatoes, corn, and cotton. | 

They found potatoes and corn as wild plants and developed them by cultivation, giving to the world two most important food plants. 

They used the llama (A) as a beast of burden. 

The Spanish explorer Pizarro, with a small party of soldiers and adventurers, invaded the country in 1532. By the use of firearms, the Spaniards captured and later killed the king of the Incas, and conquered the land for Spain. It remained under Spanish rule for nearly three hundred years. 

Two Independent Republics. As you know, Bolivia has no coast lands (page 47) and you have studied those of Peru as a part of the West Coast Desert. Two parts of Peru and Bolivia remain to be studied. The eastern and western ranges of the Andes spread out to inclose a great plateau with an average elevation of about 12,000 feet, and, farther north, numerous shorter and lower ranges. Between those shorter ranges are mountain valleys with bare slopes. 

Farms and Grazing Lands.- The people of the plateau and valleys are chiefly Indians and mestizos. Most of them are farmers and have a great affection for their small holdings. 

In the mountain valleys where there is enough rain, or where irrigation is possible, the floor of the valley and its terraced lower slopes are cultivated. Being near the Equator, the lower valleys are warm, and the crops of warm regions are grown there. These include corn, beans, some orchard fruits, and vegetables. In the higher valleys the crops are those of cooler lands-wheat, barley, rye, and potatoes. The plateau is bare, windswept, and rocky. Comfortably warm when the sun is shining, it is cold at night; frosts are frequent, and the growing season is short. 

Some crops are grown, but grazing is more common, although the grass is poor and scanty. In the summer the shepherds drive their flocks up the mountain slopes almost to the snow line.

A. Part of the Central Railway of Peru, on which you see a train carrying copper bars from a Cerro de Pasco smelter. 

On the lower slope there are some terraced fields. 

Some large grazing areas are owned by men who live in the cities. The herds and flocks of such an owner are left in the care of a mestizo manager and the Indians he employs. 

The beef animals are generally poor and their meat tough. The sheep are small and the wool is of various colors and of poor quality. 

A demand for better meat and a better kind of wool has led to attempts to improve the breed of the animals. 

Two Valuable Animals. The llama (54 A) 

is small but strong for its size, and very surefooted. It belongs to the camel family and can travel long distances if necessary without much food or water. Llamas are the pack animals of the Andes mountain trails. Each animal will carry about 100 pounds, but if overloaded it will lie down until a part of the load is removed. The alpaca, which belongs to the same family as the llama, is raised for its long, fine wool.

A Famous Mine in Peru. - The Central 

Railway of Peru (A) and the Southern Railway of Peru connect the coast with the mining and agricultural regions of the Andes. 

The Central connects the port of Callao with Oroya, on the eastern slope of the western range of the Andes. Its construction was difficult and very expensive. Part of the road bed was blasted out of the mountain side, and passengers look down into gloomy gorges. There are many tunnels, bridges, and switchbacks. The grades are steep, and where the railroad crosses the western range its pass is 15,680 feet above sea level the greatest height reached by any railroad in the world. A railroad from Oroya goes to one of the world's great copper mines at 

Cerro de Pasco (map, page 50). 

The Cerro de Pasco mines and a great smelting plant at Oroya are owned by an American company. The same company

The volcano El Misti towers above the city of Arequipa, which lies at its base. Arequipa is about sixty miles inland, on the railroad from Mollendo to Lake Titicaca and Cusco. owns other mines not far away. It mines nine tenths of the copper of Peru. Some gold and silver are obtained from the same ore as the copper. Men sent from the United

States manage the mines and the smelter, but the hard work is done by Indians who have always lived in these high altitudes. 

Vanadium and lead also are mined in small quantities, and some coal from which coke is made. Vanadium is used in making certain kinds of hard steel. Peru produces more than half of the world's supply. From mines not reached by railroads, ore is brought out by llamas or donkeys. The metals are shipped, and supplies for the mines are received, at Callao.

From Mollendo to the Bolivian Plateau. - 

The Southern Railway of Peru connects the port of Mollendo with Arequipa and Cusco, once the capital of the Inca empire. From 

Mollendo it crosses the desert and winds upward more than 7000 feet before reaching Arequipa. This city (A) is the center of the wool trade and has some manufacturing. For over 35 years (1891-1927) Harvard University, of Massachusetts, had an observatory near Arequipa. The air there is usually clear and the night sky cloudless. Although the 

North Star and others near it cannot be seen there, most of the stars can be seen very well, including the Southern Cross and all other stars that cannot be seen in our country.

After crossing the western Andes the railroad continues to Lake Titicaca (57 A). 

Steamers on this lake, the highest navigable body of water in the world, are owned by the railroad and connect with a short line to La Paz. This is the least used of the Bolivian railroads.

La Paz is the largest city of Bolivia and its chief financial and business center. It was built in a valley below the level of the plateau to protect its people from the cold biting winds and dust storms that sweep across the higher land. Because La Paz is a railroad center and Sucre, the legal capital of Bolivia, is not, most of the government business is done in La Paz.

A. 

 - A small native boat on Lake Titicaca. Both the boat and the sail are made of reeds tied together. 

The Mines of Bolivia. The richest mineral region of Bolivia is in the eastern Andes, where tin, silver, gold, copper, and lead are found. Only the tin is mined in large quantities, and Bolivia now produces about one fourth of the world's supply. The amount of silver mined is now small, although the silver mines of Potosí were once the marvel of the world. Gold is found in the ores of copper and silver. The copper mines of Bolivia produce much less than those of 

Peru and Chile.

The chief railroad serving the mines is the 

Antofagasta-Bolivia Railway (page 50), although many of the mines are at some distance from it in the mountains. Donkeys and llamas are used to carry the ore down the mountain trails. 

Another railroad from La Paz and the shortest route to the sea-goes to the port of Arica. Its mountain section has steep grades and is expensive to operate. Most of the freight still takes the longer route to 

Antofagasta. A railroad connects that route also with the railroad system of Argentina and gives an outlet for Bolivia on the Atlantic at Buenos Aires. Bolivia, as you know, is in the unhappy position of not being able to reach the sea except across the territory of neighboring countries.

Industries and Products. As in other | gathered the latex from wild rubber trees parts of South America, large estates, some of a half-million acres or more, are owned by rich men who live in the cities. From its leaves is made the drug cocaine, used in medicine and surgery. 

Southeastern Bolivia is a part of the Gran

Chaco (map, page 4). Some of it is scrub, a part is grassland, and another part is forest. 

The population of this area is small. Potatoes, cereals, fruit, sugar cane, rice, and coffee are raised, but there are no industries that send important products to world markets.

The forested lowlands of the Amazon and Orinoco basins are inhabited chiefly by Indians who live by hunting and fishing. 

Not many years ago the Indians in this area and prepared "hams " of crude rubber (page 22). So much plantation rubber is now produced in the Far East that the wild rubber industry of South America is no longer very important.

Iquitos, the largest settlement in the whole area you are now studying, was once a famous rubber-shipping port on the Amazon in eastern Peru. It can be reached by goodsized steamers, but with the falling off in rubber production its commerce is dwindling.

Another forest industry once very important, especially in eastern Ecuador, has been almost destroyed. Quinine, a drug much used in medicine, is made from the bark of the cinchona tree. These trees grow wild in the forests of the eastern Andes, where the natives strip the bark from the trunks and branches. The industry is declining because many of the wild trees have been killed, and because of the cinchona plantations in the 

Far East.

SOUTH AMERICA 

In Colombia, some cattle are pastured on the savanna lands along the Orinoco, but to get them to market they must be driven into the highlands. Even at the start of the drive they are generally in poor condition, and when they reach the highland markets their condition is worse. The meat is stringy and tough and brings a low price, but their hides have some value. 

The Future. This part of South America 

(eastern Bolivia, Peru, and Ecuador, and southeastern Colombia) has great forests that could yield an enormous amount of lumber. There are grasslands on which millions of cattle could find pasture. It has a fertile soil and abundant rains where tropical products can be raised almost without limit. 

There are many streams whose waterfalls and rapids could furnish all needed power. 

Yet much of this region has a population of less than one person per square mile. When will it be developed? So far as can now be seen that time will not come until some energetic people can clear parts of the forest, control the river floods, and build railroads that will carry goods cheaply to market.

The population of the world must grow much more dense than it is now before any nation will seriously attempt to do these things.

Products and People. Find the Gulf of Guayaquil. On a river flowing into this gulf find a city of the same name. It is the largest city and chief port of Ecuador. Near it are large cacao plantations. At one time 

Ecuador was the leading cacao-growing country in the world. Now the Gold Coast of Africa and near-by islands produce over twelve times as much, and Brazil three times as much (page 16).

Ecuador is losing its cacao industry as it has lost much of its cinchona and rubber industries. One reason for this is that the population of this west coast region is made up chiefly of Indians, Negroes, and mestizos who do not like to work. who do not like to work. Nearly all of them suffer from hookworm disease, which makes them tired and weak, but which can be cured. Until a few years ago yellow fever, one of the most deadly of tropical diseases, was found here also. American army surgeons in Cuba discovered that yellow fever is carried from person to person by one kind of mosquitoes. Methods of killing off these mosquitoes were worked out, and with the help of American sanitary officers many South American cities have been freed from this disease including Guayaquil. Malaria, also caused by a mosquito, is another disease from which the people of Ecuador suffer, but it too can be controlled. 

White managers can now live here in safety. When there is more labor and the natives are able and willing to work — as native laborers do on plantations in other parts of the world - many tropical products

NORTHERN COUNTRIES OF SOUTH AMERICA 

The northern part of South America is bordered by the Caribbean Sea and the 

Atlantic Ocean. It includes the northern part of Colombia, and all of Venezuela, British Guiana, Surinam or Dutch Guiana, and French Guiana. Southeastern Colombia has been studied as part of a larger region including similar areas in Ecuador, Peru, and 

Bolivia; and southwestern Colombia has been studied as part of a tropical jungle bordering the Pacific (pages 58-62).

The northern countries of South America are in the Torrid Zone, and the prevailing winds there are the northeast trade winds. 

What does this region produce that is of interest to the people of the United States, the nearest of the great trading nations? 

Caribbean Colombia. In Colombia, the northern Andes divide into three great ranges that extend from south to north. 

Between these ranges and along their sides are the cool uplands where most of the white the land lies close to sea level, and it is hot population of the country live. On the coast and damp. Bananas, sugar cane, and rice are grown there. In the cooler uplands the crops are corn, wheat, cotton, and the fruits and vegetables of temperate lands. 

Out of one of the mountain valleys, the 

Magdalena River flows into the Caribbean

Sea through swamps and over sand bars. 

It is the outlet of a rich agricultural and mineral region. It is about 1100 miles long and is navigable for a part of its lower course, but not all of the way to the sea. 

Its chief port, Barranquilla, is connected by rail with the seaport Puerto Colombia, and by airplane routes with Bogotá, the capital, and with Buenaventura on the Pacific. 

The mineral resources of the Colombia mountains and valleys are not yet fully known. Gold is found in the mountains as well as in river gravels (page 61), but the

Back in the mountains, on a plateau 8600 feet above sea level, is Bogotá, the capital of Colombia. It is beautifully located, with high mountains to furnish a picturesque background. On account of its elevation it has a temperate climate, but until the coming of the airplane it was hard to reach. 

The usual journey from Barranquilla to 

Bogotá, made up of rail and water trips of various lengths, takes over a week. The airplane trip is of course very much shorter.

Bogotá is the chosen home of much of the white population, and a trading center for the surrounding country.

Natural Regions of Venezuela. — Turn to the map on page 50. Notice that the northern part of the boundary between

Over all of this northern part of South 

America blow the northeast trade winds, bringing rain to the northern mountain slopes. From parts of Colombia the rain is shut out by the mountains that these winds cross. This is also true of the grasslands of the Orinoco, except when the equatorial belt of rains, in moving north and south with the seasons, crosses these plains.

The northern slopes of the Andes and the Guiana Highlands have dense forests. The plains of the Orinoco have a rainy season when the grass grows rapidly and the river overflows, flooding large parts of the plain. 

This is followed by a dry season when the grass withers and dies. If it catches on fire at this time, it burns over enormous areas. 

Products of Venezuela. - Crops of tropical lands are grown along the Caribbean coast and in the lowlands around Lake Maracaibo.

Here are the chief sugar-cane region and a cacao-growing district. In this same lowland, much petroleum has been found and many wells have been drilled. 

In the highlands west and south of Lake 

Maracaibo, coffee of an excellent quality is raised, and the industry is increasing. Cotton and corn also are grown in this region. 

There are minerals in the highlands and mountains of Venezuela, and some gold and copper are mined.

On the llanos, cattle raising is at present the only possible occupation. This is handicapped by a long dry season, by flooded plains during the growing season, by distance from a market, and by the lack of labor. 

The Orinoco is navigable for a long distance, but there is not enough traffic to make river transportation profitable. At the mouth of the river is a great delta much like that at the mouth of the Mississippi.

The Guiana Highlands have but a small native population, and no industries of importance.

Cities of Venezuela.- La Guaira, at the base of the mountains that border the 

Caribbean, is the chief port of Venezuela.

Through it most of the commerce of the country is carried on, although there is another shallow port at Maracaibo.

From La Guaira, a railroad climbs the mountains to Caracas, the capital, which is about 4000 feet above sea level. Although 

La Guaira is less than 7 miles from Caracas the railroad between the two cities is 23 miles in length. It is a very picturesque route. route. Caracas (65 A) is high enough above sea level to have a comfortable climate. The 

Venezuelans are proud of their capital and speak of it as the "pearl of the Andes."

The Guianas.-The Guiana Highlands extend east from southern Venezuela into 

British, Dutch, and French Guiana. their names indicate, each of these three small countries belongs to a country in Europe. 

All of the rest of South America is occupied by independent republics.

The northeast trade winds bring heavy rains to all the Guianas. Their coastal lowlands are hot, damp, and unhealthful, especially for white people. They are frequently flooded during the very rainy season, and no period of the year is entirely free from rain.

Caracas is a beautiful city with well-kept squares and public gardens. Clouds often conceal the tops of the near-by mountains.

The chief crop-growing regions are on the lower lands near the coast, and in the river valleys where there are fine soils and fertile fields. Sugar and rice are the two most important crops, but other food crops for the people include yams, corn, bananas, and other fruits. Cattle are raised on grasslands near the coast, only to meet the needs of the people. The only product of value obtained from the forests is balata, used to cover (insulate) electric wires. 

In each of these three countries some gold is mined in French Guiana by the forced labor of convicts. More diamonds are found in British Guiana than in Brazil. Much bauxite is mined, and is sent to the United States for manufacture into aluminum. 

Most of the people of British Guiana are 

Negroes, descendants of slaves; laborers from tropical islands of southeastern Asia; and mestizos. All of these can live and work there in greater safety and comfort than white men could. In French Guiana, the population has been increased by its use as a colony to which many of the worst criminals of France have been sent.

Agriculture has been more successful in Surinam or Dutch Guiana because the Dutch settlers built embankments to keep their fields from being flooded. fields from being flooded. Pumps also are used to remove any surplus water that gets on the fields. The same is true of agriculture in part of British Guiana which was once owned by the Dutch.

SOUTH AMERICA SOUTH AMERICA AS A WHOLE 

When you began the study of South America, you learned that in some ways it is much like North America, and in other ways it is very different (pages 1-3). You found that South America is southeast of our continent. If you use the meridian of 74° west longitude - the meridian of New York City — in the same way as you did the meridian of 80° west (page 1), you find again that most of North America is west of it and nearly all of South America is east of it. 

Before you leave the study of South

America, you should gather together some of the facts that you have learned about the different countries. 

Size. On the map, page 2, use the scale of miles to find how long South America is from its southernmost point at Cape Horn to its northernmost point on the Caribbean 

Sea. Find the latitude of each of these points, and, taking 70 miles as the length of a degree of latitude, find the length of the continent. How do the two results compare?

Use the map scale also to find the width of the continent from Cape St. Roque on the 

Atlantic to Point Pariña on the Pacific. 

What continents are larger than South 

America? What continents are smaller? (See Table 1, page 376.)

Lands That Cannot Be Used. The greater part of South America is in the Torrid Zone and, as the map on page 2 shows, most of the continent is less than 1000 feet above sea level. Much of the Amazon basin is less than 500 feet above sea level (map, page 8). A region in the Torrid Zone only a little above sea level is hot. In this tropical part of South America, the prevailing winds are the northeast and southeast trade winds. 

They meet in the equatorial calms that move north and south with the seasons, and there are daily rains. A large part of the Amazon basin therefore is hot and rainy, and dense rain forests cover much of it. 

Up to the present time, this region has yielded few products for the use of man. 

The most important one has been rubber, but now the production of rubber there has greatly decreased. Some day, perhaps, the world will need the products of tropical lands now overgrown by rain forests, and they may be cleared away. In the Amazon lowlands not only must that work be done, but vast floods must be brought under control. To do all this calls for earnest and intelligent labor, and much money, and both are now lacking for this task. The future of this region cannot be foretold, but at present it is not bright. No area of rain forests anywhere near as large as the Amazon lowlands has ever been cleared, although some jungles have been cut down and converted into plantations. The flood waters of some rivers, like those of the Mississippi, have been held within artificial banks, but this has never been done for a stream carrying even half as much water as the Amazon. 

Jungle lands along the coast of the Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and for some distance south along the Pacific Ocean are also largely waste. They produce but a small part of the crops that could be grown there. 

Some are not used because not enough labor is available or the laborers are not intelligent, others because diseases drive laborers away. 

There are deserts that cannot be irrigated, such as some of those along the west coast. 

There are lands that are too cold for crops, such as the plains of Patagonia. There are snow-covered mountains, too cold and bleak for crops or man. There are lonely forests on plains and mountain slopes, too far from the markets of the world to be of commercial value. Neither the timber that is now growing there nor the crops that could be grown could be sold at a price that would pay for necessary labor. 

What may be done to change these conditions, no one can say. South America is a land of the future.

A. Plowing on a large farm in Peru. The plow used is a stick that merely breaks up the soil. however, steel plows drawn by tractors and turning a number of furrows are in use as they are in the United States. 

Natural Resources not Fully Developed. - 

In the agricultural and grazing sections of 

South America, a full use of the land has never been attempted. Land is held in great estates; most of the labor is hired (A). 

There is hardly any careful mixed farming by the owners of small farms, as in our country. 

In regard to the mineral resources of South America, the case is much the same. Many Many mineral regions are known, some of enormous extent, of which a number are being worked. 

Other deposits are known that are not being worked because they are hard to reach and cannot be mined at a profit. Many parts of the continent where minerals may be found have never been explored. Most of the mines now being operated have been developed by companies in the United States or Europe.

Manufactures, using the raw materials of the country, have been started in several of the more progressive cities. The growth of manufacturing, as well as the carrying on of large-scale mining, requires much coal. But not much coal has been found in South America, and most of the little that has been found is of poor quality. 

The best mines are so located that mining is difficult and expensive. In most places it is cheaper to import better coal from the 

United States or Europe. To a small extent, electric power plants have been built to furnish electricity to cities and manufacturing plants. But here again a limited supply of skilled labor has made it necessary to use imported machinery and foreign mechanics, machinists, and managers.

Those parts of South America where the most rapid progress may be expected in the arts and industries are the A B C countries 1 

Argentina, Brazil, and Chile - and Uruguay. Parts of each of these countries are in temperate lands, and a considerable white population in each has the energy and

SOUTH AMERICA 

A. Puerto Colombia boasts the longest pier in the world, 4000 feet long. 

Loading and unloading here can be conveniently done because freight trains can run out on the pier alongside the ships. ambition to seek improvements, and the ability to bring them about. The future there should bring a better use of land, an increase of manufacturing, more education, and more orderly and settled governments.

Many of the cities in South America have gained in trade because of the growing industries of the surrounding regions. In 

Brazil, Rio de Janeiro, Santos, and São Paulo have grown in size and commerce because of coffee; Bahia because of cacao; and 

Pernambuco because of sugar. Buenos Aires and Bahía Blanca in Argentina, and Montevideo in Uruguay, have grown because of the surplus wheat, corn, cattle, sheep, wool, and hides that they ship to Europe and the 

United States. Valparaiso in Chile, Callao in Peru, and Puerto Colombia in Colombia (A) are other ports that are increasing in size with an increase in the industrial importance of their hinterlands. 

Education has been largely confined to the wealthy and to the white population of the more progressive countries.

For most of the poorer people there have been no schools at all. Even for the wealthy not much technical education has been provided. Not until more people receive an education, and technical training is more generally given, will skilled native laborers be available.

At present, most of the Indians and Negroes, and many mestizos, cannot read or write.

A study of the map on page 

24 will show that most of the people of the continent live near the oceans. The interior of the continent has very few people, and almost all of them are Indians or Negroes.

Transportation and Trade. - Railroads and good roads are very limited in South 

America. The railroads that have been built are chiefly short lines extending back from the coast, or connecting a few of the larger inland cities with near-by ports. 

Only two lines, built at enormous expense, cross the Andes. Not many of the railroads of South America have ever paid a fair return on the money invested. In most of the continent there are too few people to pay the cost of good highways. It is only in recent years that the more progressive cities have paved their streets. 

Fortunately, South America has thousands of miles of navigable waterways reaching into many parts of the country. Air routes also are developing, both for travel in South 

America and for travel between the two 

American continents.

SOUTH AMERICA AS A WHOLE 

69 The great highway of world trade is the ocean, and the countries of South America are kept in touch with world markets through their seaports. Most of the trade of South

American countries is with the United States or Europe. The goods, however, must be carried long distances, because the greater part of South America is in the Southern Hemisphere. The meats shipped must be kept chilled or frozen during the long voyages. 

The expense of transportation by steamers, though less than it would be for an equal distance by railway, is nevertheless higher than it would be if the distances were shorter. 

Because of differences in products and needs, the commerce between North and South 

America is constantly increasing. Because such products as corn, wheat, and meat find a better market in Europe than in the United

States, a large part of the commerce of some South American countries is with Europe. 

Pan-American Union. In the city of

Washington, there is a beautiful building that is the home of the Pan-American Union. 

The members of this Union are the republics of North and South America. It was formed so that through meetings and the exchange of information the people of the member countries can know more about each other. This has brought about better understanding and more friendly relations.

THE NEW WORLD AND THE OLD WORLD 

Last year you studied North America, and you have just completed the study of 

South America. These two continents with their near-by islands include nearly all of the land of the Western Hemisphere. Ever since their discovery and early exploration they have been called the New World. 

In the Eastern Hemisphere you find the continents of Europe, Africa, and Australia, and almost all of Asia. Europe and Asia form a single large mass of land to which the name of Eurasia is frequently given. The continent of Africa is also joined to Asia by the Isthmus of Suez, across which a canal has been cut to connect the Mediterranean 

Sea with the Red Sea.

All three of these continents border on the 

Mediterranean Sea. Europe is on the north,

Africa on the south, and Asia touches it at its eastern end.

In the valley of the Nile, in northeast Africa, the ancient Egyptians built large temples and palaces several thousand years ago. On the edge of the desert, too, they built huge pyramids, covering the burial chambers of some of their kings. In southwestern Asia, about as long ago, some great cities were built by other nations. In southern Europe, a little later, the Greeks and the Romans built temples of rare beauty. 

Vast open-air theaters were constructed also, where plays were presented, where orators spoke to the people, and where games and other exhibitions were held. Most of these beautiful buildings are today in ruins, yet people travel halfway around the earth to see and admire them.

One by one these ancient peoples were conquered by less civilized invaders, who in turn built up new civilizations. The three

A. 

- Westminster Abbey, in London, England, is the most famous church in the British Empire and the one most closely associated with its national life. Here most of the English kings have been crowned, and here many of them are buried.

EUROPE 

Across the Atlantic Ocean, to the east of 

North America, is the continent of Europe.

Over the more than 3000 miles of ocean that separate the North Atlantic ports of these two continents, ships are constantly moving. 

99 

Some of these ships we call "tramps."

They have no regular" run between ports. | 

They pick up a cargo where they can. They take it to the port where it is to go, and hope that there they can find some cargo that they can carry on to yet another port, wherever it may be. Other North Atlantic ships are the "luxury liners" great passenger steamers that carry also some express and freight. These are are vast floating hotels.

Each has fine public rooms, a library, a gymnasium and a swimming pool, and great dining rooms in which the best of food is served. At night all parts of the ship are lighted by electricity. In your comfortable room, called a stateroom or cabin, is an excellent bed. excellent bed. These steamships, driven by powerful engines, move rapidly through the water, and can make the trip across the ocean from New York to a port in southern England or northern France in from five to seven days.

More people travel back and forth between 

North America and Europe than between any other two continents. Many business men in our country buy or sell in European markets, and find it necessary to make many trips abroad. Students go to Europe to study.

They and other travelers go to visit the famous old cities that still retain something of the past to see their picturesque houses and the interesting streets and shops. In some of these cities there are museums and art galleries. In a number of them there are magnificent churches, on which architects, builders, sculptors, and painters have used their great abilities to make them worthy of the purpose for which they were built (A).

POSITION AND SIZE OF EUROPE 

75 Just as we find the people and the cities of the Old World interesting to us, so do the people of many European countries find the New World interesting to them. Some of them have come to our country to make their homes here. Others have gone to some South American country. They be lieve that in these new and less crowded lands they can live better and be happier.

They have bought farms. They have found work in our mills and factories, and in our shops and offices, or they have started some business of their own. Others are students or travelers. They come to see our cities and their skyscrapers, to visit Niagara Falls, Yellowstone National Park, the Grand Can yon, or some other marvelous work of nature.

The ancestors of most of us came from Europe. In some European country many of you may still have relatives or friends. 

You could go back to the place from which your ancestors came and find the records of your family. For these reasons and many others you will enjoy studying the continent of Europe.

The Position and Size of Europe. - If 

If you look at Europe on a globe, you will find it a very much cut-up peninsula extending west from the great land mass of Asia. But, although the large southern peninsulas of Asia almost reach the Equator, no part of Europe is as far south as the Tropic of Cancer. A small part of the continent extends northward beyond the Arctic Circle, but much less than in North America. Almost all of Europe, therefore, is in the North 

Temperate Zone.

Europe is sixth in size among the continents only Australia is smaller. Asia is more than four and a half times as large, and North America is nearly two and a half times as large. How does Europe compare in size with the United States? How does it compare with Brazil? (See Table 1, page 376.) 

Map Study. 1. Look again at the coast line of South America (map facing page 1). Then look at the coast line of North America (page 375).

You can easily see that the coast line of North America is much more irregular than that of South America. Now look at the coast line of Europe on the opposite page. How does it compare in regularity with the coast lines of the Americas? 

Europe is less than half as large as North America and little more than half as large as South America, and yet it has a longer coast line than either. 

How do you explain this fact? 

2. What large sea separates Europe from Africa to the south? Name three other seas that touch 

Europe on the south. What sea between the 

British Isles and the mainland? What sea extends from the west far into the interior of Europe?

Europe. Look up names you cannot pronounce, in the Index and Pronunciations at the back of this book.

NATURAL REGIONS OF EUROPE 

77 

A Mother Continent. Year after year the population of many European countries has increased, except when disease or war has caused great loss of life. There are now more people in Europe, for each square mile of its surface, than in any other continent. 

Prove this by dividing the number of people in each continent by the number of square miles. This gives an average number for each square mile, or what is called the "density" of population. The density of population for each country can be found in the same way.

The increasing density of population in some of the European countries has had an effect upon the settlement and progress of many other countries. Through discovery and settlement, or through wars, some of the countries of Europe have spread their influence far beyond the boundaries of that continent. Some of them own or control large areas in other continents and many of the islands of the sea. Europe has been like a great mother. She has sent her children to fill empty lands and build new nations. 

The Highlands and Lowlands of Europe. 

Study the maps on page 74 and page 76. 

These maps show the larger natural regions of Europe and their relation to each other. 

You will remember that in both North 

America and South America the highlands | and lowlands have a north-south direction. 

In Europe, their direction is east-west. 

The High Ranges of Southern Europe. - 

Trace the mountains of southern Europe across the continent. Notice that they are made up of several mountain masses having different names. There are the Pyrenees, the Alps, and the Carpathians. Find each of these, and remember where they are. 

Notice also that there are mountains in 

Italy and in the Balkan Peninsula. What are the names of these ranges? Find a route past the western border of the Alps from the Mediterranean Sea to the North 

Sea. Find another from the Mediterranean 

Sea to the Black Sea, then east of the Carpathians to the Baltic Sea. In following these routes is it necessary to cross any of the great mountain ranges?

The Central Highlands. - North and northwest of the Alps and the Carpathians are the Central Highlands. They extend from south-central France across the continent to the great plains in its eastern part (map, page 76). There were once high mountains in this region; but long before any time of which we have a record, they were worn down to lowlands by the winds, and rains, and rivers, and ice. Later some parts were lifted again, and once more the forces that wear away the highlands of the earth began to work upon them. As a result, these lifted blocks of land have been carved into hills and valleys, with some lowland valleys where rivers flow out of them. 

The Spanish Plateau is another region in which almost the same changes have occurred. 

Northwest Highlands. -The region known as the Northwest Highlands includes the mountains of the Scandinavian Peninsula, the highlands of the British Isles, and an area in northwest France. It is believed that these highlands are the remnant of a mountain range that at one time ran along the western coast of Europe from the Arctic Ocean to the Bay of Biscay. They are now much lower than they once were, and parts of the old highlands are covered by waters of the North Sea and the English Channel. 

The present mountains of this region are broadest and highest in the Scandinavian Peninsula. But they are much lower than the high mountains of southern Europe. 

It is fortunate for central and eastern Europe that there is now no great mountain wall like the Andes along the western coast. 

Such a body of mountains would almost entirely shut out the rain that reaches central Europe. The lowlands lying east of it would be largely desert instead of being fertile and densely populated as they now are.

Influence of the Ocean on the Climate of 

Europe. 

Europe. Have you ever stood on the banks of a river, or the shores of a lake or ocean, when the wind was blowing? Did you notice that the wind brushed the surface of the water and heaped it up in waves? 

If you did, you probably also noticed that when the wind was strong the waves were high, and that soon after the wind died down the waves did also.

Waves are not the only movement of ocean waters caused by the winds. Over some parts of the oceans the winds blow so steadily in one direction that the surface waters are driven along as a current or drift. 

On the map above, find the current off the eastern coast of North America called the 

Gulf Stream. One part of it comes out of the Gulf of Mexico through Florida Strait.

Its waters come from the equatorial regions and are warm. 

As the Gulf Stream moves northeast, it spreads out more, and is moved along in part

The lands along the Mediterranean

These southern peninsulas are themselves largely mountainous, and there are marked differences in the climate of the various parts. As a whole, however, the climate is more oceanic than continental. Farming.-Farms average much smaller in size than they do in the United States, and as a rule the land is more carefully cultivated. 

Low lands along the North Sea have been protected, and some areas covered by shallow seas have been reclaimed, by building banks or dikes to shut out the ocean. 

Hillsides and lower mountain slopes have been terraced. Some lands have been irrigated, and where possible more than one crop a year is raised. Fertilizers are used freely to increase the yield of the fields. A. 

66 Welsh shepherds are driving their sheep down from the mountains to the valley for their annual dipping," a precaution against disease. 

You can see the brands on some of the sheep. In the valley below you can see some fields.

Some of the food crops can be raised under a variety of conditions as to climate and soil. Such crops are widely scattered because each nation wishes, so far as it can profitably do so, to raise food for its people. Other crops must have certain conditions of temperature and rainfall to do well. They will be grown in more limited areas. The distribution of the more important crops of both kinds will be shown on maps on later pages of this book. 

The Animal Industries. Grazing is car ried on where the land is too rough or too cold to be farmed; where the rainfall is too heavy or too light for cultivated crops; and in high mountain pastures. Most of the domestic animals, however, are raised on farms where mixed farming is carried on. 

Areas devoting special attention to sheep (A), goats, donkeys, horses, and hogs will be studied as they are found in learning more about the different countries. 

Unproductive Lands. - Europe has only small areas that can properly be called unproductive. The high, rocky, snow- and ice-covered mountain areas are unproductive, but mountains that are covered with forests are not. The swamp lands around the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Bothnia are partly forested. Even the cold, barren tun- dra region bordering the Arctic Ocean furnishes pasture for herds of reindeer. 

Mineral Resources and Manufacturing. 

Minerals have been found in different parts. of the continent but chiefly where old mountains have been worn down and where coal beds were formed. In these areas, metal and other manufacturing industries have been developed, and great modern industrial cities have grown up. The importation of raw materials not produced in Europe, or produced in only small amounts, has made possible the growth of other great manufacturing industries. 

Distribution of Population. You have already learned that Europe is the most densely populated continent. In what parts of the continent are most of the people to be found? Naturally there are more in the great manufacturing districts than in farming regions. The better agricultural regions are more densely settled than the grazing and forest regions. The least densely settled areas are the high mountains, the swamp lands, and the tundras. Study map 81 A.

Cities. Most of the large cities of Europe have grown up where manufacturing and trade furnish their people something to do. Manufacturing has centered around districts rich in minerals, or near ports where raw materials from distant lands are received. 

A few cities owe their present importance to the time, many centuries ago, when they got their start in art and industry and trade. 

In part, they have survived because of this early start, and in part because art galleries, museums, and wonderful buildings draw thousands of travelers to them yearly.

THE BRITISH ISLES 

The British Isles include all of the islands shown on the map facing this page. They are separated from the mainland of Europe on the south by the narrow English Channel and on the east by the waters of the North Sea.

On the map of Europe (page 74) find the black line in the Bay of Biscay marked 100. 

It is the 100-fathom line and shows where the waters along the shore of the continent reach a depth of 100 fathoms, or 600 feet.

Trace it around the west and the north of the British Isles, along the shore of the 

Scandinavian Peninsula, into the Arctic

Ocean. Within this line the edge of the continent extends out under the sea and is called the continental shelf. There was a time in the history of our earth when no water covered the continental shelf and the British Isles were a part of the European mainland. 

The largest island is Great Britain, and in it are England, Wales, and Scotland. 

The other large island is Ireland and in it are the Irish Free State and Northern Ireland. The Irish Free State has its own government. The three parts of Great Britain, together with Northern Ireland, make up the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, often called simply "United Kingdom," or "Great Britain."

Learn the way in which each of these names should be used. 

British Empire. The many parts of the earth over which the British government has more or less control are, taken all together, called the British Empire. This empire includes the United Kingdom itself, the Irish Free State, Canada and some smaller lands in America, Australia, large parts of Africa, India and some smaller lands in Asia, and several thousand islands. A few of the islands are large, but most of them are small. 

The Irish Free State, Canada, Newfoundland, Australia, New Zealand, and South

Africa are almost independent of British control, and together with the United Kingdom are called the British Commonwealth of Nations.

AMERICA 

A. — Nearly half of this hemisphere is land.

Great Britain and the Land Hemisphere. 

On this page there are outline maps of two hemispheres. One shows the half of our earth that has the greatest proportion of land. 

It is called the Land Hemisphere. The other shows the half of the earth with the greatest proportion of water surface. It is called the Water Hemisphere. 

Notice that the British Isles are at the center of the Land Hemisphere. They are on the eastern edge of the north Atlantic Ocean the ocean over which most of the world's commerce moves. East of these islands is the mainland of Europe. West of them, across the Atlantic, is North America.

These two continents are the homes of the world's most progressive nations.

From the great ports of the British Isles and those of near-by lands more of the chief trading centers of the world can be reached in a shorter time than from any ports in any other continent. The central position of the British Isles in the Land Hemisphere has been of the greatest importance in aiding the growth of Great Britain and its expansion into the British Empire. B. 

- Most of this hemisphere is water. 

The British Empire and the Navy. - It has also been of great importance to the people of the British Isles that their homeland is separated from the mainland of the continent. All through the early history of 

Europe, different tribes and groups of people made war upon each other. Once in a while in those early days, armies and peoples from the mainland crossed the narrow seas and landed in the British Isles. 

Several of these invasions were successful, and for a time the countries from which these armies came controlled parts of the islands. Always, however, the people of the islands succeeded in again setting up their own governments. The English people were the most numerous, and their kingdom the strongest, so that in time they gained control also over Wales and Ireland. Finally, in 1707, the kingdoms of England and Scotland were united in the one kingdom of 

Great Britain.

In early times the English built many boats for fishing, for they had discovered that fish in great numbers could be caught in the shallow waters of the North Sea

A. 

Courtesy Travel Association of Great Britain & Ireland, N. Y. Cuy

Fishing vessels in port on the south coast of England. and other near-by waters. Gradually the fishing boats went farther and farther to sea, and the fishermen became brave and skillful sailors. The English built ships also to use in protecting their country from enemies, and manned them by sailors from the fishing fleet.

The English, later the British, navy has for many years been the largest and most powerful navy in the world. It has been nearly nine hundred years since an enemy army has been landed on the shores of 

Great Britain.

One great reason for the building of such a navy was the growth of the British Empire. 

When the age of exploration began, with the discovery of the New World by Columbus, England took part with other nations. other nations.

During the course of many years, new lands were found, claimed for England or for Great Britain, and explored and settled by people from the British Isles. Many of these lands now form parts of the British Empire.

With this expansion of territory, the settlers in the new lands called more and more upon the mother country for manufactured goods, and offered raw materials in exchange. Trade increased, and ships to carry goods and passengers were built in constantly increasing numbers. More and more of the people in Great Britain gave their attention to mining, manufacturing, shipbuilding, and commerce instead of to agriculture. 

Soon there was not enough food raised in the British Isles to feed the people. Much food had to be purchased in other lands, along with raw materials for mills and factories. These imports were paid for with manufactured goods and by carrying goods across the oceans for other people. 

To protect the distant lands of the British

Empire and the ships carrying on a worldwide trade, the government of Great Britain kept increasing its navy. But during the 

World War even this navy was not large enough to protect all food and supply ships, and many of them were sunk by enemy submarines. For a time there was danger that the people of the British Isles would be short of food. But with the help of friendly nations and the building of many ships, actual hunger was prevented. The invention of the airplane has made possible a new method of attack upon these islands, and has made necessary also a new kind of defense.

An Indented Coast Line and Good Har bors. -At the time western Europe was high enough above sea level so that the continental shelf was dry land, rivers flowed across it. When, later, this west-coast region sank to its present position, some of the tributary streams of old river systems were left as independent rivers flowing into the surrounding seas. Their lower valleys were drowned, like the drowned valley of the Hudson River, about which you learned last year. This sinking of the land and the drowning of river valleys gave the British Isles their present irregular and deeply indented coast line.

EUROPE 

A. 

Courtesy White Star Line 

The harbor of Southampton, on the southern coast of England, has up-to-date equipment and improvements. 

Point out Southampton on the map. In this picture you see a huge transatlantic liner lifted out of the water, in a floating drydock, for cleaning and repairs. At the right is a pier, with cranes for loading and unloading ships. 

The lower courses of some of the rivers became broad estuaries with channels deep enough for ships to sail a long distance inland. An ocean steamer going up the

Thames about 50 miles to London is almost in the center of southern England. Yet one that goes up the Hudson River 150 miles to the port of Albany has just entered the edge of our continent. Since much larger ocean liners have been built in recent years, it has been necessary to dredge the channels of some of the streams and to build docks and basins and other harbor works.

The outflowing tides in river estuaries have helped to keep them clear of sediment.

The larger ships also take advantage of the deeper water at high tide in getting in and out of the harbors. Ships moving with the tide are helped by its movement. Many excellent natural harbors along the western coasts of Scotland and Ireland have little value for commerce because the regions they might serve are small or unproductive. 

No part of the British Isles is more than seventy miles from a seaport, and this nearness to the sea has helped greatly in keeping down the cost of shipping goods to foreign markets. There are no long and expensive railroad journeys for either exports or imports between seaports and the places where goods are manufactured or used. In our own country, it is sometimes necessary to haul goods by rail from 500 to 2000 miles to get them to ports for shipment to other lands. This extra cost of transportation of course increases the price at which the goods must be sold. 

Surface. You have learned that there are no great mountains in the British Isles (page 77). The Highlands of Scotland are in the central and northern parts of that country and they are the highest and roughest part of the islands. This highland area is a region of valleys and ridges having a general northeast-southwest direction. It is cut into two sections by a trench-like valley.

A. - Valley and pass in the mountains of northern Wales. 

Some of the mountains in Wales are bare like these; others are covered with forests. 

Through this valley the Caledonian Canal was built to connect the Firth of Lorne and Moray Firth. In southern Scotland there is a hilly region known as the Southern Uplands, but it is not so high or rough as the highlands of the north. Between these highland areas is the Scottish lowland, deeply indented by the Firth of Forth on the east, and the Firth of Clyde on the west. There is also a coastal lowland along the North Sea.

The Pennine Chain is a range of low mountains running north and south through the middle of northern England. In northwest

England is a small highland area with a number of beautiful lakes - the English lake country famous in literature and art. tral and southeastern England is a lowland, flat in some parts and hilly in others. A part of the lowland between the Humber River and the Wash is so low that banks are built to keep out the sea, and the area is drained by pumping. Wales is a region of low Cen- mountains and many valleys (A). Ireland has a central plain surrounded by a rim of low mountains much broken in places so as to give easy communication with the sea. 

The great ice sheet that once covered so large a part of Europe (map, page 101) covered most of the British Isles. In parts of both the larger islands there are beautiful lakes formed by glacial action, as were many of the lakes in New York state and in New England.

The highlands of Scotland are famous in song and story. From the abundance of vegetation shown here what can you tell about the rainfall? Sheep raising is an important industry in Scotland. 

Climate. Do you remember about the oceanic climate of the western part of Europe? Read again about the westerly winds and the influence of the Gulf Stream Drift (page 79). These westerly winds blow across the British Isles, on their way to the mainland of the continent, and give the islands a very oceanic climate. They blow against the mountains in Ireland and Great Britain, and the annual rainfall on the western slopes varies from 60 to 70 inches. Its distribution between the summer and winter seasons is shown on the maps on page 79. 

The rainfall decreases in amount from north to south, and from west to east.

Ireland has so much rain and so much bright green grass that it has been given the name of the Emerald Isle. In the western highlands of Wales, England, and Scotland also, because of the heavy rainfall, grass grows abundantly. In the Highlands of 

Scotland, especially, the rains are so frequent and heavy that agriculture is not profitable, but there are fine pasture lands and many of the people are shepherds (A). There is so little snow, even in the winter time, that the flocks can be pastured out of doors during the greater part of that season. In eastern 

England, the rainfall is only about 25 inches a year; and yet the fields and gardens are green and fresh throughout the summer because there is no great heat to dry the ground and wither the plants. 

In winter the winds, warmed in their passage over the Gulf Stream Drift, never let the British Isles get very cold. The weather may at times be damp and chilly, but the temperature seldom sinks below freezing, and there is not much snow. When snow falls, it does not last long. In summer the ocean is cooler than the land, and the westerly winds bring coolness to the land. American visitors to England find the midsummer days cool enough to be very comfortable, though the English people may call them hot.

Compare the climate of the British Isles with that of western North America and that of eastern North America in the same latitude. Do you remember about the climate of the Pacific coast of Canada? It is mild

because of the westerly winds from the Pacific Ocean, as the climate of the British Isles is made mild by westerly winds from the Atlantic Ocean. What about eastern

Canada and Labrador, north of the Gulf of 

St. Lawrence? These lands are cold, barren, rocky, and with few people except in fishing settlements along the coast. There is no agriculture and there are no flocks. 

Snow and ice cover the highlands. What makes the difference? You have learned how the climate of the British Isles is influenced by the winds from the sea. In Labrador, the winter winds come from the cold lands of interior North America, and those that come from the sea cross the cold waters of the Labrador Current. 

Why Great Britain Has Grown in Power and Population. Three main causes led to the prosperity of the people of the British Isles and their increase in numbers. These are: (1) the invention of the steam engine, a supply of coal to run it, and the invention of steam-driven machinery to take the place of hand-worked machines in the homes of the people; (2) the discovery and settlement of new lands where manufactured goods were needed, and from which raw materials could be obtained; and (3) the building of many ships in which to carry on world trade. 

Coal and Iron. Among the mineral resources of the British Isles, coal is of first importance; but the deposits of iron ore, once much larger, are still of great value. 

One third of the coal of Europe is in Great

Britain, and even at the rate at which it is now being used, the supply should last for many hundreds of years. Study the map of the coal regions of Great Britain on this page. 

There are three principal producing districts. One of these is in the Scottish lowlands, a second is in central and northern England on both sides of the Pennine Chain, and a third is in southern Wales.

Much of it is carried in British ships to France, Italy, Argentina, and other foreign countries. 

Much is sent also to coaling stations all over the world where steamers may stop for coal on long trips. Such coaling stations are necessary because even the largest ships carry only coal enough to go a few thousand miles. miles. Welsh coal is also used at Swansea and other places to smelt imported ores.

The coal district of central and northern England is the largest of the three districts. 

One of the great fields is about Newcastle, on the Tyne. This city not only exports much coal, but uses much in making iron and steel. 

Here, too, are built some of the largest steel ships that cross the oceans.

Another great coal field is in Yorkshire, east of the Pennine Chain. This field supplies coal for the iron and woolen industries of Sheffield, Leeds, and many other cities.

Sheffield has made fine steel for hundreds of years, including the best pocket knives, shears, and other kinds of cutlery. 

Coal fields are found in central England near Birmingham. The special industry of this city is the working of iron. Here and in the neighboring towns the coal pits, their piles of waste, and the black smoke from many chimneys have given the neighborhood the name of "black country." It is very different from the clean and quiet parts of rural England which lie around it. Birmingham will be interesting to you because one of our large southern cities was named after it. 

This was because our Birmingham in Alabama is also an iron and steel city. It has coal, iron ore, and limestone near by, as Birmingham in England once had. Unfortunately, although there is still plenty of coal and limestone, and some iron ore, to supply the blast furnaces and steel mills of Great Britain, much of the best iron ore has been used up. Iron ore is now imported from

Sweden, Spain, and other countries. It pays to do this because coal is plentiful and cheap in Great Britain, and low ocean freight rates make it possible to bring in the better ores at no great cost. You will remember that iron ore is carried long distances in our own country. The ore from Lake Superior mines is shipped down the Great Lakes to smelters at Cleveland, Erie, Lackawanna, and Pittsburgh. 

There is one other important coal field in England. It is in the county of Lancashire, west of the Pennine Chain in the region about Liverpool, the great port, and Manchester, the chief center of the cotton industry. 

With what remains of its own iron ores, and with the iron ores and pig iron that it imports, Great Britain keeps its great iron and steel industry going. Modern building, manufacturing, and transportation, both by land and by sea, require the use of iron and steel in great quantities. Great Britain uses its iron and steel for the manufacture of ships, tools, railroad equipment, and machinery; and exports much in these forms. Coal and iron have done much to make Great Britain the greatest manufacturing nation of the world, even in industries for which raw materials must be imported. It is the lack of either coal or iron, or both, in most of the South American countries that has prevented the development of great iron and steel industries in that continent. Which of these two minerals is found in large quantities in Brazil and Chile?
