The Woolen Industry. From very early times the people of the British Isles have made the wool of their sheep into yarn and cloth. Years ago, the spinning and weaving were done in the homes of farmers, and every household had its spinning wheel and loom. 

All of the work was done by hand. Later, machinery was invented to do this work, and mills and factories were built. Some of the people became spinners or weavers and spent all of their time at this work. As the machinery was operated by water power, the factories were located on the edges of the highlands of both England and Scotland, where the streams furnished the necessary water power. These factories were therefore also near the sheep pastures from which their raw material came.

With the invention of the steam engine, the factories, grown much larger and needing more power, moved to the coal regions, where the largest ones are now found. Here they are still near the sheep pastures on the drier eastern slopes of the Pennine Chain. 

Some skillful weavers, driven out of their own country on the mainland of Europe, came to England to settle. They helped the mills to improve the quality of the manufactured goods and build up the industry. 

Long ago the fine quality of British woolen goods created so great a demand that the manufacturers were forced to import wool from other countries. More than three fourths of their supply is now imported, chiefly from Australia, South Africa, and 

Argentina. Fine woolen goods from Great

Britain are sold in our stores and tailor shops. One kind is called "worsted." It took its name from a village in eastern England. Another kind called "tweed" is made at several places in the lowlands of 

Scotland. Broadcloths, cashmeres, merinos, and serges also are made of wool, as are many carpets and rugs. The fleece from a sheep is divided into many parts so as to get the length and fineness of fiber needed for the different kinds of cloth or other articles that are to be made. On the map, page 82, find Leeds. It is a city of almost a half million people, and the center of British woolen manufacture. Find Bradford, Halifax, and

Huddersfield, all near at hand, and all with woolen factories. Leicester, farther south, makes woolen hosiery. 

Cotton Manufacture. The manufacture of cotton goods is the largest industry in Great Britain, yet every fiber of the raw cotton must be imported. The plant requires a long growing season with many long, hot, sunny days-climatic conditions not found in the British Isles.

Most of the world's cotton is grown in the United States, India, China, and Egypt. In what countries of South America does it grow? The United States supplies most of the cotton for British mills, though much comes from Egypt and India. It is brought by sea to Liverpool, and thence by rail or ship canal to the manufacturing, towns in 

Lancashire, west of the Pennine Chain.

Manchester is the chief city in the cottonmanufacturing district, and the business center of the cotton industry.

EUROPE 

The city of Manchester dug a ship canal, thirty-five and a half miles long and twentyeight feet deep, from the city to the sea. 

On it ocean freighters take their cargoes directly to Manchester or Salford without stopping at Liverpool. Bolton, Blackburn, and Preston are other cotton-manufacturing centers of this district. In Nottingham, south of the Pennines, cotton hosiery and lace are made.

Taken as a whole, the region around Manchester and Liverpool is the greatest cottonmanufacturing district in the world. Scattered in the near-by cities and towns are mills for spinning the fiber, mills for weaving the cloth, mills for dyeing, and mills for finishing the cloth. Hundreds of thousands of people find employment in these mills. 

Ninety per cent of the British cotton goods are made there.

There are several reasons for the greatness of the industry in this region. (1) Englishmen invented the machinery that was needed. More than a hundred years ago two men, named Hargreaves and 

Arkwright, invented machines for spinning cotton. These machines made it possible for laborers to make more and better goods than before, and thus lowered their cost. 

At first the workmen were very angry over these inventions. They were afraid that the machines would make it possible for a few men to do all the work, and that many men would have no work to do. But the use of cotton goods increased so rapidly in all parts of the world that soon many more men were needed than before. (2) Lancashire is in the rainy part of western England. In spinning and weaving, the cotton threads work best and are least likely to break when the air is moist. (3) The manufacturing region is favorably located for ocean trade. The estuary of the 

Mersey allows ships to reach Liverpool, and the ship canal carries them to Manchester. 

Cotton is thus brought close to the mills by the cheapest of all methods of transportation over long distances. In the same way, the shipment of finished goods to foreign markets is made cheaper also. (4) The energy and business ability of the British people have led to the growth of trade with all parts of the world. Especially favorable trade agreements have been made between the mother country and the dominions; but the fine quality of the best 

British cotton goods makes it possible to sell them even in the United States, where so much cotton is grown and manufactured.

Pastures and Plowland. You 

You have learned that British farmers raise only a part of the food needed by the British people (page 85). This is not because of any lack of industry or care on the part of the British farmer. It is because the population of 

Great Britain is so large, and because there are many large estates where only a small part of the land is under cultivation. In the south and east of England, where the rainfall is least abundant (maps, page 79) and the winters cool, much wheat is grown. 

The fields yield an average of 32 bushels an acre, about twice the average yield in the United States. Yet the greater part of the wheat and wheat flour used in Great Britain must be imported from the United States, Canada, Argentina, and other lands.

In the more moist parts of England and in the Scottish lowlands, barley, oats, and many potatoes are raised. These crops will grow and ripen in a cool, moist climate where wheat will not. Large quantities of garden vegetables also are raised in various parts of the country. Corn is not grown, because the summers are too cool. Nowhere in 

Great Britain do you see silos. To take the place of the juicy corn which keeps our dairy cattle in such good condition during the winter, the British farmer uses root crops such as turnips and mangels (a kind of beet).

A large part of the rougher and more rainy sections of the island is used for meadows and pastures. Cattle, sheep, horses, and hogs are raised, and many fine animals are exported. The dairy industry is large, but not enough butter and cheese are produced to supply the needs of the population, and some must be imported. Young cattle from

Ireland are fattened in English pastures. 

British mutton is of excellent quality, but a large part of the mutton supply is imported.

Seaports and Trade. - 

Great Britain usually has a larger foreign commerce than any other country. However, since Great Britain is small and has less than half the population of of the United

States, its internal or home trade is much less than ours. 

Most of the British foreign trade is carried in British ships; and these, as well as many ships for other countries, are built in the shipyards of 

Great Britain. Newcastle has the largest shipyards of England, but Glasgow, together with the bank of the lower Clyde, is one of the world's chief shipbuilding districts. Hull is another shipbuilding center.

Margate is a resort on the North Sea, two hours by rail from London. 

At the foot of the chalk cliffs along the beach are many tiny dressing rooms. 

More land is being used for crops in recent years. Some of the great estates, where much of the land was formerly used for meadow land, for pastures, and for hunting, are being sold and broken up into small farms. In agricultural regions of small farms, the fields are very carefully cultivated. 

The roads are narrow and winding, and roads, fields, and railroads are commonly bordered by neat hedges. Many trees are grown in the meadows and pastures, and buildings and walls are covered with the beautiful green English ivy. The soft green of grass and trees, and the well-kept fields and roads, make the English countryside rural England - look like a great park. 

Fishing. - In the shallow waters surrounding the British Isles, and in more distant waters, fishing has become an important British industry. Cod, haddock, mackerel, and herring are taken in great numbers. 

About 60,000 men from Great Britain are engaged in this business. Many seaports share in the industry, though much of it has been centered at a few large ports on the North Sea. Among these are Hull, Grimsby, and London in England, and Aberdeen in Great Britain has an irregular coast line, with many bays and tidal rivers or estuaries, and fine harbors. and fine harbors. Every British citizen thinks much about London and talks about "going up to London." This is because the city is so great and the land so small. London has nearly one fifth of the population of Great Britain. 

It leads all other cities in commerce. Its docks stretch down the Thames more than twenty miles, and the cargoes unloaded there come from all parts of the world. They are brought there, not only for use in Great Britain, but to be reshipped to many other ports, for Great Britain is a great trading nation and London a great center of world trade.

The largest and most famous of the British universities, Oxford and Cambridge, are only a short journey from London. Government of Great Britain. The form of government in Great Britain is now such that the people have almost entire control, while the king and the nobles have little power. The House of Commons is made up of members elected by the people and is the chief lawmaking body. The House of 

Lords is composed of members of the nobility and the bishops of the established church the Church of England. The two houses form the Parliament of the kingdom. The king appoints as Premier the leader of the party in power in the House of Commons, and the Premier selects a cabinet or ministry of leading statesmen for the management of the departments of government.

Irish Free State, and Northern Ireland.

Most of the people of Ireland have long objected to English rule. In 1922 the control of the island was divided. The smaller part, Northern Ireland, remained with Great Britain in the United Kingdom, but the rest of the island was formed into the Irish Free State, with a government like that of Canada. 

Taken as a whole, Ireland has low mountains on its borders, but in the central part there are low plains, suitable for meadows, pastures, and some crops. Some of the best farming land is in Northern Ireland, where crops of hay, oats, barley, flax, potatoes, and roots are large, and fine grass seed is grown. 

Northern Ireland is the chief flax-growing region of the island because the plant thrives in a cool climate. In preparing the flax the plants are pulled, dried, and the seeds removed. They are then put into pools of soft water to loosen the fibers. This makes it possible to comb out the fibers and get them ready for weaving. Much fiber goes to Belfast, where it is made into linen. The best Irish linens are very beautiful and highpriced. Belfast is noted also for its great shipyards, where large ocean ships are built. 

The Irish Free State is largely an area of grass land, with grazing and dairying as. the chief industries. It is this region that furnishes the young cattle sent to England to be fattened. There is some farming in the southern section of the country, but much of the land has been made less productive by poor farming methods, and the crops are not large. In the western part, some bog lands have been drained and some mountain lands have been terraced.

There is but little coal in Ireland, and therefore but little manufacturing. In the swampy lands, of which there are many in the low-lying parts of this island where the rainfall is heavy, mosses and other plants have grown freely. As the country is never hot or dry, the moisture of the swamps prevents decay of these plants, and in time they form a brownish vegetable substance called peat. This peat when cut out in blocks and thoroughly dried burns well and is used in the homes as a fuel.

Dublin is the chief city of the Irish Free State and has become an important shipbuilding and brewing center. In recent years it has grown rapidly in size, while the country districts have been slowly losing in population. 

Distribution of Population. The distribution of population in the British Isles is largely the result of the industries that have grown up within these islands. The industries are in part the result of natural resources and natural conditions and in part the result of the energy, enterprise, and business ability of the people. 

There are highlands where it is too cold, too wet, or too rough for agriculture, and where there are no minerals to be mined, and no manufactures. Such lands are used for grazing, and their population is small because only a few people can earn a living there. There are lowlands that are swampy or where the soil is thin and stony; they also can support only a few people. In

agricultural and dairying regions the population is more dense because more people are needed to plant, tend, and harvest the crops, and to care for the domestic animals. 

Most of the people of the islands, however, have gathered into the towns and cities that have grown up around the mines, the mills, and the seaports. Workers must be able to go quickly between their homes and the places where they work. England especially has become a land of cities. 

You must remember also that many of the sons of British people went out to the far places of the earth where their energy and abilities have created the British Empire. In all parts of this empire, and in other lands, you find them owning and operating farms, ranches, mines, and business enterprises, building the cities, and organizing the governments. Many are to be found in Canada, Australia, and South Africa.

It is not easy to explain why one race or group of people is progressive and another is not. But it is probable that, in a large measure, the abilities of the English, Scotch, Welsh, and Irish peoples are due to the fact that each is a mixture of several of the races of northern Europe. It is also probable that the climate of the homeland gave to all of these peoples great energy, and made them willing to work and eager to undertake vast enterprises. Many

In the early days of the New World, Englishmen founded a number of colonies later included in the United States. The earliest of these were Virginia and Plymouth. 

English, Scotch, Irish, and Welsh people came to the colonies, or later to the United States, in order to have religious freedom, or a better opportunity to earn a living. All these races are sturdy, resourceful, independent, and industrious. They have been leaders in science and invention; in literature and art; and in government. The 

English language is spoken by more people than any other tongue.

THE SCANDINAVIAN PENINSULA

THE SCANDINAVIAN PENINSULA 

You have already learned that the land of western Europe at one time stood at a higher level (page 85). The rivers of that ancient day had cut many deep and narrow valleys in the old hard rocks of the Scandinavian Peninsula. The glacial ice filled these river valleys and by its movement widened and deepened them. The soils were moved, the rocks worn, bowlders scattered, and lakes formed, as in those parts of New York state over which the ice sheet passed. In the parts of southern Europe not covered by the ice sheet there are few lakes.

The Scandinavian Peninsula is in the northwestern part of the continent of Europe (map, page 74). It lies between 55° and 72° north latitude, and has a length of about 1200 miles, in a generally northeast-southwest direction. 

This general direction is about the same as that of the British Isles and the islands between. The Northwest Highlands of Eu rope (page 77) form the backbone of the peninsula for much of its length. The main ridge of these highlands is known as the Kjölen Mountains, but it is more of a plateau than a mountain range. For much of its length it is followed by the boundary line that separates Norway and Sweden, the two countries into which the peninsula is divided. 

When the land finally sank, the ocean waters covered much of the western coast of the peninsula and flooded the valleys that reached back into it. Off the western coast of 

Norway the tops of old mountain ranges show as islands. There are about 150,000 of these islands, of which those in the Lofoten group are the largest. This coast is like that of 

British Columbia, the Panhandle of Alaska, and southern Chile. Here also, as in the other regions just mentioned, there are the quiet and protected waters of an inland The kingdom of Norway is on the western side of the peninsula. It has its greatest width in the south, becomes narrower farther north, and widens again toward its northern end. The kingdom of Sweden is in the eastern part of the peninsula and is much larger than Norway.

The old block of land that forms the penin- | (page 79). The westerly winds that blow sula is tipped so that its steep slope is toward the west and its longer and gentler slope toward the east. The ancient river valleys that were drowned as the land sank in the west are the beautiful fiords that reach back into the land, some for more than a hundred miles. Along many of them steep rock walls rise from the water with no bordering lowland and no roads. Here and there streams flowing into these fiords have made little deltas on which small villages have been built. 

Quiet waters showing mirrored clouds, cliffs, forested slopes, and plunging waterfalls make a trip through the inland passage or in and out of the fiords one of great beauty.

The Norwegians find the easiest route from the sea into the interior of much of their country by way of the fiords. In many of them the water at the entrance is about 600 feet deep, but farther inland it may have a depth of from 2000 to 4000 feet. If this land should rise again, high enough to shut out the ocean, the fiords would become long, deep, winding lakes. Sweden has many streams; but they are less rapid than those of Norway, because of the gentler slope of the land. Notice that they are roughly parallel to each other and that the main streams are about the same length and flow generally toward the southeast. The boundary line between Norway and Sweden follows the watershed that separates the drainage systems of the two countries. The ice sheet has greatly changed the surface. Valleys have been scooped out, and streams left with waterfalls and rapids or with obstructions that have caused lakes. 

The Swedish coast line is regular, with wide river mouths and good harbors. The chief lowlands of the peninsula are in the south, but include also much of eastern Sweden along the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Bothnia. Climate. 

You will remember reading about the Gulf Stream Drift of the North 

Atlantic Ocean, west of the British Isles over it bring the temperature of its waters to the coast of Norway. As a result, the coast and western-facing slopes of Norway, though cool in summer, are much warmer in winter than lands in the same latitude on the other side of the ocean.

Hammerfest, a small town on an island off the northwest coast of Norway, is the most northerly town in Europe, but its harbor is ice-free the year round. A little farther south, on another of the west coast islands the climate is favorable enough so Tromsö has grown to be a city of more than 10,000 inhabitants. These two places are near the parallel of 70° north latitude. Find where this parallel crosses Greenland and Baffin Island, in North America, and notice the difference in conditions. Greenland is almost entirely covered with ice and Baffin Island is barren, almost without inhabitants, and bordered by ice-covered seas. On the eastern, or 

Swedish side of the Scandinavian highlands, the influence of the ocean is felt much less. 

The summers are hotter and the winters colder than in the same latitudes in Norway. In Norway has a heavy rainfall which increases with an increase of elevation. some parts of the highland it is as much as 

200 inches a year. In northern Sweden the rainfall averages only about 20 inches a year. Fortunately this is sufficient for agriculture because evaporation is less rapid than it would be in regions having higher temperatures. Study the maps on pages 78 and 79. 

The winter temperature along the Swedish coast is so much lower than that along the coast of Norway that the Swedish harbors are frozen for weeks at a time. The rivers are frozen in winter, thus preventing their use for navigation, for floating logs, or for power. Yet conditions are better than in some corresponding latitudes in North America. There is a large enough population across the Baltic from Stockholm to make it profitable to use ice-crushing ships in winter

Logs are floated down many rivers in Sweden as they are in our country. The lumbermen are skillful in keeping the logs from forming jams and in breaking up jams when they are formed. so that commerce may be carried on. In the 

Hudson Bay district of North America, on the contrary, there is very little population. The 

Forests. The forests of the Scandinavian 

Peninsula cover about one third of its surface, but the Swedish forests are much more extensive than those of Norway. chief Norwegian forests are near Trondheim on the west and in the drainage area of the Skagerrak in the southeast. In Sweden the forests cover the rougher and higher lands. The chief lumbering region is in the central and southern parts of the country. 

Both Norway and Sweden have laws, loyally lived up to, to prevent the wasteful cutting of timber and requiring the replanting of cut-over areas. With such care the forests will never be destroyed.

Much timber is cut for lumber and many of the houses are built of wood, especially in the smaller towns. In recent years more and more of the trees cut have been used in the manufacture of wood pulp and paper. Large mills for these industries have been built near the forest regions, and there are many sawmills and match factories.

Fishing. Two of the very important

Norwegian industries are connected with the The first of these is fishing. The second is the operation of cargo boats engaged in world commerce. Thousands of fishing boats visit the Lofoten Island district every winter, when many of the summer farmers turn to fishing for winter work. Fish can be caught at all times during the year, as these waters are ice-free. South of these islands are famous cod fisheries- the most important fisheries along the Norwegian coast. 

Farther south, herring are caught, and still farther south, mackerel. Salmon are caught in the fiords. The fishing boats follow the migration of the fish, and the fishermen may be away from home for weeks at a time. 

Find Bergen on the map. This city is the center of the fishing industry, and here many fish are prepared for export. Some are sent 

Some are sent to near-by countries as fresh fish. Cod are salted and dried (A). Herring and salmon are smoked or prepared in other ways, and great quantities of fish are canned, especially the small fish that are sold as sardines. 

The whale fisheries in the Arctic, and especially in the Antarctic, have become an important part of the Norwegian fishing industry. In recent years they have equaled in value all of the other fisheries combined. 

Whale oil, obtained from the fat or blubber, is the most valuable product. It is used in lamps, for making soap, and for dressing leather. Some is prepared to be used in place of other fats in foods. The best of the whale meat is good food; much is eaten fresh, and much is canned. 

The Swedish fisheries are much less important than those of Norway. Few fish are found in the Gulf of Bothnia, and not many in the Baltic Sea, although some are caught along the coast. The chief Swedish fishing grounds are near the west coast in the Kattegat. 

Mineral Resources. There is some coal in the peninsula but the amount is small and the quality is poor. the quality is poor. The most valuable mineral resource is the iron ore found in both Norway and Sweden. The Swedish deposits are large and of great richness. 

These ores and iron made from them-especially from the deposits in the central part of the country-have long been exported. 

When you were studying the British Isles,

Courtesy Norwegian Government Railways, N. Y. City

A. - Hydroelectric power plant in southern Norway. Water under pressure comes to it down the hill in eight large pipes. you learned that both ore and iron are imported into Great Britain from Sweden. 

Steel made from these ores is of such fine quality that it has become famous and is extensively used in the manufacture of cutlery, both in Sweden and at Sheffield in England. Some of the ore from this central region of Sweden is smelted by the use of charcoal (wood that has been half burned) and experiments are being made with electric furnaces. High-grade coal is also imported for this use. 

The ore deposits of northern Sweden are in the Lapland area and are largely exported a part from the Baltic port of Luleå, and a part from Narvik in Norway (map, page 100). 

The two ports and the mines are connected by an electric railroad, but most of the ore is shipped through Narvik, a port that is icefree, rather than through Luleå, a port that is closed by ice for half of each year. These 

Lapland deposits are believed to be the largest high-grade iron ore reserves in the world. 

Water Power and Its Use. - Both Norway and Sweden have an abundance of water power in their many falls and rapids. Until very recently, practically all of this energy went to waste. Mills and factories that could make use of it were few and small. 

Now, however, some of this vast water power is being changed into electric power in hydroelectric plants, in the same way as it is being done in other parts of the world. In both 

Norway and Sweden many electric generating stations have been built (A), although as yet only a small fraction of the available power is being used.

The electricity is used for lighting and heating in city and country, for running the machinery of mills and factories, for operating trains and street cars, for manufacturing nitrates, and to some extent for smelting. 

Electric power is cheap and plentiful, and is helping in the development of industries in which power is necessary in a land where there is no petroleum and little coal. The fact that Swedish rivers have only a small flow in the coldest part of each year makes it necessary for some of the plants to use imported coal if they are to operate all the year.

Agriculture and Grazing. Almost half of the people of Scandinavia spend at least a part of their time in farming, although many of them turn to lumbering, mining, or fishing for winter industries. The most densely settled farming regions are the plains in the southern and eastern parts of the peninsula. 

Oats, barley, rye, potatoes, sugar beets, and some wheat are raised. All of these are crops suited to a cool climate, and, as you would expect, more of them are grown in Sweden than in Norway.

In both countries the chief use of the land is for meadows and pastures. There are meadows in the lowlands, in small fields in valley bottoms, and on hillsides. The grass of the meadows when cut for hay must be carefully hung on fences and trellises to keep it off the damp ground, so it will cure without molding. The pastures, hay, and some small root crops are used for cattle and other animals, and a prosperous dairying industry has grown up in both countries. In Norway, especially, cattle are driven to highland pastures for summer feeding, where some members of the farmer's household look after the cattle and make the butter and cheese.

There are places where a wire rope can be stretched between mountain pastures and the valley farm, on which the butter and cheese can be lowered and supplies drawn up. 

Butter, cheese, and condensed milk are exported, but much food must also be imported. Sheep are raised in both Norway and Sweden. 

On the treeless tundras of northern Norway and Sweden live a group of people whose ancestors came from Asia many centuries ago. They are the Lapps or Laplanders (107 A). They keep herds of reindeer and live on the flesh and milk. From the hides they also make their clothing and tents. 

Inland Routes and the Merchant Marine. 

The physical features of the peninsula are of such a character that the building of roads and railroads is difficult and very expensive. 

There are not enough people in the higher regions to make the building of either roads or railroads worth while. Railroads have been built across the peninsula only where there was some good reason for them, such as that which led to the construction of the Luleå- 

Narvik Electric Line (page 105). Another such line connects Bergen with Oslo, and goes

Other lines connect the cities of southern Sweden, and one, in the eastern part, sweeps around the northern end of the Gulf of Bothnia into 

Finland. (See map, page 100.) Keeping the roads and railroads free from snow and ice is a large item in the cost of upkeep. 

In carrying the roads and railroads from sea level on the Norwegian side to the top of the high plateau, it was necessary at times to blast out roadbeds along the sides of rocky cliffs. For the railroads, many tunnels were cut through solid rock. In some cases these tunnels are long loops that carry the railroad to a higher level where it can again be brought out along the side of a valley. 

The Göta Canal, 10 feet deep, forms part of a waterway from Göteborg to Stockholm.

It is over 50 miles in length, added to 300 miles of natural waterways. In the trip between the two cities boats must be put through 60 locks, making the trip a very slow one.

Wherever and whenever possible, the Norwegian turns to the sea to get from point to point along the coast or to make his way into the interior. Mention has already been made (page 104) of the Norwegian cargo boats. This fleet, largely engaged in foreign trade, is enormous as compared with that of most other countries. It has been said that the whole population of Norway could be sent to sea in this fleet. The revenue earned in this way helps to pay for foodstuffs and manufactures that must be imported.

Land of the Midnight Sun. - The cool summer climate, and the beauties of the fiords and islands along the Norwegian coast, have made a summer trip to Norway popular with many tourists. Sweden is also a pleasant land to visit, and good hotels and courteous treatment, as well as lovely scenery, help to make a visit an interesting holiday.

Stockholm is sometimes called the "Venice of the North," because there are several waterways through it. It has also many parks and gardens. The larger building in the center of this picture is the royal palace. you can. 

There is one trip you should all take when

It is to the North Cape, the northernmost point of one of the islands off the northern coast of Norway. This cape is not quite the most northerly point of Europe as many people think, but it is interesting to visit in the season of the "midnight sun."

For three months in the summer the sun shines continuously in the latitude of North 

Cape. You can see the sun shining continuously during midsummer from any place north of the Arctic Circle, for a longer or a shorter period, depending on how far north of the circle you are. At the circle itself it will be for nearly forty-eight hours; at the 

North Pole for six months. So many tourists visit northern Norway to see the midnight sun that it has become known as the "Land of the Midnight Sun." 

Cities. You will naturally expect to find the largest cities of the Scandinavian

Peninsula in its southern and most densely settled part. And so they are. The largest three are Stockholm, Göteborg, and Oslo all three of them near the parallel of 60° north latitude. Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, is a beautiful city on the shores of the Baltic 

Sea (A). It carries on trade with other countries even during the winter, although it is necessary to use ice-breaking ships to keep the harbors open. Göteborg is the port of western Sweden and is the center of the fishing industry of that country. 

Oslo is the capital of Norway. It has an attractive seaside location and is the chief seaport of Norway. 1 

The People. The area of the Scandi navian Peninsula is about two and a half times that of the British Isles, but it has less than one fifth as many people. From what you have learned about the peninsula and its resources you can understand why this is so. 

The people of this northland are brave and strong and hard-working, and gifted with great abilities. A nation of sailors is a nation of courageous and venturesome people, and

Swedish farmers in a hayfield. The women are wearing their native costumes, with gayly colored neckerchiefs and aprons. men from both Norway and Sweden have followed the sea. Among the great explorers of our modern times are Roald Amundsen, a Norwegian, and Sven Hedin, a Swede. 

Winning a living from the fields and pastures of this northland has always called for strength, tireless care, watchfulness, and patience. So the men and women of Norway and Sweden who have come to our country to settle on the farm lands of the North Central States have brought these qualities to their new homes. 

Scientists, inventors, writers, musicians, and artists from these countries have done their share in adding to the advancement, culture, joy, and beauty of the world.

LOWLAND COUNTRIES OF WESTERN EUROPE 

In your first study of Europe you learned about the central lowlands that extend from the Atlantic Ocean into the interior of the continent (page 77). They are narrow in the west but broad in the east. Yet it is in the west that the denser population is found, and it is there that the land is most carefully used. 

In the lowland bordering the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and connecting waters, there are three small countries - Denmark, the Netherlands, and Belgium (map, page 72). 

Using Table 1, near the end of the book, compare the areas and populations of these countries with those of other European countries. 

DENMARK 

Denmark is made up of a small peninsula and a group of islands. It is separated from the much larger Scandinavian Peninsula by the Skagerrak and the Kattegat. On the map, page 100, see how much the Kattegat varies in width at different points. 

The people of Denmark are related in blood and speech to their northern neighbors.

Their ancestors once lived in the northern peninsula. At times in the past, the people of 

Denmark and Norway and Sweden have had the same government. The Kjölen Mountains form a natural boundary between Norway and Sweden, and the Skagerrak and Kattegat separate the two peninsulas. The result has been the formation of three countries, each with its own government. 

Islands Belonging to Denmark. - The 

Danes, as well as their neighbors, were sea raiders at one period of their history. They made their way to the British Isles and more distant lands. They still own the great island of Greenland, northeast of North 

America, and the Faroe Islands, north of

Scotland. Most of Greenland is covered by an ice sheet, but a few Eskimo fishermen live along the southwest coast, and from them 

Danish traders get furs, fish, and seal oil. 

From the Faroe Islands, Denmark gets some fish, mutton, wool, and cod-liver oil. 

At one time Denmark owned Iceland (map, page 72). The people of that island have now been given full control of their land and industries, but with Denmark retaining control over its foreign affairs until 1940. Iceland is a land of ancient laya flows, glaciers, and geysers. Sheep, cattle, and horses are raised, codfish and herring are caught, and the eider duck furnishes eider down for export.

Denmark also owned some of the Virgin 

Islands in the West Indies, but in 1917 they were sold to the United States.

Industries. Look again at the map on page 101. You will see that the lowland area along the North and Baltic seas was covered by the great ice sheet, which disturbed the soils over all this region. When the ice sheet melted, there were many areas that were poorly drained and many places where the soils were made up chiefly of sand and gravel. Out of the poor soil of the 

Denmark part of this lowland area the people have made a prosperous country. Three fourths of the area is in farms and one half of the farm land is in pastures. The climate is cool, with damp, chilly winds and an annual rainfall of about 25 inches (maps, pages 78, 79). Such crops as oats, rye, barley, and vegetables are grown, rather than wheat. 

Dairying and the raising of swine and poultry are important industries in Denmark. 

Butter, an unusually excellent bacon, and millions of eggs are exported. All the animals are looked after with the greatest care. 

In this the government has helped, through schools in which young farmers are trained in the agricultural sciences. But the people | have also learned to help themselves. 110

Coöperative Marketing. - Societies have | been formed by Danish farmers who agree to maintain high standards for their products, and to follow certain rules in marketing them. 

These coöperative societies require that the products of each member be marked so that buyers will know what they are getting and from which member the products came. 

Members who do not live up to the standards and rules are first warned and then expelled from the society. They must then sell their own produce when and where they can, and usually get lower prices than they would get as members of the society. 

Manufacturing. Denmark has no coal, no oil, and no water power, and therefore no large-scale manufacturing. The Danes are very artistic, however, and make fine silverware and beautifully decorated pottery.

Most of the clay for the pottery comes from deposits in their own country. 

Copenhagen. On the map, page 100, find Copenhagen (A). It is so located that ships sailing between the North Sea and the Baltic must pass by it unless they use the Kiel Canal, which was built by Germany across the peninsula to the south. Copenhagen is Denmark's chief port and gets its name, which means "Merchant's Harbor," from the fact that merchant ships from near-by waters seek its protection during storms. Since the Kiel Canal was built fewer ships use the route by way of Copenhagen. 

Commerce. The chief exports are butter, cheese, bacon, eggs, some fish, and artistic manufactures. The Danes import food for themselves and their animals, and fertilizers and fuel. Among the cattle foods imported is cottonseed meal from the United States.

Southwest of Denmark, and facing the North Sea, is the Netherlands (map, page 112). The name means low lands,' and is a very good name for this country, as you will soon see. The country is also often called Holland, but this is really the name of only a part of it. The Netherlands is about one fourth the size of New York state, about three fourths the size of Denmark, and a little larger than Belgium (Tables 1 and 6, near end of the book). Here live several million thrifty and hard-working people. From Table 1 work out the density of population that is, the number of people there are, on the average, for each square mile of area. If you have forgotten how to do this, read again on page 77 how it can be done. You will find the Netherlands one of the most densely settled parts of the world. 

How does it compare with the United States? 

What can so many people do to earn a living?

A Delta Land. - Look carefully at Map A 

below, and notice the three large rivers that cross the Netherlands. They are the Rhine, 

the Meuse, and the Scheldt. You have learned about the deltas of the Mississippi and Nile rivers in your earlier study of geography, and you know how their deltas were formed. You saw that near their mouths, each of these rivers divides into several channels. Notice the number of parts into which the rivers of the Netherlands have divided, as shown by Map A on this page. Delta lands have been built out of earth or rock material brought downstream by the rivers. A large part of the Netherlands was formed in this way. 

Along the seaward border of delta lands you expect to find swamp land and places where the water is shallow. The swamps are flooded when the streams overflow or when water is driven inland by storms from the sea. 

To prevent the lowlands along the Mississippi from being flooded during times of high water, you remember that levees have been built. 

The Dutch, as the people of the Netherlands are called, have controlled their rivers in the same way, by building embankments called dikes. The soils of delta lands are usually fine, deep, and rich. When they are pro- NEOER=T Η SEA

The Polders and the Canals. The Dutch people have done more than build dikes to control river floods. They have inclosed 

They have inclosed swamps and parts of shallow seas with dikes high enough to keep these regions from being flooded unless a dike breaks. After the dike has been built, the inclosed space is pumped dry, leaving fields called polders. Map B on page 114 shows what polder lands, once below sea level, have been made in this way. 

Along parts of the North Sea coast it has not been necessary to build dikes. There the sand dunes, or sand hills, are high enough to keep out the sea, even during storms.

Further additions to the polders are being | made by draining the Zuider Zee. Some parts of this work have already been finished, and the work is still going on. 

The surplus water that falls on the polders as rain, or that gets there in any other way, is drained into ditches or small canals. From these it is pumped into the streams or into larger canals that join the streams. For many years nearly all the pumping was done by power furnished by long-armed windmills (A), many of which are still in use. There is no water power, and for a long time little coal was used. In recent years, however, much of the pumping has been done with steam and electric pumps. They are more powerful but less picturesque than the windmills. The larger drainage canals are at the same level as the rivers, and like them are bordered by dikes.

EUROPE 

Courtesy Netherlands Railways 

A. A narcissus field in bloom near Haarlem.

There is a great network of rivers and canals which the Dutch use for the transportation of goods (114 B). There are also roadways or pathways along the tops of the dikes, and bridges over the canals. Ship canals, large enough for ocean steamers, connect the ports of Rotterdam and Amsterdam with the North Sea, and are kept open all the year. When, during the winter, canals are frozen, the people skate from place to place and push loaded sleds over the ice.

Climate and Crops. - The prevailing winds are the westerlies. The temperature is mild in summer and cold in winter. The rainfall in the western part of the country is about 25 inches a year and inland it is less. 

How is it divided between the warmer and cooler parts of the year? (See maps, page 

79.) The crops grown are those that can best be raised under the conditions of temperature and rainfall. 

In the polders, much of the soil is too wet to be cultivated, and only grass is grown. 

The grass of the meadows and pastures is so good and so abundant that a great dairying industry is carried on. The cows are of breeds that give large quantities of milk, and they are well cared for. The Dutch people, like those of Denmark, make butter, cheese, and condensed milk for export. They also keep poultry and export an enormous quantity of eggs. On some of the polders there are market gardens in which many vegetables are raised. Not far from the city of Haarlem is a somewhat sandy region protected by dunes, in which flower bulbs are grown. One of the most beautiful sights in this little land is its fields of tulips, hyacinths, and narcissi (A), when millions of these plants are in bloom. 

The bulbs are exported to many countries. 

In the eastern and northern parts of the Netherlands the land is a little higher, the soils are not so good, and the rainfall is less than in the polders. Here potatoes and other vegetables, sugar beets, and cereals such as wheat, oats, barley, and rye are raised.

Much fertilizer is used, however, and the average yield per acre is about twice that of the United States. In places where the soil is poor and pastures not good, sheep instead of cattle are raised. In soils too poor for crops many trees are planted. 

Manufactures. The Netherlands has no deposits of iron or other metals, and no smelters, blast furnaces, or iron and steel works such as you will find in neighboring countries. Coal has been found in the southeastern part of the country, and the amount mined has rapidly increased in recent years. 

A large part of it comes from state-owned mines. This supply of fuel has led to some increase in textile manufactures, and is partly taking the place of peat, which was formerly the chief native fuel. 

Much fine butter and cheese (117 A) are made in the Netherlands. Margarine, a butter substitute, is made from imported vegetable oils. Most of the other Dutch manufactures are those requiring a high degree of skill rather than much raw material or fuel. One of these is the diamond-cutting industry of Amsterdam. Another is the manufacture of fancy cotton goods and artificial silks. Local clay deposits led long ago to the manufacture of brick, decorated tile, and pottery. Delft is one of the famous china-manufacturing cities.

A. Edam cheese for sale in the cheese market of a city in northern Holland. This cheese is made from sweet milk and is mild in flavor. Each Edam cheese is spherical in shape, and is coated red. 

Fishing. 

Fishing is carried on chiefly in the North Sea and near-by waters. Herring are caught in large numbers and many are packed for export. With other fish, also, they form an important part of the country's food supply.

Trade, Transportation, and the Merchant 

Marine. The Dutch people have always given much attention to trade and commerce, for which they are very favorably located. 

Their country, like the British Isles, is near the center of the Land Hemisphere (page 84), and it is surrounded by a number of the most progressive nations of the world. Across the 

North Sea to the west are the British Isles. 

To the southwest are Belgium and France. 

To the east is Germany. All of these countries are engaged in manufacturing and have a large foreign trade. All of them trade more or less with each other. Much of the trade between France and Germany, and much of that between Great Britain and Germany, passes through the Netherlands as a transit" or cross-country trade. It gives work to many of the Dutch people, and makes use of their ports, warehouses, boats, canals, and railroads. Many goods and passengers from other and more distant parts of the world reach Germany and countries east, across the Netherlands. Some of the goods and passengers are carried by the Dutch merchant marine. 

Three facts, especially, have led to the development of this international transit trade. 

One is that the Dutch people have studied the needs of those whose goods they handle. 

They have provided the necessary machinery for handling goods safely and quickly; established low rates for handling, storage, and freight; and have learned the languages of those with whom they deal. The second is that the Netherlands is low, and goods can easily be carried inland by either water or rail. 

The third is that the Rhine River, the great river of Germany and the greatest commercial route of central Europe, crosses the Netherlands to reach the North Sea. Rotterdam, the chief port of the Netherlands and one of the finest ports of the world, is on this river. 

Its large, well-developed, and protected harbor is reached by a great ship canal.

EUROPE 

The Hague (in Dutch, 's Gravenhage), the capital of the Netherlands, has no canal connecting it with the sea, although it is nearer the sea coast than either Amsterdam or Rotterdam. At the Hague is the Palace of Peace where the meetings of the World Court are held. This court helps to settle disputes between nations without war. 

Dutch Possessions. The Dutch took part in the exploration and settlement of new lands that followed the discovery of the New 

World. Henry Hudson was in command of a ship sent out by a Dutch trading company at the time he discovered and explored the river in New York that now bears his name.

The first settlements at the mouth of this river and along its course were made by the Dutch, but later came into the possession of the English, and some were renamed. The city we know as New York was founded by the Dutch as New Amsterdam, and Albany was founded as Fort Orange. The Dutch The Dutch made other explorations and some settlements in the West Indies, on the north coast of South America, and among the islands southeast of Asia. 

In America. Surinam, or Dutch Guiana, is in the northern part of South America, between British Guiana and French Guiana. 

It has an area more than four times as large as the Netherlands, and a population of about 150,000, mostly Negroes and Indians. 

It is a region of forests and savannas producing a small amount of sugar, cacao, coffee, rice, balata, and bauxite, and some bananas.

From one third to one half of its trade is with the United States, but some of the products are sent to the Netherlands. 

The Dutch West Indies are a group of six small islands in the Caribbean Sea off the coast of Venezuela. Curaçao is the largest. 

The products are chiefly cattle, corn, salt, and phosphates. Petroleum from the Lake 

Maracaibo basin of Venezuela is imported and refined. Trade is chiefly with the United 

States and Venezuela. 

In the East Indies. The Dutch East 

Indies are a group of islands lying between 

6° north latitude and 10° south latitude.

Their area is about fifty-five times that of the Netherlands, and over one fifth that of the United States. Their population is about eight times greater than that of the Netherlands. Turn to the political map of Asia and find the East Indies. What smaller group of islands is north of them? What continent is northwest? What continent southeast?

Find Sumatra, Java, Borneo, New Guinea, and Celebes. These are the larger islands of the group that belongs almost wholly to the 

Netherlands; but parts of Borneo and New 

Guinea belong to Great Britain.

Ages ago, much lava was poured out over the islands by the many volcanoes that were active in those days. Some volcanoes are still active, and earthquakes sometimes disturb the islands. The lavas have decayed to form soils of great richness. Heavy rainfall and rich soils combine to produce a tropical growth of great luxuriance.

At the time these islands were discovered by Europeans, spices were much used in preparing foods. As the islands produced spices, they were for a time known as the 

Spice Islands, a name now little used.

In some of the islands, especially Java and Sumatra, fertile areas near the coasts have been cleared and planted to plantation crops. 

These include sugar, rubber, coffee, tea, cacao, cinchona, and tobacco. Indigo, spices, and copra are also prepared for export, and rice is grown as a food crop for the people. 

Much of the labor on plantations is done by natives and by people from the mainland of 

Asia, working under white managers (119 A).

Here are to be found some of the largest and most productive rubber plantations in the world. Much of the raw rubber is sent directly to the United States. Java is second to Cuba in the production of sugar for export, and 99% of the world's supply of quinine comes from this same island. In the

Celebes, at Makassar, there is a mill that presses the oil from coconut meat brought from the various islands.

The Dutch trade with Java and Sumatra is of great value, but that with Borneo and New Guinea is much less, as plantation industries on these two islands have not yet been developed. They are inhabited chiefly by savage people.

Coal has been found in Borneo as well as in Java and Sumatra. The annual production of petroleum in the Dutch East Indies is about 40,000,000 barrels, and they rank next after the Malay States and Bolivia in tin production.

The products of the islands have yielded much profit to the Netherlands, through whose home markets they are distributed. 

Dutch ships have also found employment in bringing needed supplies to the islands, and in carrying the exports back home or to other parts of the world. Much has been done in developing the resources of these islands, and much more can be done. Taken as a whole, they are one of the most productive of the tropical regions of the world.

BELGIUM 

Belgium is about the size of our state of Maryland. It is smaller than Denmark or the Netherlands, but is more densely populated than either. Using Tables 1 and 6, near the end of the book, find its density of population and compare it with that of the Netherlands, that of the United States, and that of New York state. With so dense a population, there are many workmen for all industries. Most of them have developed great skill in the kind of work that they do. 

Agriculture. In the lowlands of northern

Belgium there are dikes, polders, and canals like those in the Netherlands. The soil of this delta region is fine, deep, and rich. Here many horses and cattle are raised. Butter and cheese are made. The farms are so small and so carefully cultivated that you might almost call them gardens. 

In all parts of Belgium much fertilizer is used, and the average yield of each acre cultivated is two or three times as much as in A. our own country. Among the crops grown are potatoes, sugar beets, tobacco, chicory, flowers, and the finest flax in the world. One of the large crops is the coarse beets called mangels, which are grown as food for cattle and hogs. Oats, rye, and some wheat are raised also, but not on the garden farms of the polders. Many workmen in all kinds of industries make gardens out of the small patches of land near their homes. Yet all the food that can be produced in Belgium is not enough to feed the dense population, and much that is needed must be imported. 

Harbors and Commerce. The coast line of Belgium is much shorter than that of the Netherlands, and there are few good harbors. 

A boat service is maintained between Ostend and the English port of Dover, and a ship canal connects Ostend with Calais, a port of northern France. Many years ago Bruges and Ghent, now centers of textile manufacture, were ports; but their harbors silted up, the coast line moved seaward, and they became inland cities. A ship canal has been

The chief port of Belgium is 

Antwerp, on the Scheldt River, near its mouth. Docks, basins, and wharves have been built with all necessary harbor works to care for passengers and goods (121 A). The Scheldt crosses the Netherlands to reach the North Sea, but a large Belgian ship canal has been built from Antwerp to the sea. In recent years, the trade of Antwerp has so increased that it has become one of the chief ports on the mainland of Europe. Like Amsterdam, it is a famous diamondcutting center.

The canal and railroad systems of northern Belgium center upon Antwerp; and Belgium, like the Netherlands, has much transit and foreign trade. 

Brussels. Not far from the port of

Antwerp, and connected with it by railroad, canal, and fine highways, is Brussels, the beautiful capital of Belgium. It is famous for the manufacture of carpets and rugs, and as the center through which lace, made by hand in various parts of the country, is sold. Fine gloves also are made there.

Industrial Belgium. -Southern Belgium is a region of uplands, crossed by the Meuse River and its tributary the Sambre. This upland region lies somewhat to the west of the central uplands of the continent. It contains limestone and deposits of coal and iron ore, which are the raw materials of a great iron and steel industry in the Sambre-Meuse valley. Smelters, steel mills, and factories where many kinds of articles are made from iron and steel may be seen in different parts of the valley. These industries center around the cities of Liége, Namur, and Charleroi. 

Find these cities on the map, page 112.

The products include locomotives, building hardware, automobiles, bicycles, firearms of many kinds, and hundreds of small articles. 

Much of the Belgian iron ore has been used, and ore is now brought to Belgian smelters from the near-by mines of France. 

So much of the coal of southern Belgium has been used also, that only the deeper, thinner, and more broken seams remain, and the cost of mining has increased. Fortunately there are other mines of fine coking coal farther north, which can be drawn upon. 

The Belgian deposits of zinc ore have been almost completely worked out. But zinc and copper ores are imported, smelted, and the metals used in the metal industries. 

Belgian deposits of sand and clay are used in the manufacture of glassware and pottery. 

Much plate glass is sent to the United States. for use as window glass and in automobiles.

Manufacture of Textiles and Lace. The 

The textile industry is one of the oldest of the 

Belgian manufactures. The skillful weavers who helped the English in the development of their woolen manufacturing (page 91) came from Flanders the name given to northern

Belgium. The manufacture of woolen goods is still carried on in Flanders, but most of the wool must now be imported.

Cotton goods also are manufactured in Belgium, and the moist climate makes it possible to spin and weave fine threads there as well as in Lancashire in England (page 92). All the raw cotton for this industry is imported. 

The fine flax grown in Belgium is the basis of the country's linen manufactures. But so much fiber is needed to supply the linen mills that much must also be imported from the flax-raising countries of eastern Europe. 

One of the smaller industries for which

Belgium has long been famous is the making of beautiful lace. It is largely carried on in the homes of the people. Some of the loveliest pieces are almost priceless.

Two Languages. The people of Belgium are not of one race with a language of their own, as is the case with most of the countries of Europe. At different times in the past, part or all of the country has belonged to France, and to the Netherlands. In the south and west the Belgian people are of the French race and speak French. In the north and east they are Flemings and speak Flemish - a language much like the Dutch. Merchants and business men usually speak English and German also, because they must deal with business people and travelers from 

Great Britain and Germany. 

Belgian Congo. During the time Leopold

II was king of Belgium he became interested in Africa as a result of discoveries made by the English explorer Henry M. Stanley.

With the help of a small group of Belgians, he raised some money to help Stanley in his work. 

The final result was a Belgian territory now known as Belgian Congo (see map of Africa).

It occupies most of the Congo River basin in the central part of Africa, is crossed by the Equator, and has only a very short coast line on the Atlantic. It has an area of more than 

900,000 square miles and is nearly 80 times as large as Belgium. As a region from which 

Belgian industries may sometime hope to get large amounts of tropical products and valuable minerals, it is very promising. At the present time the chief products are copper, diamonds, pitchblende (an ore from which radium is obtained), palm oil, cotton, and ivory. Coffee, cacao, and rice also are raised. 

Luxembourg. Luxembourg is a small independent country, a grand duchy, with an area of 1000 square miles. Its territory touches that of Belgium, France, and Germany (map, page 112), but in its trade it is most closely connected with Belgium. Its surface is rather rugged and it has many small farms. There are large deposits of iron ore, and about two thirds of the people are engaged in the metal industries.

LOWLAND AND PLATEAU COUNTRIES OF WESTERN EUROPE 

Of the three small lowland countries of western Europe that you have been studying, Denmark and the Netherlands are wholly within the Central Lowlands, as is also most of Belgium. As you know, these Central 

Lowlands continue east across northern Germany and occupy the eastern half of Europe between the Black Sea and the Arctic Ocean. 

West of Belgium, the Central Lowlands are found in northern France, and, beyond the 

North Sea, in southern England.

FRANCE 

France is separated from England by the English Channel, which at its narrow eastern end is connected with the North Sea by the Strait of Dover. It is across this strait, between Dover in southeastern England and 

Calais in northern France, that boats carrying passengers, mails, and goods make their quickest trips. 

Coasts. The northern coast of France is not all alike. In the east there are dune lands, in the central part there are chalk cliffs, and in the west there is the rocky coast of 

Brittany. In spite of these differences there are several good harbors in each part of this coast. Some of the smaller ports are used chiefly by fishermen, or have their chief trade with the near-by countries of Europe. 

Of the larger ones, Le Havre is the port of the French Atlantic passenger liners and for heavy freight (A); and Cherbourg is used by some of the great passenger steamers belonging to other countries.

The western or Atlantic coast of France is rocky at the north, and lower and more regular toward the south. In the north there are the ports of Brest and St. Nazaire, and farther south is that of Bordeaux. This last-named city is some distance inland, at the head of the estuary of the Garonne River. 

Along the southern part of this coast are some famous seaside resorts. 123

A.

- Monte Carlo, one of the most famous winter-resort cities in the world. Luxurious private yachts and great ocean liners on Mediterranean cruises often stop at Monte Carlo.

The southern coast line is much shorter than either of the other two. Here, near the mouth of the Rhone, is the great port of Marseille. The eastern half of this Mediterranean coast, known as the "Riviera," is so sheltered by the mountains that cold winds from the north do not reach it. It has a delightful winter climate, and visitors from many parts of the world go there to escape the colder winters of their home lands.

On the Riviera, near the Italian border, is the principality of Monaco, with an area of eight square miles. For many years its people paid no taxes, as the income from the great casino at Monte Carlo (A) more than met the expenses of government. | few passes. The many valleys on the French side of the boundary can be reached only by steep paths or rough roads. In the larger of these valleys there are some small villages as well as many farms, but in other valleys there are only very small farms and mountain pastures. Here the farmers and shepherds and their families live their lives without much care for what goes on in the rest of the world.

The Eastern Mountains. East of the 

Rhone Valley is the huge mass of the Alps, the highest mountains of Europe. On the map, page 112, trace the boundary of France from the Mediterranean Sea to the North Sea.

Its southern part crosses the main body of the Alps and the folded ridges of the Jura Mountains to the Rhine River. It follows the Rhine for some distance, but finally turns northwest to cross a part of the Central Highlands and the Central Lowlands, to the sea.

In the many centuries of European history, army after army has crossed this boundary. 

Some moved from the east toward the west. 

Others moved from the west toward the east. 

The southern part, because it is mountainous, with few valleys or low passes, has always been more easily defended. It is only in the north, where the plains of France and Belgium meet, that there are no natural barriers. 

Across these plains warring nations have many times sent their troops. It was across them that German armies moved toward Paris in the early days of the World War. 

The Auvergne Mountains. There is another highland region in France about which you should know. It is in the south-central | part of the country, west of the Rhone Valley and the valley of the Saône River, a northern tributary of the Rhone. This highland is a block of old land tipped so that its longer and gentler slope is toward the west, and its shorter and steeper slope toward the east. 

The surface of this old highland, the Auvergne Mountains or central plateau of south-central France, is rough, much cut up by streams, and partly covered by lava flows from old volcanoes. The highest peaks are what is left of old volcanic cones. On the western edge of this highland there is a limestone area with caves and subterranean streams. In some of the caves articles have Notice the many streams that flow out of this area. 

Here are the headwaters of the

Loire River and those of many of its tributaries. Here also you find tributaries of the 

Garonne River. The steep eastern slope of the highland is not crossed by any important stream. Seen from the Rhone Valley it looks like a range of low mountains, and is known as the Cevennes. 

Find the city of Lyon. It is east of the

Cevennes, where the Saône River joins the Rhone, and is a famous silk-manufacturing center. Trace the Saône to the north, and notice that the Doubs River flows into it from the east. The valley of the Doubs leads northeast and is connected with the valley of the Rhine by a low pass at Belfort. 

The Côte-d'Or. - North of the Doubs 

River there is an elevated region that connects the Auvergne Mountain area with the Vosges Mountains. It is really a region of hills and valleys, and separates the streams that flow south into the Mediterranean from those that flow north into the English Channel. Here are some of the most famous vineyards of France, and because of that it is called the Côte-d'Or the "region of gold." 

The railroad connecting the cities of the Rhone Valley with Paris crosses this region. 

The Paris Basin. - Paris lies somewhere near the center of the plains area to which the name "Paris Basin" has been given. If you will think of a nest of saucers, each one of which is smaller than the one in which it rests, you will have in mind the arrangement of the rock layers beneath this basin. Some part of each of the layers is seen as a part of the basin surface. As each layer comes to the surface it has a long slope toward Paris, and a short steeper slope away from Paris. At certain points along these steeper slopes, especially where streams have cut across them, the French built fortresses to protect their capital, Paris, from attacking armies.

EUROPE 

Around some of these fortresses much fighting occurred during the World War. Their location furnishes another example of the way in which the location of hills and plains was so important in connection with the war. The river valleys crossing these steep marginal slopes have also greatly influenced the location of the trade routes that lead toward and away from Paris. This basin contains some of the best agricultural lands in all France. 

The Lowlands of the Garonne. In southwestern France there is a hilly lowland region drained by the Garonne River. It is connected by lowlands with the Rhone-Mediterranean district on the east, and, by lowlands along the Loire, with the Paris Basin on the northeast. North of the Pyrenees there are gravelly soils of glacial origin which slope away in every direction from the mountains and form what is called a "fan delta."

Into this the streams of the region have cut deep valleys. The soils are poor and cultivation is limited. Farther west and extending to the coast is the region called the Landes. 

A hundred and fifty years ago this was a desolate area of sand dunes which the winds from the Bay of Biscay were blowing farther and farther inland. Some years ago the dunes were planted with grass having long roots, to bind the sand together; and later most of the region was planted to pine trees. 

Beautiful evergreen forests now cover large areas of this one-time waste land. From these forests much turpentine and other naval stores are obtained. France ranks next to the United States in these products. 

Climate. The climate of France as a whole is oceanic. It is much like that of the 

British Isles, although somewhat warmer because it is nearer the Equator. The prevailing winds are from the west. Throughout

France, except in valleys shut in by highlands, there is enough rain for successful agriculture. 

The heaviest rainfall is, of course, in the highlands. These include the highest parts of the peninsula of Brittany, the Auvergne 

Mountains, the northern Pyrenees, and all the highlands along the eastern border. 

The lower Rhone Valley is sheltered from the prevailing westerly winds by the Auvergne Mountains, with the result that its rainfall is less (map, page 79). In the 

Mediterranean region, especially along the Riviera, the mountains to the north shut out the cold winter winds. It is a land of flowers, and one of the most famous winter resorts in the world. Agriculture. Although the people of 

France are engaged in many industries, the greatest industry of all is agriculture. Nearly half of the area of France is in farms, and nearly half of the people are farmers. Most of the farms are small, varying in size from twenty to forty acres, and nearly all of them are cultivated by their owners. 

In our country the land belonging in one farm is usually all together, although it may be divided by fences into different parts or fields. In France, most of the farms are much smaller, and many of them are made up of several little fields, separated from each other by those of other owners. Each owner marks the boundaries of each small piece so that he can always be sure of the land that he owns. Fences are not built because along both sides of a fence there would be strips of land that could not be easily cultivated. | 

Many of the French farmers live in little Agriculture in France and in the British Isles. It is interesting to notice some of the differences between farming in France and in the British Isles. (1) Although both have an oceanic climate, France is nearer the Equator and has a longer growing season. This makes it possible to grow crops in France that cannot be grown farther north. (2) Much of the land in the British Isles is in large estates, only a part of which is rented out to be used as farm land. Most of the farms in France are small and are cultivated by their owners. (3) In the cooler and more moist regions of the British Isles, the chief farming industry is grazing, and the chief crop is grass. In 

France, nine tenths of the farm land is in crops and only one tenth is used as pasture. 

Cereals, vegetables, fruits, and nuts are the chief crops.

Wheat-producing regions of Europe. 

The Cereals and Other Crops. In a country as large as France a variety of crops will be raised because of differences in soil, in temperature, in rainfall, and in market demand. Wheat can be raised in most of lowland France (map A). The French people prefer white bread, and France raises almost enough wheat to meet their needs. About half the crop is grown in the Paris Basin. 

Other cereal crops include oats, rye, barley, and a small amount of corn. The oats grow best in the cool regions in the north. Rye and barley are raised where wheat will not grow well in the poorer soils of Brittany and the Auvergne, and corn is found chiefly in the southwest (map, page 207). Vegetables are grown in most farming regions, along the coast of Brittany, and in market gardens near the cities.

Fishing. 

France has long coast lines and is close to the fishing grounds of the North Sea as well as those in the near-by shallow waters of the Atlantic. It is natural, therefore, that some of its people about 130,000 - should turn to fishing. In the North Sea several kinds of fish are caught, including many herring. Along the coast of Brittany, sardines and tunnies are caught, and nearly every seaside village is a fishing port. The canning of sardines in oil and the preparation of other fish for market give employment to thousands of people on shore. 

Boulogne and Dieppe are two of the more important fishing ports, and have a direct railway service to Paris and other cities.

The French deep-sea fishermen go also to the waters around Iceland and Newfoundland. 

Tree Crops. -France has several tree crops of high value. There are chestnut, walnut, and almond trees; and in the south, lemons, oranges, and pomegranates are grown.

There also, in localities with the right kind of soil and climate, are groves of olive and mulberry trees. Both nuts and fruits are exported. Some of them go to Great Britain, Germany, and other northern countries, and some are sent to the United States. import the walnuts under the name of "English" walnuts. Both ripe olives and green olives are put up in glass bottles, or jars, and many olives are used in the manufacture of olive oil.

We 

Artistic Products. The French people are very artistic. They make beautiful jewelry, delicate perfumes, lovely glassware, fragile porcelain, and wonderful pieces of lace. 

Their textiles are excellent in design, color, texture, and finish. In their smaller metal industries the French have shown unusual skill in making surgical and other implements, and they have a world-wide reputation for making measuring instruments of great accuracy. 

Today, as for many years past, much

French manufacturing is done in little shops and small factories where trained workmen have gathered together. Such workmen take pride in their work, and put into it the touch of their personal genius. The products of such shops and factories are not standardized but are individual. Quality rather than quantity, and beauty rather than cost, are the ideals that are followed. 

Scattered about France there are many places which through the years have come to have a wonderful reputation for their manufactures. Grenoble, in the valley of the upper Rhone, is famous for its gloves; and 

Grasse, in the mountains north of Nice, is widely known for its perfumes. Fine porcelain ware is made at Limoges in southcentral France, and at Sèvres, a few miles from Paris.
