The Don, much shorter than the other two, flows into the Sea of Azov. These are the three chief rivers of southern Russia.

The commerce of the Volga is from place to place along its course, or to and from points on the Caspian Sea. The commerce on the 

Dnieper and the Don can reach the Black 

Sea. From Black Sea ports, by way of the water route past Istanbul to the Mediterranean, commerce can be carried on with any port in the world.

The rivers of the northern plains of Asiatic Russia follow the slope of the land toward the Arctic Ocean. On the map of Asia find the Ob, Yenisei, and Lena rivers. Which one of these is nearest to 

European Russia? Which one rises far to the south in the highlands of southeastern Asiatic Russia? The lower courses of all of these rivers and parts of most of their tributaries are frozen for many months in the year. This is true also of the northwardflowing rivers of European Russia. Why? 

If you will notice the high latitudes of the lower courses and the mouths of these rivers it may help you to find the answer to this question. Keep in mind the location of the 

Lena River. The coldest part of the world in which people live is found in the basin of this river. There is little commerce on these rivers because the country is sparsely inhabited, because they are frozen for many months at a time, and because they flow north while the commerce of this part of 

Russia moves east and west.

Find Lake Aral and Lake Balkhash in southwestern Russia in Asia. Notice that streams flow into them but that they have no outlets. As you might correctly tell from that fact, the basins in which they lie are regions of light rainfall, like the basin of 

Great Salt Lake in our country.

Climate and Vegetation. The range in latitude in European Russia is from about 

40° north latitude on the west shore of the 

Caspian Sea to about 70° north latitude on the Arctic Ocean. Within this 30° range of latitude there are marked differences in climate, vegetation, industries, and density of population.

The prevailing winds are from the west, but they do not bring to Russia the even temperatures that are found in the lowland countries of west-central Europe. In western 

Europe their influence is to make the temperatures cool in summer and mild in winter (page 79). As they move eastward these westerly winds become warmer in summer and cooler in winter, and give Russia a continental climate a climate of extremes of temperature. The difference between summer temperature and winter temperature for places in Russia, therefore, becomes greater from the west toward the east. As you would naturally expect, the temperature decreases from south to north, although at Astrakhan, near the mouth of the Volga, that river is closed by ice for over two months in winter. 

Throughout northern Russia, both in Europe and Asia, the winter temperatures are so low that the ground is frozen to a depth of many

feet. The short summers are usually warm enough to thaw out the surface, and as a result much of the land is swampy in the summer time.

The rainfall varies greatly in different parts of the country. It is about 24 inches a year in the west-central part of the country in the region of the Valdai Hills. From this region it becomes less toward the north, the east, and the south. In the north the average annual rainfall drops to less than 10 inches a year, too little for the growth of crops. This makes little difference to the farmers of Russia, because it is so cold in these regions that no crops will grow. 

The rainfall in the central and southern parts of the country is of much greater importance. In these parts the temperature is favorable to the growth of trees or crops, and most of the soils are excellent. The average annual rainfall for much of this area is only 20 inches or less, and it varies so greatly from year to year that crop damage or failure frequently happens.

In the Caspian Sea region, where the summer temperatures are often very high, the rainfall is less than 10 inches a year, and part❘ of the country is almost a desert. Farming is impossible without irrigation. 

The Tundras. You will remember that when you were studying North America last year, you learned about the tundras of northern Alaska and northern Canada. You found these tundras to be low, treeless plains, where the ground is frozen to great depths, and where there is a very sparse population. 

The surface thaws out during the brief summer, and there is a growth of reindeer moss and some grass. These furnish food for the 

These furnish food for the herds of reindeer and the caribou that are to be found there. In studying Norway and 

Sweden you found a similar region in which a nomadic people live with their herds of reindeer (page 106).

A broad belt of country in northern Russia, extending across the country from west to east, is just such a tundra region. The natural vegetation is lichens and some grass, with a few small shrubs. Here also you find many scattered groups of people with their reindeer. They live in sod houses or skin tents, and move from place to place whenever necessary to find food for their herds. In western European Russia, as in northern

Norway, Sweden, and Finland, these people are Lapps. In eastern European Russia, and in Asiatic Russia, there are various tribes or groups of the same yellow race, speaking different languages. For their food the people depend chiefly upon the milk and meat of their reindeer, but they also catch fish, and gather some berries. With the coming of winter these people move southward with their herds into the edge of the forest. There they are better protected from winter storms, and their animals have a better chance to dig through the snow with their sharp hoofs to get at the grass or moss underneath. The reindeer hides are used both for tents and for clothing. 

Forests. The forests of Russia are the largest in the world. The forest belt, like the tundra region, stretches across the whole of Russia, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean. In the northern part, the trees are chiefly evergreens. Toward the south, the evergreens thin out and are replaced by deciduous trees; that is, trees that lose their leaves each winter.

In European Russia there is much lumbering going on in the evergreen forests. In the warmer season, logs are floated down the Dvina to Archangel, where they are sawed into lumber or made into wood pulp for export. Very little of this forest area has been cleared for crops, although some flax is grown for its fiber and crops of oats are raised. 

Taken as a whole, however, this European evergreen-forest region is very sparsely populated. As you know, this area was once covered by the European ice sheet, and there are many swamps and undrained lakes, as

A. 

Floating timber down a river of north-central Russia. Some of the logs are fastened together in rafts, but most of them are floated separately. What do you know about the size of the Russian forests? there are in similar regions in North America.

In such a forest area, with so sparse a population, with its cold winters, and its swamps and lakes, it is natural that there should be many fur-bearing animals. Hunting and trapping have long been a very important industry in this region. Farther east little lumbering is done, because of the difficulty and expense of getting the lumber to market. 

Trees have been cut chiefly to meet local needs for timber and firewood.

The hardwood region has been extensively cut over, especially in the west, along the rivers, and along the southern margin.

Throughout the cleared areas are many villages where the farmers live. During the day they go out to work in the fields. Flax, rye, oats, wheat, and potatoes are the chief crops, as they all grow well in cool lands and can ripen during the short summers of northern latitudes. Some live stock are kept, but the raising of crops is much more important.

A Region of Dense Population and Some Great Cities. - The western part of the forest zone was largely cleared away many, many years ago. It is today the most densely settled part of all Russia, and within this area are two of the greatest cities. It has also become the chief industrial region. 

Leningrad, first named St. Petersburg (and later Petrograd), is second in size among the Russian cities. For many years it was the capital of the country, but the government was transferred to Moscow after the revolution. Leningrad is located on the 

Neva River, the outlet of Lake Ladoga.

It is not far from the eastern end of the Gulf of Finland, an arm of the Baltic Sea. Improvements at the mouth of the Neva have made Leningrad the chief port of European

Russia. It is connected by a direct railroad line with Moscow, the present capital.

Moscow, southeast of Leningrad, has grown rapidly since it became the capital of modern Russia. It is now much larger than Philadelphia, and about as large as Chicago. 

It is the railroad center of European Russia, and from it railroads lead out in every direction. Moscow is the European end of the 

Trans-Siberian Railroad. Trace this great route along its 6000 miles of length through 

European and Asiatic Russia to the Russian port of Vladivostok on the Pacific Ocean (see maps of Eastern Europe and Asia).

The government of Russia, in control of its industries, is increasing its manufactures (A). In recent years, Moscow has become a textile-manufacturing center, with cotton, woolen, linen, and silk mills. It also manufactures leather goods and machinery.

EUROPE 

A. Farm workers, in teams or "troops," stirring the soil in the broad fields of the Ukraine. The harrows are hauled by small tractors. What is the main agricultural product of this region ? 

Moscow has naturally become also a trade center for the surrounding country. Here are gathered grain, furs, oil, and other products for export to other points in Europe, or to be sent to ports for shipment abroad. 

Near Moscow, on the Volga, are other cities where industry is developing. One of these to the east of Moscow is Gorki - formerly Nizhni Novgorod, famous for the annual fairs held there. It was a meeting place for traders of eastern Europe and Asia. It is now rapidly becoming an important manufacturing center. 

Grasslands and the Black Earth Region. 

The region south of the old forest belt is a large area of grassland that occupies most of southern Russia in Europe and extends east ward into Asia. Find this Black Earth Region on the map, page 76. The soil is called "black earth" because it has been colored very dark by the decay of grass roots in it year after year for centuries. It is one of the most fertile soils in the world. Where there is sufficient rainfall, very large crops can be grown. 

This is the great wheat-raising region of Russia, and in the years of good harvests Russia is second only to our own country in the amount raised. Cattle are found on the farms all through the southern half of Russia.

The chief rye-growing district in Russia is in the northern part of the great farming area, especially to the east of Moscow. More than half of the rye grown in Europe is raised in European Russia.

Although west-central Russia is the most densely settled part of the country, the blackearth region, especially in the south and southwest, has a great many people. Kiev on the Dnieper is one of the chief cities of this region. It is a trading center for the district; manufactures iron and steel goods and textiles; and has flour mills, sugar refineries, and tobacco factories. 

Odessa, for many years the chief Russian port on the Black Sea, is not now growing as rapidly as are Vernoleninsk and Kherson. 

Through these ports grain and other products are shipped to world markets. They have flour mills and other industries.

Oats are grown in much of the region south of the tundras, but the area of greatest production is a belt north and west of the chief wheatgrowing region.

Corn is grown chiefly in the southwestern part of the country, along the Black Sea (A), but also in the region of the Caucasus. 

There is a heavy production of barley north of the Black Sea, in an area almost as large as the sea itself. Nearly all of the sugar beets grown in Russia are raised in the southwestern part of the country (128 B) north and west of the barley-growing area. 

Production is increasing, and a number of sugar refineries are in operation. Tobacco is another crop grown largely in the southwest. grazing region, but experiments in farming are being carried on by the new government of Russia, and much progress is being made. 

It is in this region that the growing of winter wheat on farms owned and operated by the government is proving most successful. It is done on a large scale, with the aid of modern farm machinery, and by modern dry-farming methods. The barley-growing region is being extended into this steppe region also, and here sunflowers are grown for their seeds, from which oil is extracted. 

The steppe region around the Caspian extends eastward into Asia as the Kirghiz Steppe (map, page 198). On these plains large herds of cattle, sheep, goats, and horses find pasture. The herds are cared for by tribes of wandering people whom we call nomads, because they move about from place to place in search of grass for their animals.

There are three important cities of Russia in the steppe region or on the edge of it. 

One of these is Stalingrad, on the Volga. 

This city was built by the Soviet government in an effort to increase manufacturing in this part of Russia. The second is Astrakhan, a fisheries and trade center near the mouth of the Volga. The third is Baku, the center of a great petroleum-producing area (A) from which oil is piped to Batum on the Black Sea, for export. Some is sent north by boats on the Volga, and much is used on Russian railroads.

Notice on your maps the region south of the Kirghiz Steppe. It is a lowland region in which there is so little rainfall that it is almost a true desert. Rains falling in the mountain area to the south and east furnish water for irrigation, and a large amount of cotton is grown on irrigated fields in this part of the Soviet Union. Vegetables, cereals, and mulberry trees are raised. The leaves of the mulberry are fed to silkworms, as they are in France, Spain, and Italy. Silk and wool are used in the manufacture of rugs on the crude hand looms of the people. 

After reading about the steppe and desert regions, you can tell where some of the raw materials used in the textile mills of Moscow and other Russian cities come from.

Find the Crimean Peninsula, extending into the Black Sea. On the south of its coastal mountains and on the slopes of the southern Caucasus are forest regions with a Mediterranean climate. Here, in some of the valleys, corn and winter wheat are grown. 

Agriculture in Asiatic Russia.-The north ern part of Russia in Asia has long been

known as Siberia, and you have traced the Trans-Siberian Railroad across it to its 

Pacific port of Vladivostok. This railroad passes through grasslands that are the eastern continuation of those in southern Russia in Europe. Many farmers have settled inland along the railroad. Grain and cattle are raised, and butter and some wheat are sent west by rail. Butter from Siberian farms is sold in Great Britain. Omsk, on the railroad, is the chief trade center. 

Mineral Resources of Russia. For so large a country, Russia is not rich in mineral resources. It is only since the World 

War that the active development of those that are known has been started. In the central Urals, iron ore, coal, copper, gold, and platinum are found. The iron and coal are being mined and used, in cities near by, in the manufacture of iron and steel. In gold production Russia now takes very high rank. The yield of its platinum mines is small, but the mineral is very valuable. 

Columbia, in South America, ranks second.

The greater part of the coal and iron now mined in Russia comes from deposits in the southern Ukraine. southern Ukraine. As this coal is the only good coking coal found in Russia, and as there are deposits of manganese near by, this region has become an iron and steel center.

The oil fields of Baku on the Caspian have been mentioned. Other oil fields have been found farther west along the Caucasus

Mountains, and are being developed. 

Water taken from the Caspian, or other salt lakes near by, is heated until the water evaporates, leaving the salt. The salt is then purified and prepared for use. 

It will be a long time before Russia becomes one of the great manufacturing nations in the field of the metal industries.

Fishing. There is some fishing in the 

Russian lakes and rivers and in the Russian coastal waters. Fishing is not, however, a large and important industry of Russia as it is of Norway, Great Britain, and France.

Transportation and Trade. You know that Russian rivers, during the time they are not frozen, are used for the transportation of goods (pages 201-202). The river routes, however, are unsatisfactory not only because they may be closed by ice for weeks or months at a time, but because they are long and crooked, and the river boats are small and slow. Some railroads (map, page 198) have been built in European Russia, and one great route the Trans-Siberian Railroad across Asia (page 205). But the railroad mileage is very small for so large a country, and most parts of Russia are a long distance from the nearest railroad. Most of the

Russian roads are poor. Only in very recent years has the building of good roads been begun. Their construction is expensive. 

Over most of the plains there is no rock except that which is buried under the surface soils. Rock for road building in Russia is therefore expensive. Road building is further handicapped because much of the land is swampy. Airplanes are in use but not so generally as they are in other parts of Europe (map, page 133). 

Leningrad on the Gulf of Finland, and

Odessa, Vernoleninsk, Kherson, and Batum on the Black Sea, have been mentioned as ports. Leningrad is kept open by the use of ice breakers during a part of the cold weather, but it is closed for months at a time. 

Even the Black Sea ports must use ice breakers during part of the winter. Ports on the White Sea and the Arctic Ocean are difficult to reach and can be used profitably for only a few products such as timber and wood pulp. Vladivostok is too far from the densely settled and industrial regions of Russia to serve any useful purpose at the present time.

Russia, therefore, is poor in transportation routes, and poor in ports. These conditions do not favor trade, nor does the fact that the people of Russia are too poor to pay for many luxuries from abroad. Most of the trade is in the export of raw materials and foods, while the imports are materials for the developing manufactures. Among the exports are lumber, petroleum, furs, eggs, butter, meat, grain and flour, and flax.

Among the imports are raw cotton and wool, machinery, metals, hides, rubber, and tea. 

People. Most of the people of Russia are of the white race, although largely of Asiatic origin. They come mainly from three Slavic groups: (1) Great Russians, (2) White Russians, and (3) Little Russians, or Ukrainians. Other racial groups include about eight per cent of Jews, and many Germans. Under the new government all the different elements of the population are working together, trying to improve conditions in their country. A large part of the population cannot read or write, but more schools are being established. In spite of their hardships these people are strong, cheerful, and hard workers; and lovers of music and the dance. 

Comparing Russia with Canada. Much of northern Europe and northern Asia belongs to Russia. Much of northern North

America belongs to Canada. Russia's land area is less than three times as large as Canada's, but its population is about fifteen times that of Canada.

Some things are very similar in the two countries. Other things are very different. 

In both countries the northernmost part is a region of tundras; south of the tundras are forests; south of the forests are grasslands. 

In the tundras there are not many people, but there are herds of reindeer. In the forests there are fur-bearing animals, and hunters and trappers. In the grasslands there are cultivated fields and pastures. 

Canada has richer mineral resources, and better waterways, seaports, and railroads;

FINLAND 

Turn to the maps on pages 100 and 198 and find Finland. It lies to the north of the Gulf of Finland, and to the east of the 

Gulf of Bothnia, Sweden, and Norway. Be fore the World War Finland was a part of European Russia. So also were the three small republics of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. All three of these, because they are on the Baltic Sea, are called the Baltic states. 

Finland too is sometimes called a Baltic state. 

Finland lies between 60° and 70° north latitude. This means that part of the country is north of the Arctic Circle. Finland is therefore a region of long, cold winters and short summers. The summer days, however, are long, and the short summer season is therefore hotter than you would naturally expect. Winds from the Baltic help, also, to keep the winter temperature somewhat warmer than that of the Russian plains in the same latitude farther east.

This is especially true of the lowlands along the Gulf of Bothnia and the Gulf of Finland. 

Work of the Ice Sheet. Much of interior 

Finland is a plateau, higher in the north than in the south. It is what is left of an old mountain mass that has been worn down to its present level. All of Finland was covered by ice during the glacial period (101 A). 

When the ice melted, it left the lowlands covered with coarse glacial soils, and the uplands covered with lakes and marshes, and with thin and scanty soils.

Industries of Finland. 

Agriculture and grazing are carried on in the lowlands. 

There is grass for summer pasture, and much is cut, dried, and stored in barns for winter feed. There is a dairying region in the southern lowland where fine butter is made for export. Crops of oats, rye, barley, and potatoes are raised. Of these, the oat crop is increasing and the rye crop decreasing. 

All of these crops can be raised in cool regions

It is inhabited by a group of wandering people called Lapps, who keep reindeer and move with them from place to place.

The southern part of the plateau region has a heavy growth of pine and spruce trees. 

Here extensive lumbering operations are carried on to furnish the raw material for Finland's lumber mills and for its manufactures of wood pulp and paper. Not only do these industries give employment to many thousands of men, but they also furnish a large part of the exports of the country. 

As Finland has no coal it depends upon white coal," or water power, to run its mills and to generate electricity for other uses. 

Finland has no iron ore, and therefore no iron and steel industries. A little gold and copper are mined, but the total value of its mineral products is small.

Fishing (A) is an important industry for many of those who live along the shores of the Gulf of Bothnia and the Gulf of Finland.

Transportation. - Finland has only a few short railroads. In getting logs from the forests to sawmills, the lumbermen use the streams and lakes, some of which have been connected by canals. The logs are floated in summer, and dragged over the ice in winter. 

Much lumber is moved over the navigable waterways by boats.

Most of the people of Finland live in the southern part of the country (81 A). The densest population is in the lowlands, especially around Helsingfors, the capital, largest city, and chief seaport. Although the harbors of Helsingfors and other ports are frozen over during the colder winter months, ice breakers are used in an attempt to keep them open as much as possible.

Finland was ruled by Sweden for hundreds of years before it came under Russian rule in 1809. During the time Sweden was in power a fine school system was established. The people of Finland were treated much better

THE BALTIC STATES 

Among the changes that came in Europe as a result of the World War was the creation of the three small independent republics that border the Baltic Sea. These are Estonia,

Latvia, and Lithuania. The position of each of these is shown on the maps, pages 100 and 

198. They separated from Russia in Europe before the present Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was formed. Their independence has been recognized by the great nations of the world. These Baltic states, as they are usually called, are small, with very limited resources, and they can never expect to become important countries or to have any large influence in world affairs. You may think of them as "buffer states," in which the people greatly wish to improve their position in life. Some improvements have already been made in education and agriculture, and to a small extent in manufacturing.

with other serfs in Russia. 

Since the independent governments have been set up, the large estates of the old landholders have been broken up and the land distributed among the people. Under the present laws the amount of land that can be owned by any one person is limited. 

Surface and Climate. This part of Eu rope is low, and its surface and drainage were greatly disturbed by the ice sheet that at one time moved over it. Today there are many lakes and marshes, such as are found in Finland and in parts of Russia in Europe. The remainder of these countries is made up of low ridges and rolling lowlands. There is, however, a region of slightly greater elevation in western Latvia and Lithuania.

The climate of this lowland area is affected chiefly by its latitude and its nearness to the Baltic Sea. The climate is more like that of

Forests and Farms. The glacial soils of these Baltic states are rather poor, and they have never been improved as those of the north German lowland have been (page 140).

Almost one fourth of the land is covered with forests; and lumber, wood pulp, and paper are important exports, as they are from the forests of Finland, Russia, and the Scandinavian Peninsula.

Most of the people are engaged in farming (A). Flax, rye, oats, barley, and potatoes are the chief crops. All of these crops, you will remember, grow well in cool lands. You will notice that four out of the five crops given in the above list are food crops. The other one, flax, is grown both for seed and for fiber. Some cattle are raised, and in all three countries dairying is an important industry. 

Cities and Commerce. The capital of each country is also its largest city. Of these, Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, and Riga (Latvian spelling, Rīga), the capital of Latvia, are seaports. Riga is the larger of the two cities, and its port is seldom closed by ice. 

Klaipėda is the seaport of Lithuania. When the Russians find it impossible to keep the ice broken up so that ships can reach Leningrad, they use all three of these Baltic ports - but chiefly Riga. A very large part of the overseas trade of the three countries is therefore a transit trade which is handled by railroads between Russian points and the ports.

The Future. It is impossible to foretell what may be the future of the Baltic states. 

The position of buffer states is never a comfortable one. They are usually too weak to protect themselves if the nations they separate go to war, and absolute neutrality is difficult to maintain.

POLAND 

Almost all of Poland is part of the great lowland plain of Europe. It is separated from Russia on the east and Germany on the west by boundary lines for which no good reason can be seen on the map (page 113). 

On the south there is a natural boundary along the crest of the Carpathian Mountains. 

On the Polish slopes of these mountains are fine farm lands (217 A). At the north the boundary crosses the plains. This northern boundary separates Poland from Latvia, Lithuania, East Prussia, and the territory of the Free City of Danzig, a city state under the control of the League of Nations. because it is in the center of Europe, it has become a crossroads for trade and travel. 

Railroad lines from Paris and Berlin cross Poland through Łódz and Warsaw on their way to Moscow and other points in Russia in Europe. Through Moscow these eastwest trade routes connect with the Trans- Siberian Railroad and the Far East. 1 North-and-south lines connect ports of the 

Baltic with others on the Black Sea, and through the Moravian Gateway with Vienna and the Danube Valley. In fact, much of the trade between the Baltic and Black seas is most easily carried on through Poland. 

Items in Poland's History. 

The ease with which it is possible to enter Poland from the west, the east, and the north, has had much to do with its history. Poland became a separate kingdom nearly one thousand years ago. Its boundaries changed from time to time, but during long periods it included large areas in central and eastern Europe. 

In general, the Carpathian Mountains have formed the southern boundary, and the Baltic shore the northern boundary. During this period of its history, Poland's neighbors were Germany and the state of Prussia, which later became a part of Germany, on the west; 

Austria on the southwest; and Russia on the east. the east. During wars between these powerful neighbors, Poland was frequently invaded,

Forest Resources. There are forests on the slopes of the Carpathians and in northeastern Poland, where they join with the forests of the Baltic states. They are used for a lumber supply and in the manufacture of wood pulp. 

Agriculture. The leading industry in

Poland, as in many other parts of the Central Lowlands region of Europe, is agriculture. 

The glacial soils of the north, like those of the Baltic states, are poor, but there are much better soils in the south, in the rolling lands north of the Carpathians. The principal crops are potatoes, rye, wheat, oats, barley, sugar beets, and flax. The flax is raised chiefly for its fiber, and much of it is sent to the linen-manufacturing centers of western Europe. Many of the potatoes are used in the manufacture of alcohol. Among the farm animals raised are horses, cattle, sheep, hogs, and poultry.

HUNGARY AND RUMANIA 

When you were studying Germany, and later when you were studying Austria, you learned about the Danube River. You traced its course across southern Europe, from the place where it rises in Germany to the place where it enters the Black Sea. 

This is one of the famous trade routes of southern Europe. Railroads and highways have made use of the valley, and the river itself, as you know (page 161), has been internationalized. As the waters connecting the 

Black Sea with the Mediterranean are also free to the ships of all nations, the Danube forms a part of a great water route that gives much of southern Europe an outlet to the world's seas. 

Before reaching the Black Sea the Danube turns north and then east through the lowlands of Rumania. It enters the sea through three mouths, one of which has been improved, so that ocean-going steamers can go up the river to Rumanian ports. 

Other trade routes both from the north and from the south connect with that of the Danube. They cross the mountains through natural gateways or passes, or follow the valleys of tributary streams. Most of these are railroad routes, the most important ones from the north centering upon Vienna, while the chief routes from the south and east center upon Budapest (221 A). It is well to keep in mind, however, that the Danube route and the railroad routes that center upon it are not as important as the Rhine route and those that center upon it. The

HUNGARY AND RUMANIA

A. Elizabeth Bridge, Budapest, spanning the Danube River. This is one of six bridges connecting the two old towns, Buda and Pest, which united in 1872 to form one city. Budapest has many impressive public buildings and fine churches.

Rhine routes serve the most densely settled parts of Europe and the most highly developed industrial regions of the continent. 

They lead to the north Atlantic, across whose waters most of the world's commerce moves.

The Danube flows through a much less densely settled part of the continent, which has had a smaller industrial development, and the river carries its trade away from, not toward, the Atlantic. 

Surface. Study carefully the map on page 113. It shows that Hungary is largely made up of plains, although there are some hill lands west, southwest, and northeast of

Budapest. Rumania, however, has a central mountain region -the Transylvanian plateau partly bordered by the higher Carpathian Mountains and the Transylvanian 

Alps. Taken as a whole from west to east, the two countries consist of (1) a plains region between Vienna and Budapest that extends south toward the boundary of Yugoslavia; (2) a region of low hills east of the plains just mentioned, rising from a level region of slightly greater elevation than that of the plains; (3) a larger plains area that stretches eastward into Rumania and southward into Yugoslavia, across which the Danube and the Tisza flow from north to south; (4) the highlands of central Rumania, consisting of a plateau bordered by mountains; and (5) a large plains area to the south and east of this central highland, occupying much of the remainder of Rumania, and reaching the Black Sea.

Europe. You have learned that after the war these two countries were separated, and that Austria lost much territory to other countries. Hungary lost much territory also.

Climate. Hungary is now an inland country without a seacoast, and although 

Rumania borders the Black Sea, both countries are far removed from the influence of the Atlantic Ocean. Both countries have a continental rather than an oceanic climate.

The summers are hot and the winters are cold. Cold northeast winds blow out of central Russia during the winter, and the mouths of the Danube are usually closed by ice during several weeks each year. Naturally, because of the greater elevation, the highlands of Rumania are cooler than the rest of Rumania, and cooler than Hungary.

Agriculture. The chief industry of Hun gary is agriculture, and more than three fourths of its people are farmers. Some of the soil is exceedingly rich and fertile, and the growing season is long. Over half of the country is under cultivation, the remainder being given over to pasture land and forests. 

At times the rivers overflow their banks and do damage to the crops, but lands that are frequently covered by water in this way are not usually under cultivation. Among the crops raised, wheat is the most important. 

Corn is also grown in large quantities (222 A), as are other grains. Potatoes, sugar beets, grapes and other fruits, and tobacco are also raised. Hungary has always had a surplus of grain for export, and has long been looked upon as a source of food for its neighbors. 

Cattle, sheep, hogs, and horses are raised.

The cattle, sheep, and horses are raised in the central part of Hungary, where there is not enough rainfall for crops. Hogs are raised, as in the North Central States in our own country, and fattened on corn, so that a part of the great corn crop can be used to produce meat.

In the plains of Rumania, east of the Carpathians, dry seasons are more frequent than in the more moist parts of Hungary. Yet the crops are much the same, and there is some stock raising also. Corn is the chief crop, but wheat, barley, and other grains are raised. Cattle and horses are pastured on the grasses that grow in the region of light rains, near the Black Sea, while cattle (A) and sheep are raised largely in regions near the mountains, where there is excellent summer pasturage. Both cattle and sheep are driven into the highlands in spring. In what other countries have you found the same custom? 

Hogs also are raised and exported.

Later it was taken by Russia and held by that country until the close of the World War, when it was returned to Rumania. Its southern part is largely a marsh land. Its northern part is hilly, but the farmers raise corn, wheat, hay, and live stock.

Minerals. A small amount of coal, some of a fair quality, is the most important mineral resource of Hungary. There are also valuable bauxite deposits. Rumania has a poor quality of coal or lignite. Other mineral products of Rumania are rock salt and petroleum. There are oil wells in the highlands and near the shores of the Black Sea. 

Oil and oil products are exported. 

Cities. The city of Budapest, the capital of Hungary, is divided into two parts by the Danube (221 A). These were formerly two separate cities- Buda and Pest. The two parts of the united city are connected by fine bridges, much as you found the parts of Paris on opposite banks of the Seine connected by bridges. Budapest is a very attractive city with fine public buildings, and large city in Hungary, and the only one with important manufacturing industries. It is a center for the manufacture of flour, and of some beet sugar. Textile industries based on imported cotton are growing steadily. 

Bucharest, the capital of Rumania, is the chief trade and industrial center of that country. Its modern part has many fine public and private buildings, and many of the rich land owners of Rumania have made their homes there. It has flour mills and oil refineries. 

Constanţa, on the Black Sea, is a shipping point for the petroleum industry (A), and

Galați on the Danube is the port from which most of the wheat of Rumania is exported. 

The People. - Most of the people of Hungary today are true Hungarians, or Magyars. 

They are descendants of Asiatic people who came to Hungary many centuries ago. As a people they are brave and proud, and very courteous (225 A). They are fond of music

A. 

Hungarian fruit sellers in an open-air market at Budapest. and dancing, and much fine music and many fine musicians have come from Hungary. 

The Rumanians, although partly Slav by race, claim to be descendants of ancient Roman colonists, and they speak a language somewhat like Latin. They are a strong and vigorous people.

In both countries, there are some citizens who are wealthy and well educated. But there are also many peasants who have very little education and enjoy very few of the luxuries of life. Some efforts are being made to improve the education of the people and to improve the conditions under which they live and work. Unfortunately, the population is large and the countries small. The great mass of the people must depend upon agriculture for a living, and even if the land were divided equally among them, the farms would be very small. The future does not look bright for either Hungary or Rumania under present conditions. The discovery of greater mineral wealth, and the increase of manufacturing to give employment to more people would help. The improvement of agricultural methods may bring larger returns.

YUGOSLAVIA, BULGARIA, AND ALBANIA 

South of Austria, Hungary, and Rumania is a highland region that includes four countries and a part of one other country. They are generally called the Balkan countries. 

One of them, Greece, you have already studied, as it is a part of the Mediterranean region (pages 191-193). The three others wholly included in the Balkans are Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, and Albania. A part of

Turkey occupies the eastern corner of the peninsula, separated from the much larger part of Turkey in Asia by the Bosporus, Sea of Marmara, and the Dardanelles. 

Surface. The Balkan Peninsula is some times likened to a bridge joining Europe to Asia. It faces Asia across three seas the 

Black Sea, the Sea of Marmara, and the 

Aegean. It is bordered also by the Adriatic 

Sea (A) and the Mediterranean.

The land is mountainous, but among the mountains there are many beautiful valleys and old lake basins. In the west are the 

Dinaric Alps. This range of highlands continues the folds of the Alps southeastward into Greece, where they are known as the 

Pindus Mountains. The Balkan Mountains are in the northern and eastern part of the peninsula. From eastern Yugoslavia, they extend eastward through Bulgaria to the 

Black Sea. Extending south and east from the Iron Gate, they are sometimes thought of as a continuation of the Carpathian and 

Transylvanian ranges. 

The chief lowlands are those along the

Danube and its tributaries, making up the large plains area in northern Yugoslavia and northern Bulgaria. Lowlands are also to be found along the Maritza River in Bulgaria and Turkey. Two streams whose headwaters are very near each other are the Morava that flows north to the Danube, and the Vardar,

The valleys of the Vardar River and the northward-flowing Morava form a famous trade route. The connecting of the two rivers by a canal has been planned. A railroad follows this route from Salonika northward. 

The main railroad line from Istanbul to Sofia, Belgrade, Budapest, and Vienna can be easily traced on the map. After crossing from Istanbul to the Maritza Valley, it follows that stream toward its headwaters, and then cuts across the highlands, by way of 

Sofia, to the valley of Morava.

Climate. The climate of much of the 

Balkan Peninsula is influenced (1) by the fact that its western part borders the Adriatic, and (2) by the fact that westerly winds sweep across it from that sea and from the 

Mediterranean, and (3) by the fact that the mountain ranges of the Dinaric Alps border the Adriatic in a series of parallel ridges beginning close to the coast. 

The southern part of the peninsula has a 

Mediterranean climate, as you have learned.

The mountains along the Adriatic have rainfall on their southwestern slopes, but the amount decreases toward the northeast, where there is much less. The rain of this region comes largely at the time when the westerly winds prevail.

History of the Balkan Region. 

This part of Europe has been for thousands of years closely related to Asia. Across the narrow waters that join the Black and Aegean seas, men have gone for trade, for settlement, and for war.

The whole Balkan region fell under the control of the Turks several hundred years ago. Their rule was so cruel that different peoples, one after another, fought for and gained their independence, and set up gov- Turkish power in Europe came in a war with near-by countries of the peninsula in 19121913. At its close the Turks were forced to give up five sixths of their European possessions, keeping only a small area in the east. 

As a result of the World War, Yugoslavia was formed, including Serbia, Montenegro, and several southern provinces of the former 

Austria-Hungary; and Bulgaria and Turkey both lost territory to Greece. (See map, page 156.) 

The several peoples of the Balkan area are of different races, speaking different languages; and they are of different religions also. This is often true of groups that have been included within the boundaries of a single country. 

The nature of the surface of the country keeps the several groups apart. You may expect, therefore, that there will be jealousies and disputes; and wars between the different nations and between smaller groups seeking power within a nation. Indeed, quarrels and wars have been so constant that no one country has had peace long enough or a government strong enough to develop its resources. Farmers and herdsmen retire to remote valleys, and oppose bitterly any change. Nearly all industry is of the most primitive kind. A wealth of metal lies hidden and untouched in the mountains.

Since the World War, exports have not increased as they should have done.

Yugoslavia. — Yugoslavia is the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and is sometimes called "Greater Serbia." These three peoples are Yugo-Slavs or South Slavs; that is, Slavs of the southern or Balkan region. 

This name sets them apart from the northern 

Slavs of Czechoslovakia, Poland, and Russia.

The Serbs of Yugoslavia live in the eastern part of the country. The Croats and Slovenes live in the western provinces.

Much of Yugoslavia, as you have learned, is a tangle of mountains and valleys that has no natural center from which all parts of the country can be easily reached. Its natural resources have remained largely undeveloped. 

The people carry on agriculture (A), for which the climate and soils of the mountain valleys seem well suited. Corn and wheat are raised. Rainfall decreases toward the interior, and the summers grow hotter and the winters colder, but plums, grapes (B), hemp, flax, and tobacco are among the crops raised. 

In the mountain valleys, and even on steep sloping mountain pastures, cattle, sheep, and goats are raised. Many hogs are kept, and some of them get a large part of their food from forest nuts where forests are still found. 

Much of the land was stripped of its forests many, many years ago, when the Romans cut the timber for their own use and carried it to Italy. No attempts of an extensive nature have yet been made to reforest the barren hillsides. Yet there is some timber on the mountain slopes, which so far has met the most pressing needs of the people.

Very little manufacturing of any kind is carried on in Yugoslavia. There are small household industries, including the making of yarn from sheep's wool, and much knitting. 

There are also, in many households, small looms used for weaving cloth in bright colors, and of many patterns. The cloth is used for garments, aprons, and kerchiefs (228 B).

Of mills and factories there are very few large ones. There are some that are engaged in making flour, or in weaving carpets. On some rivers where the rapids have many little falls, it is not uncommon to find that each farmer of the neighborhood has a mill of his own. 

Coal and copper are important mineral products. The mountain regions of Yugoslavia, when carefully explored, will probably reveal other mineral deposits of great value.

Cereals, prunes, prune marmalade, some timber, and hogs are exported; and most manufactured goods must be imported. 

Belgrade, the capital, as you see from the map, does not have a central location. Here are the homes of some wealthy people, as it is the largest city and on the main railroad route through the country. Belgrade is on the 

Danube River and trade that passes up or down the river must go through the city (A).

As it is on the great railroad line from Vienna and the west to Istanbul and to Salonika, it is the chief trade center of the country. Yugoslavia has no port on the Adriatic of firstclass importance, but it is able to use Fiume, one of the Italian ports.

Most of the people of the country are poorly educated and know little of modern agricultural or other machinery. 

Bulgaria. Modern Bulgaria has been an independent kingdom only since 1908, but the land it includes has been inhabited for a long, long time. Invading hordes have swept back and forth over its plains, and pushed remnants of former populations back into the mountains for many centuries. Nature has divided the country into three well-marked physical regions. In the north there are lowlands forming part of the plains of the Danube. In the south there are the plains of the Maritza River, which extend into Turkey and to the shores of the Aegean. 

Between these two lowlands are the Balkan Mountains, which connect in the western part of the country with the highlands south of the Maritza.

The climate of Bulgaria is continental in character, the winters being cold and the summers warm. This is especially true in the northern part of the country, where cold winter winds sweep south from central Russia. 

In the Maritza Valley, however, the winter temperature is higher, as the mountains at the north shut out the cold winds. The rainfall is rather small (maps, page 79), and crops and pastures sometimes suffer from long periods of drought.

In Bulgaria, as in Rumania to the north, the chief crops of the Danube plains are corn covered with vineyards. Some coal mines are in operation, and there is other mineral wealth in the Balkan Mountains, but mining has scarcely begun. 

In addition to the trade that is carried on by way of the Black Sea, some trade goes by rail to Istanbul, or to the Aegean Sea, and some moves northward toward central Europe.

Sofia, the capital, is on the main railroad between Istanbul and Vienna, and thus has connections with all parts of Europe. Philippopolis, on the Maritza, is a business and industrial center.

The population includes, in addition to the 

Bulgarians, many Turks, Rumanians, Greeks, and Gypsies. Such a mixture of races is common in all the Balkan countries. Education has been neglected and the majority of the people are poor and ignorant. Modern industry has made but little progress, but the full resources of the country have not been developed, and there is hope for the future. 

Albania. Northwest of Greece, on the western side of the Balkan Peninsula, is

Albania, the smallest of the Balkan countries. It is not very much larger than the state of New Jersey and has only about one

ALBANIA AND TURKEY 

231 fourth as many people. Along the Adriatic

Sea is a narrow coastal plain with a Mediterranean climate, where most of the people are farmers. The rest of the country is mountainous, with many small valleys separated from each other by high mountain walls. 

These mountain valleys furnish excellent pasture for flocks of sheep or goats (230 A), and for some cattle. Most of the mountaineers are shepherds, but they are a wild and turbulent people who are very proud and sensitive, and unfriendly to strangers. They are mostly Mohammedans in religion, although there are some Christians. 

Fine pine forests on the mountain slopes would furnish much excellent timber, but these people produce little of anything more than they need for their own use. There is very little trade with other countries. This is partly due to the backward state of all industries, and partly to the fact that, unlike other Balkan countries, Albania is not on any trade route. There are few good roads and but one short railroad, although others are projected. Valuable mineral deposits have been located, but no mining is being done. 

The capital city, Tiranë, is on the inner margin of the coastal plain.

TURKEY 

Look once again at the map on page 163. 

Find Turkey in Europe. It is a small area in the Balkan Peninsula just north of the waters connecting the Black and Aegean seas. It is only a remnant of the immense territory that the Turks once ruled in Europe. 

You have learned that in ancient times one power after another held control of the Mediterranean world and its trade. Greece followed Phoenicia, and Rome followed Greece.

The power of Rome, during the period of its greatest expansion, extended far beyond the shores of the Mediterranean Sea. It was decided to found a second capital of the empire in the East. This capital of the eastern Roman Empire was established at the city of Byzantium, renamed Constantinople in honor of the Emperor Constantine, and now called Istanbul.

In the west, the Roman Empire began to break down with the loss of province after province to invaders from the north. Finally, with the capture of Rome by the invading barbarians, the Western Empire tottered to its fall. But in the Eastern Empire the rule of the emperors lasted much longer. During the more than 1100 years of its existence this Christian Empire stood as a wall to protect civilized Europe from Asiatic invasions. It successfully met and defeated the attacks of Persians, Saracens, and Seljuk Turks, but it was finally overthrown by the Ottoman Turks, whose ancestors had been driven out of central Asia by the Mongols. This was in 

1453, just thirty-nine years before the dis covery of the New World. Constantinople, as the center of Roman power in the East, had defended Europe while the new western nations of that continent were growing into power and importance. 

Pushing on beyond Constantinople, the

Ottoman Turks invaded and conquered the greater part of the Balkan Peninsula, and brought most of the people under their rule.

EUROPE 

A. 

This picture, continued on the opposite page, shows a panoramic view of the Bosporus, looking Turkish government to grant, other nations demanded as an equal right and usually succeeded in getting.

Before the Ottoman Turks had conquered the Balkan Peninsula, however, they had already established their power in southwestern Asia.

A great Turkish Empire was created, and the Turk ruled both in Asia and in Europe. 

It was the setting up of this Turkish Empire at the eastern end of the Mediterranean that blocked the trade routes to the Far East.

The leaders of the Turks had great military ability, and they led their fierce and warlike followers from one conquest to another. 

Their rulers, however, failed utterly to make the conquered peoples happy under the new government. So bad was their rule that the conquered peoples were always restless, and there was more or less constant rebellion, especially among the people of the Balkan 

Peninsula. One after another, successful wars for freedom were fought by various 

Balkan groups, and independent governments were set up.

The wars against the Turks had the support of many Christian people who urged their governments to go to the assistance of those oppressed by Turkish misrule. But the control of the Balkan Peninsula and its open ways to the East, and the control of Constantinople and its crossing trade routes by any one European power, would not be allowed by the others. In the weak hands of the 

Turks these routes were gradually more or less opened to all powers. Whatever concessions any European nation forced the 

Meanwhile, new routes to the East having been found, trade followed them for a long, long time, until the power of the Turks began to decline. In recent times, as you know, Great Britain gained a shorter and a safer sea route by way of the Suez Canal. Germany sought an overland railroad route to the 

Persian Gulf. This was the "Berlin to 

Baghdad" route, which reached from Berlin to Constantinople, and parts of which had been built in Turkey in Asia, before the opening of the World War. During this time, the 

German Emperor was especially friendly with the Turkish ruler the Turkish ruler the Sultan. Russia was also seeking an outlet to the south-control of the water route to the Mediterranean.

Great Britain and France were opposed to both the German and the Russian schemes. 

You can now understand why European nations did not join to put the Turks out of Europe. 

A City at the Crossroads.-Constantinople, now known by its Turkish name, Istanbul, is on the Bosporus (A). It is by far the largest city of the Balkan Peninsula, and is one of the most ancient and famous cities of Europe. It is at the crossroads of the trade between two seas and two continents. The trade between the two seas moves between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and

TURKEY 

233 Istanbul lies just beyond the promontory at the extreme right. across it from Europe to Asia. at Istanbul it meets the trade from Asia that comes overland by rail, and from central and southern Europe that comes largely by rail.

This city was for a long time the capital of Turkey, but after the World War the capital was changed to Angora, a city of Asia Minor.

Istanbul is divided into two parts by its long harbor, called the "Golden Horn." On one side (sometimes called Stamboul) are the | native homes and shops along narrow, winding streets that are crowded with people, animals, and carriages that often get in each other's way. In little booths that open upon the streets, merchants show their goods for sale and craftsmen work at their trade. If you stop to buy you must be prepared to bargain for a long time and with true Oriental spirit, unless you are willing to pay a high price for what you purchase. 

B. Istanbul, Turkey. The tall spires at the right are minarets. This view shows the modern part of the city, where there is a fine broad paved highway with a narrow park between the two roadways.

EUROPE 

On the opposite side of the harbor, in another part of the city (often called Pera), are the homes of the foreign peoples, and fine public buildings. The streets are broader than those in the native part of the city and there are street cars and automobiles by which you can get around quickly. 

Istanbul is a Mohammedan city and you can see all about the city the domes of the mosques and the tall minarets (233 B) from which the call to prayer is cried out to the faithful. St. Sophia, which for hundreds of years was a Greek Catholic Church, and later was made over into a mosque, is now used as a museum of Byzantine art. 

Turkey in Asia. — Turn to the map of Asia and find the peninsula of Asia Minor.

Notice how it extends west from the mainland of Asia, between the Black and Mediterranean seas. This part of Turkey is far larger than the part in Europe. Its industries are much like those of other countries in southwestern Asia, and will be studied later, at the same time with those countries. 

Before the World War the Turkish possessions in Asia were very much larger than they are at the present time. They included 

Syria, Palestine, and most of Arabia, and extended east to Persia. The number of 

Turkish people in the lands that were lost was a very small part of their population. In the present Turkey most of the people are Turks. 

Government. After hundreds of years of bad government as a monarchy, Turkey became a republic after the World War. 

The first president, Mustafa Kemal, proved himself a strong man, with a knowledge of his people and a real wish to help them. There have been many changes. The people are no longer forced to be Mohammedans.

Women are now well treated and are not compelled to wear a veil over their faces in public. Both men and women use modern dress. A modern alphabet almost like our own has been introduced instead of the old Turkish alphabet, so that Turkish books and A.- Old-fashioned wheel for lifting water for irrigation in Turkey. Taken as a whole, Europe is the most densely settled of the continents. It is divided into many countries, each of which, with a few exceptions, has a language of its own. 

The Latin Nations. The Italians, the 

French, the Spanish, and the Portuguese are called Latin peoples because they are descended partly from the Roman people who spoke the Latin tongue. The languages of all four have grown out of the Latin, and are therefore somewhat alike, although in many ways each is different from the others. The 

Rumanians also have a language that grew out of Latin. They too claim descent from the 

Romans, and are proud to bear their name. ― - 

The Teutonic Nations. The nations of central and northwestern Europe are related to one another, and are sometimes called 

Teutonic. The Dutch and the German peoples still hold the land where their early ancestors lived. German tribes known as

Angles and Saxons went early from this part of the mainland to Great Britain. From one of these tribes we have the name Angle-land, or England. A combination of the names of both tribes-Anglo-Saxon-is a term much used when speaking of their English descendants. The Danes, Swedes, and Norwegians also are Teutonic peoples. 

Slavic and Other Peoples. Many of the peoples of eastern Europe, including most of those in Russia, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and Bulgaria, are called Slavs, or Slavonic people, from a powerful tribe that once lived in that region. 

All of the peoples thus far named, and also the Greeks and some others, belong to the white race. The Hungarians, the Finns, the 

Lapps, and a few other Europeans belong to the yellow race. Their ancestors came from 

Asia not many centuries ago.

All of the people of Europe are descended from strong and active races. From these races have come many explorers and colonizers. From them have come also inventors, builders, merchants, and tradesmen.

To these people and their descendants the world owes modern science and its achievements. To them the world owes also its best literature, music, and drama, and its most enlightened laws and most progressive forms of government.

Some Europeans, however, have been restless, dissatisfied with their surroundings, and anxious to possess lands that belonged to others. Sometimes they have wanted lands for settlement, sometimes for the natural resources found there, and sometimes for their trade. This has often led to wars. 

The World War was the latest, and the greatest, of the wars of Europe.

The World War. The war which began in August, 1914, involved most of the nations of Europe. Fewer than one tenth of the people of Europe were able to remain neutral. 

The war not only caused vast loss of life and property, but led to important territorial changes. Germany and Russia lost large areas, as did Austria and Hungary, the former members of the dual monarchy of

Austria-Hungary. Out of parts of the areas lost by old nations, several new nations were established. To prevent future wars, if possible, a League of Nations, including most of the countries of the world, was formed. 

Governments. Before the World War there were but three important republics in 

Europe. These were France, Switzerland, and Portugal. All the other leading countries were monarchies.

As a result of the war, Germany, Austria- 

Hungary, and Russia are no longer monarchies, and most of the new nations of Europe are republics. There are now but twelve monarchies in Europe. 235

EUROPE 

A. A modern automobile highway in Sicily. The road winds up the mountain side, and along the way the tourist can catch glimpses of beautiful scenery. Many tourists visit Sicily to see Mt. Etna (page 183). 

Postal Union. Almost all of the countries of the world have joined in the Universal 

Postal Union. The Union has an office known as the International Bureau, at Bern, Switzerland. Every few years a meeting is held in one of the great national capitals to arrange for changes and improvements in international mail service. 

Roads. The building of good roads 

(A) began in Europe many years ago. For a long time the common roads of Europe were better built than those of any other continent. 

With the coming of rapidly driven motor vehicles, however, methods of construction were changed. It became necessary to build the roads even better than before, to make them wider and straighter, to bank the turns for fast-moving traffic, and to put them under control. Many of the roads of Europe are being rebuilt to meet the changed conditions of highway traffic. In no part of Europe are there so many automobiles and trucks in use as there are in the more densely settled parts of the United States. Yet there are places in Europe where automobile traffic has now become so great that it is necessary to put it under police control. Laws have been passed to regulate the speed of motor-driven vehicles, and traffic officers in the cities signal motorists when to go ahead and when to stop. 

The best of the European automobiles are among the finest made in the world.

Railroads and Steamship Lines. Most of the railroads of Europe are very well built. 

The roadbeds are firm, and the trains are handled with such care that there are very few accidents. In mountain regions where hydroelectric power is available, trains are run by electricity. In the Alps, and in other mountain regions, it has been necessary to build great tunnels, some of which are marvels of engineering. Long-distance travel without change of cars has been made possible between the most important cities of the continent. Much travel and much freight move for short distances only.

Courtesy London Midland and Scottish Railway 

A. A compartment in a corridor car in Great Britain.

Notice the view of the ancient bridge seen through the car windows. 

Passenger cars are divided into compartments, with differences in conveniences and equipment (A). In the railroad stations the trains run alongside platforms so that passengers can step from the train to a platform on the same level. Some of the compartment cars for passengers have a corridor running along one side, with the compartments opening out of the corridor. Others have the compartments running across the full width of the car, with doors opening out of each compartment on both sides of the car. 

The seats are along the partitions between compartments, so that, when the train is full, half of the passengers must ride with their backs to the engine. Likewise the berths made up for sleeping in the compartments are crosswise rather than lengthwise of the cars as they usually are in our country. 

The best-equipped of the compartments are the "first class" carriages, others less well equipped and carrying more passengers are "second class" or "third class." To travel first class costs more than to travel second class, and second class costs more than third class. In our country you do not find passenger cars of this kind, except some compartment sleeping cars.

European freight cars usually travel much shorter distances than do those in our own country. They are therefore much smaller than those in use in the United States, and more goods are carried in open cars than is usual in our country. Even goods that might be damaged by rain are sometimes carried in open cars in Europe, as they can be covered by waterproof canvas and be sufficiently protected for short journeys.

EUROPE 

Courtesy French Line 

A. The Ile de France, one of the finest liners on the Atlantic Ocean.

The greater part of the world's ocean shipping is controlled by European steamship companies. Among the countries that have a large merchant marine are Great Britain, France, Norway, Italy, the Netherlands, and

Germany. Many of the larger passenger ships (A) have been built for use on regular runs between European ports and the chief ports of other countries. The largest and most beautifully furnished of these ocean liners, as they are called, use the port of 

New York. As the years pass, faster and faster ships are being built- ships that are also safer and more comfortable.

Only a few sailing ships are still left on the seas. Most of the freighters, as the ships that carry goods are called, are steam-driven, as are the passenger liners. They are not so picturesque as the ships of the old days, which carried several masts with billowing sails of white canvas, but they are much faster.

Many ships are used in fishing. Fishing fleets from European countries may be seen at certain seasons of the year on fishing banks many hundreds of miles from their home ports. These fishing fleets are manned by sailors who know the sea in all its moods and tempers, and from them come the best of the sailors in the world's navies. 

Airplane Routes and Travel. All the main parts of Europe and the important cities can now be reached over regular air routes. 

The map, page 133, shows only the principal air routes. There are many others also.

Air travel is becoming more and more common, and the handling of mail and valuable packages is a regular part of the business of the airways. Improvements are constantly being made in airships, of both the "lighterthan-air than-air" and "heavier-than-air" types. 

The German airships to which the name "Zeppelin" has been given (239 A) are of the lighter-than-air type. Not only are such airships in constant use in Germany, but airships of that kind have made trips across the 

Atlantic, and around the world. They have accommodations for many passengers, and their engines drive them forward at high speed. Very large airplanes of the heavierthan-air type have been built. Some of them have as many as twelve powerful engines and can carry over 160 passengers. 

From some of the larger airports of Europe, planes take off on trips covering hundreds of miles, and forming links in routes to distant points in other continents.

Agriculture and Grazing. The chief agri cultural products of the European continent are foods. The cereals, potatoes, and fruits are of first importance. Wheat, both spring and winter, rye, barley, rice, and corn are grown each where the conditions are most

favorable. Sugar beets are used to furnish the main sugar supply of the continent, and the pulp is used as cattle food. A large part of Europe's meat supply comes from the cattle, sheep, and hogs raised in those parts of the continent where grazing lands or a food supply for the animals is available. Much meat is imported from other continents, especially from Australia and South America.

Grapes, used in the manufacture of wines or dried as raisins, are grown chiefly in Italy, France, Germany, Spain, Portugal, and 

Greece. Where wine is made, most of it is used by the people with their meals. 

In manufacturing regions food must be imported. It is only in southeastern Europe that a surplus of grain is available for export. 

Manufactures. - Europe is the manufacturing center of the world. Many things are made as skillfully elsewhere, but no other continent has so many workers engaged in manufacturing. Some of the raw materials are produced in Europe, others are imported.

All of the silk and wool produced in Europe, for example, would not be enough to keep the silk mills and woolen factories going, and the balance must be imported. Almost all of the cotton that is manufactured is imported, much of it from the United States. 

In a large sense, much of Europe and parts of North America manufacture for the world. 

South America, Australia, and Africa furnish foods and the raw materials of industry. 

Asia, a continent with ancient civilizations and ancient arts, is more self-contained, and has only recently entered into the life, industries, and trade of the modern world. 

Trade. The prosperity of the manu facturing nations of Europe is bound up with their trade. Some of the raw material used in their industries comes from distant parts of the earth. Also there must be found somewhere, at home or abroad, markets in which the manufactured goods can be sold. A failure to sell them means that further manufacturing must stop until they can be sold. 

 A. The Graf Zeppelin at a mooring mast. 

To close factories and mills means a loss of work and pay, and great hardship for mill and factory workers. Anything that upsets the usual movement of trade means loss of work and income for people in all parts of the world. 

To a very great degree the prosperity of people in one part of the world is dependent upon the prosperity of people in many other parts of the world.

AFRICA 

245 and the Dutch made only a few settlements. 

Exploration and settlement of most of Africa by Europeans waited through the years. 

Down to the time when your great-grandparents were living, no white man had followed the great African rivers to their sources. 

Only their lower courses were known. White men knew little or nothing of the many trails that wound across the deserts or through the grasslands and the gloomy forests of the 

Dark Continent. 

Before taking up the story of the exploration of Africa and its division among European nations, you should learn about its surface and its climate. 

The Position of the Continent. - Study the map on the opposite page. Notice that the Strait of Gibraltar is only a little farther north of the Equator than the southern tip of the continent is south of the Equator. 

This means that the Equator crosses Africa nearly midway between its northern and southern limits. The northern part, however, because of its shape, is much larger than the tapering, triangular-shaped southern part. In a very rough way, Africa and South 

America are alike. You will see that both are broad at the north, both have a western bulge, and both narrow toward the south. 

Of the two continents Africa lies much farther toward the north than South America, and has a much greater share of its total area in the Torrid Zone.

The nearness of Africa to Europe has had much to do with its later history. It faces 

Europe across the Mediterranean Sea. It is separated from Spain by the narrow Strait of Gibraltar. About midway along its northern coast the island of Sicily lies in the Mediterranean like a giant stepping stone between Italy and Tunisia. On the northeast, the 

Isthmus of Suez connects it with Asia. A part of its northeastern boundary is separated from Asia by the waters of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Elsewhere Africa faces out on great oceans.

COASTLINE AND SURFACE 

247 

A Regular Coastline with Few Harbors. 

When you were studying the British Isles you learned about the continental shelf upon which they stand. If you do not remember what it is, turn back to pages 83, 85 and read what is said about the broad shelf just off the west coast of Europe. The continental shelf of Africa is narrow, and the African coast line is regular. There has been no sinking of the continent to allow the sea to penetrate into its interior as it did in Europe. 

The surface of Africa is such that even if the continent did sink a little, the sea would not reach far inland. There is a coastal plain, but it is narrow, and most of the interior of the continent is high, with escarpments at the inner margin of the coastal lowlands. 

Surface. The three continents that you have already studied are North America, South America, and Europe. In each of these you found long, high mountain ranges, other ranges that were lower and shorter, and great interior lowlands. The surface of 

Africa is very different. 

Most of its surface is made up of plateaus. Some of these are higher than others, but none of them reach great heights. The only interior lowlands (shown in green on the map, page 244) are in the Sahara. This map shows you that the plateau of North Africa is generally lower than that of South Africa. It shows also that there are mountains scattered over the continent and rising above the level of the plateaus.

The long parallel ranges known as the Atlas 

Mountains extend through northern Africa for about 1400 miles. They reach from the 

Atlantic Ocean to the eastern part of Tunisia.

The highest point in these mountains has an altitude of nearly 15,000 feet above sea level. 

You have already read about these mountains in connection with your study of the lands bordering the Mediterranean (pages 194195). A. 

A gorge in the Atlas Mountains. on both sides of the Equator and are therefore in the warmest part of the earth. Yet their tops are covered with snow and there are glaciers among their higher valleys. Their highest peak rises to an elevation of nearly 16,800 feet. Where else have you found mountains near the Equator whose higher parts are always covered with snow?

Eastern Africa has a highland that extends from the Red Sea to the Zambezi Valley. It is really a very high plateau with a rugged surface, above which rise many volcanic peaks. In Ethiopia a part of this plateau has been given the name of the Plateau of Abyssinia. Here are short mountain ranges, some of whose peaks are from 14,000 to 15,000 feet above sea level. Farther south, near Lake Victoria, the volcanic peak Kilimanjaro rises to a height of more than 19,700 feet. To the east of Lake Victoria is Mt.

The Ruwenzori Mountains in east-central Africa are a short and high range. They lie | Kenya, over 17,000 feet high.
