Climate. You have already learned two things about Africa that have a great influence upon its climate. The first is that most of the continent lies within the Torrid Zone, as the Equator crosses the continent nearly midway between its northern and southern limits. The second is that much of Africa is made up of plateaus with some mountain areas rising above them. The first fact means that you will expect most of Africa to be hot. The second fact means that you will not expect interior Africa to be so hot as it would be if it were a region of lowlands only a little above sea level. 

You will remember that the prevailing winds in the Torrid Zone are the trade winds, and that they meet in the zone of equatorial calms. This region of calms moves north and south with the changing seasons. ing the summer of the Southern Hemisphere because at that time the vertical rays of the sun are moving toward the south. Twice during the year the vertical rays of the sun are on the Equator - late in March and late in September. It is then that the equatorial calms are truly at the Equator. 

The equatorial calm belt will therefore be wherever it is hottest, and there the air at the surface will be heated and will expand upward. Into it from the north come the northeast trade winds. Into it from the south come the southeast trade winds. These winds bring with them any moisture that they have been able to pick up as they move from cooler toward warmer regions. As the air rises in the region of the calms, it cools and rain falls. In the remainder of this study of the distribution of rainfall over Africa, make constant use of the maps on this page.

CLIMATE 

249 Because the equatorial calm belt is near the Equator twice during the year, that region has two rainy seasons and two seasons that are not so rainy. Here high temperatures and much rain have led to the growth of great forests. These are the rain forests of central 

Africa (A). The trees, the vines, and the shrubbery grow as thickly as they do in the rain forests of the Amazon basin of South 

America. To make your way in such a forest you must cut a path through a never-ending mass of vegetation. Overhead, the branches of the trees spread out and interlace to form a great leafy cover that almost shuts out the sun. In the heart of such a forest the ground is so shaded that even on bright sunny days it is in twilight.

Late in June the vertical rays of the sun have moved as far north as they ever go. 

During that time the equatorial calms reach their northerly position, and the region over which they are will be having rain. There is enough for a quick and luxuriant growth of grass. Six months later, or late in December, the calm belt will have moved to its southerly position, and the region over which it then is will be getting rain. In another six months the calms and rains will be back in the northerly position again. It has taken a year to make the round trip. From what has been said you can see that, at the outer limits of the zone over which the equatorial calms move or migrate, there are regions where there is a short rainy season and a long dry season. In such regions forests cannot grow. During the rainy season grass grows quickly. During the dry season it as quickly withers and dies. These are the grasslands, or savannas, that are found on the northern and southern borders of the rain forests. You found them in South 

America as the llanos of the Orinoco basin, in the southern Guiana Highlands, and as the savannas of Brazil. 1 In the north of the northern grasslands of Africa is the Sudan - the region over which A. 

Ewing Galloway

A rain forest near the Equator in the Belgian Congo. the northeast trade winds blow. South of the southern grasslands is the region over which the southeast trades blow. Remember that in both regions the trade winds, as they blow over the interior plateaus, are moving from regions that are warm or somewhat cool. 

But as they move toward the equatorial calms, they are moving into warmer regions. 

Such winds give no rains except where they are forced into higher altitudes. A study of your rainfall maps will show that rain or snow falls on the mountains that lie in the path of these winds, and on the heights of the plateaus. Rain falls also on the easternfacing escarpment of the plateau of South 

Africa. Where there are no heights to cause the winds to rise and become cooler, there is little or no rainfall, and the lands that they cross are arid regions or deserts. 

The winds that blow across North Africa come off the lands of Asia on the northeast,

AFRICA 

Photo by Arthur S. Vernay 

A. Native huts on the Kalahari Desert. They are mere shelters fashioned of grasses and twigs, the only building materials to be found on this dry land. At the left is a native family. or out of the calms between the westerlies and the northeast trades. Some rain falls on the higher parts of the desert plateaus, but most of the land is left dry. This almost rainless land of North Africa and southwestern Asia is the greatest desert in the world. In Africa it is known as the Sahara. 

In southern Africa the southeast trades have crossed the Indian Ocean before reaching the land, and so come to the eastern escarpment of the plateau as moisture-bearing winds. In crossing the coastal plain, and in rising over the eastern edge of the interior plateaus, the winds are cooled, rain falls, and there you will find extensive forests. 

Wherever mountains rise above the plateaus, rain will fall on their windward slopes. In crossing those parts of the plateau lying farther inland and toward the west, the trade winds of South Africa, like those of North

Africa, are drying winds. This is the arid region called the Kalahari Desert (A). 

On the western edge of Africa, in the region of the trade winds both north and south of the Equator, the coast lands are deserts. This is in part due to the fact that the winds have traveled a long distance and have lost much of their moisture on the way, especially on the slopes of any highlands they may have crossed. It is also due to the fact that these trade winds are moving away from the continent along the west coast, not toward the continent. The same conditions are found in 

South America, and have caused the deserts along the western coast of that continent in the trade-wind regions. Notice that the deserts of Kalahari in Africa and Atacama in 

South America are in about the same latitude. 

North of 30° north latitude and south of 30° south latitude are zones in which the prevailing winds are sometimes the westerlies, sometimes the trades. It is in these latitudes that you find the migrating calms of the horse latitudes. In the horse latitudes, the

LAKES AND RIVERS 

251 air is descending toward the surface of the earth. The winds moving out of these calms toward the North Pole and toward the 

South Pole are the westerlies. Those moving toward the Equator are the trades. 

Over the Mediterranean coastal region and over the extreme southern end of Africa, the prevailing winds are sometimes the trades, sometimes the westerlies. They are areas in which you find the Mediterranean type of climate (pages 165-166). The rainy season is in the winter of each hemisphere, when the trade winds are blowing inland. The dry season is in the summer of each hemisphere, when (and where) the westerlies are blowing away from the land.

The two areas that have this Mediterranean climate, and other areas that are cool because of their height above sea level, are the parts of Africa where white people can live and work most comfortably.

Lakes. — In regions of heavy rainfall in the highlands of east-central Africa there are a number of large lakes and several small ones. 

Find them on the map. Of these lakes,

Victoria is the largest, being almost as large as Lake Superior in North America, the largest fresh-water lake in the world. The waters of Lake Victoria also are fresh, and out of it toward the north flows the White Nile, one of the headwater streams of the 

Nile that waters Egypt. 

South of Lake Victoria are Lakes Tanganyika and Nyasa. They are long and narrow, and lie in parts of a rift valley formed by breaks in the earth's crust a long, long time ago (page 146). Both of these are freshwater lakes and among the largest in the world. Tanganyika has an outlet by way of the Congo River to the Atlantic, and the near-by Nyasa has an outlet by way of the 

Zambezi River to the Indian Ocean. 

In the Sudan, the grassland or savanna region to the south of the Sahara, find Lake 

Chad. You remember that these grasslands have a short rainy season and a long dry XA

The lake, therefore, varies greatly in size between these two seasons. Even in the rainiest season it does not now reach the size that it once had. Although many streams flow into the lake, it has no outlet. 

Rivers. — Africa has four great rivers.

The longest of these is the Nile, beginning with the White Nile that is the outlet of Lake 

Victoria. In its northward course to the

Mediterranean, it flows a distance of about 3700 miles. The length of this and other large streams in Africa and the sizes of their drainage basins are given in Table 4 at the back of the book. The map (A) on this page shows you where the drainage basins are. On its way to the north the Nile is joined by the Blue Nile, which comes from the plateau and mountain region of Ethiopia on the east. 

The headwaters of the Nile are, therefore, in regions of heavy rainfall along the Equator and in Ethiopia. The supply of water is so great that it flows for hundreds of miles through a desert, and then enters the Mediterranean as a large stream. The Congo River is shorter than the Nile, but carries a still larger amount of water. 

Some of its headwater streams rise near sources of the Nile, but their waters finally reach the Atlantic Ocean instead of the

Mediterranean. Some of the streams that unite to form the Congo come from the north, and some from the south. The main stream flows first to the north, out of the east-central part of South Africa. It then 

It then makes a great bend, flowing west and then southwest to the Atlantic Ocean. Trace its course on the map. Most of its course is in the region of heavy, drenching equatorial rains, and it is bordered by the vast rain forests of the west-central part of the continent. Near the place where the main stream turns toward the west are Stanley 

Falls. Not far from the Atlantic, where the river breaks over the western edge of the central plateau, there is a series of rapids. 

Above the rapids are Stanley Pool and the city of Léopoldville. Between Stanley Falls and Stanley Pool the river is navigable and furnishes the best, and almost the only, method of transportation for a large tributary region. Railroads have been built around the falls and around the cataracts below the pool, so that goods can be more easily handled in their transportation down or up the river.

The Niger is the great river of that part of western Africa north of the Equator. It rises not far from the Atlantic coast, flows northeast for a long distance, and then turns southeast to enter the Gulf of Guinea. Much of the river is navigable, but like other great African streams it is interrupted by rapids that prevent steamboats from going from one part of the river to another. 

The Zambezi (A) is the principal river of southern Africa. It rises near the sources of the Congo and follows a winding course to the Indian Ocean. The Victoria Falls, on this river, are nearly three times as high as Niagara Falls.

AFRICA 

PLANTS AND ANIMALS 

Remember that most of Africa lies in the Torrid Zone. Only small parts of it in the north and south extend into the North Temperate and South Temperate Zones. You have learned of the distribution of rainfall and the variations in temperature over the continent, and how both of these are influenced by latitude and altitude. You will naturally expect, therefore, to find great differences in the native vegetation and animal life. The differences in the vegetation will result from the differences in climate. 

The differences in the animal life will depend, in part at least, upon differences in vegetation. Animals naturally seek the forest, the grassland, the desert, the swamp, the lowlands, uplands, or mountains as they find in one or another the food or protection that they need. 

In the Forests. - The rain forests of westcentral Africa are a dense jungle (page 249). 

Within these forests both softwood and hardwood trees are to be found. Among the

Types of land and vegetation of Africa. hardwoods there are such valuable trees as mahogany and ebony, but there is very little lumbering, because the valuable trees are scattered and it is difficult to move the logs through the dense forest. There are palm trees in this forest, however, from the fruit of which valuable oils are obtained. The natives gather the fruit and boil it to get the oil from the fibrous pulp. The first of the oil that comes to the surface is good to use as food. The rest is put into casks and sold to the traders who have their stations along the river banks. The kernels of the fruit are dried and cracked to get the nuts, which also contain a very valuable oil. 

Many millions of pounds of palm nuts are sold to the traders along the rivers, and are shipped to oil factories in Europe and elsewhere.

A part of the oil is used in preparing food products, but much of it is used in the manufacture of soaps. After the oil has been taken from the crushed or ground kernels, the cake that is left is sold as a cattle food. What oily seed in our own country is used in this way? 

Some rubber is gathered from wild plants and trees growing in the forest, as in South America. This industry, however, is not a large one and is not increasing. The rubber plantations in southeastern Asia, about which you will soon learn, produce a better grade of rubber and at less cost.

Gum copal, a resin of tropical trees which hardens in the air, is gathered and shipped chiefly to Europe and the United States. It is used in the manufacture of varnish. The bark of the mangrove is stripped from the tree and exported. It is used in the tanning of leather. Other products of this rainforest region include bananas, vanilla beans, and cacao beans. Most of the cacao comes from cleared areas which have been planted, and the industry has become one of the most important in west-central Africa. 

In the rain forests and other woodlands of Africa, as in the tropical forests of other continents, there are many poisonous reptiles

A. - Wild African elephants. It was formerly believed that African elephants could not possibly be tamed. Now, however, young ones are sometimes tamed and taught to do tasks, much like elephants in Asia. and insects. The most feared of the insects is the tsetse fly, whose bite brings on a sleeping sickness that has been fatal both to many natives and to white settlers and hunters. 

Mosquitoes which spread malaria are also present in the jungle. There are huge colonies of ants that move through the forest and destroy everything in their path. Many parrots and other birds with beautifully colored feathers flutter about. 

Wild elephants (A) roam in herds through the forests, but they are grass eaters and must live near enough to grasslands so they can get food. They are hunted both for their meat and for their ivory tusks, an important export product. Gorillas, chimpanzees, baboons, and monkeys, such as you see in zoos and circuses, are among the other animals found in African forests. 

In the Grasslands. Wild animals are found in all the grasslands of Africa. The "Big Game Country," however, is the grassland that lies around the outer edge of the jungles of the Congo basin. Over these vast savannas roam huge herds of antelopes, gnus, giraffes, lions (256 A), and zebras. Here also are elephants, hyenas, panthers, and leopards.

In the more bushy regions the huge rhinoceros is found. It is a grass-eating animal that usually feeds at night and hides in the bush during the day. The hippopotamus, another large and rather ugly-looking animal, is found in the rivers of central Africa, where it feeds upon the water plants. Lions live in the grasslands because they are meat eaters and can live on the flesh of other animals they can catch.

Some White men from Europe and from America come here to hunt the big game. come merely for the danger of the sport, others come to get specimens for museums and zoos, and still others come to take moving and still pictures of the animals in their native haunts.

AFRICA 

A.-Lions in the grassland of Tanganyika Territory. Lions in their native surroundings are said to be peaceful and harmless unless they are hungry or attacked by enemies.

A hunting expedition in Africa is called a safari, and the hunters usually travel in large groups with native porters and with beaters who know the favorite haunts of the animals. 

A safari lasts many days, even weeks, and the hunters camp in tents. 

Near the Deserts. You have learned that the vegetation near deserts is sparse, and that only a few kinds of low, scrubby thorn bushes can grow in such very dry regions. 

You will therefore find few varieties of animals near the great deserts in Africa.

Camels can thrive, for they pasture on the bushes and can go without water for several days at a time. On the edges of the deserts antelopes, gazelles, panthers, and jackals roam. There are also lizards and snakes, scorpions, and centipedes. Occasionally swarms of locusts fly over the dry country to the grasslands, where they destroy all vegetation in their path. Few flying birds can be seen, but ostriches are found.

In the oases around the wells and springs are tall date-palm trees, apricots, peaches, pears, and pomegranates. Much of the fruit is consumed at home, but many varieties of ripe and dried dates are exported in large quantities. 

EXPLORATION AND PEOPLE The entire Mediterranean and Red Sea coasts were known to some of the people of Asia and Europe long before the birth of Christ. The early stories of the Bible have much to say about Egypt. Phoenicians and

Greeks had colonies on the southern shore of the Mediterranean from Egypt to Gibraltar. 

They had some commerce in ivory and ostrich feathers, which must have come from the interior. Little was known of Africa beyond the northern edge of the Sahara.

Explorations. When the age of African exploration finally began, it was carried forward principally by the larger European nations. It was by explorations for which they were responsible that the veil of secrecy was lifted from the Dark Continent. It may have been given this name because of the dark-skinned people who lived in so much of it, or because it had been so long unknown and unexplored. Whatever the reason, once exploration was seriously begun, many of the nations of Europe became interested. 

Africa differs from the other continents because so little of its area is controlled by independent countries. On the map, page

EXPLORATION AND PEOPLE 

257 

242, find Liberia in western Africa, and 

Ethiopia and Egypt in northeastern Africa.

These three are the only regions of the continent that are independent. All the rest of Africa has been divided among European powers. 

In the last century two British explorers did a great deal to make the interior of the continent known to the world. The first was David Livingstone, a Scotchman, who went to southern Africa as a medical missionary in 1840. He carried on his work as a missionary and carried forward his explorations until his death in 1873. He learned much about the Zambezi River region and the region of the great lakes at the sources of the Nile and Congo rivers. The other great explorer of that time was Henry M. Stanley.

Although British by birth, he was sent by a New York newspaper in 1869 to find Dr. Livingstone. Livingstone had not been heard from for a long time, and many people interested in his work were greatly worried. He was found by Stanley, but was so sick that he died on the way out to the sea. His body was carried to the seashore by some of the black people for whom he had done so much. 

At this time and later, Stanley continued his explorations, which were chiefly in central 

Africa in the Congo basin.

Since then, from time to time, many other explorers have added to our knowledge of African geography, until now there are only small regions that have never been visited by white men.

European Powers in Control. The coun- 

The coun- tries that control most of Africa are Great 

Britain, France, Belgium, Italy, and Portugal.

They are countries with dense populations. 

Portugal has had her African colonies since the days of early discovery. Great Britain acquired the Dutch colony at the southern end of Africa more than a hundred years ago.

The other parts of Africa have been occupied by the various European owners in more recent times.

One reason for the dividing of Africa among the European powers is that these European nations want land where some of their people can find new homes. Another reason is that they want more raw materials that their colonies can produce for the factories at home. They hope to raise a great deal of cotton, for example, so they will not need to buy so much cotton from the planters of our southern states. They expect to find forest wealth and useful minerals, and perhaps some precious metals. The British have found gold and diamonds in South Africa; Belgium makes much money from the rubber of Congo forests. They also want new markets for the things which are made in European factories. 

They want to train the African Negro to work, and produce things needed in Europe. 

At the same time, they want him to wish for things made in Europe. Thus commerce will grow, and both the Europeans and the Africans will be helped. It is, therefore, the growth of European nations and the desire for expansion of territory and trade that have led to the dividing up of Africa among the 

European powers.

As long ago as 1885 a meeting was held in Berlin, to settle questions in connection with the peaceful division of the continent among the nations. Partly as a result of that meeting, Germany came into possession of nearly one tenth of the continent. But in the World War, Germany lost all of her 

African colonies. Some went to the French, a small part of East Africa went to the 

Belgians, and all of the remainder went to the British. 

At the present time France and Great

Britain together hold three fourths of all African territory. On the whole the British possessions are of the greater importance, because they have good soils and, in South Africa especially, a climate in which white people can live and work in safety and comfort. Among the regions in the British 

Empire are South Africa, Rhodesia, East

People. In each of the European possessions in Africa at least a few of the people are of the white race. North of the Sahara nearly all the native peoples are of the white race; but south of the Sahara nearly all are of the black race, that is, Negroes (A). The 

Negroes number more than 100,000,000, but are divided into many, many different tribes, speaking different languages or dialects, and varying greatly in degree of civilization. 

Many are savages, living largely by hunting and gathering fruits that grow wild.

Many are herdsmen, some of them nomadic. Many are farmers. The Negroes have no large cities of their own; most of them live in small villages. Among the tribes most remote from white influence are the Pygmies, people only about half as tall as most 

Negroes and white men.

COUNTRIES AND PRODUCTS 

You have learned that Africa is largely under the control of European peoples who are spending vast sums of money to develop its resources and build up its industries. How successful have they been? There are also some small parts of the continent that have independent governments. What are their present industries and how successfully have they developed their resources?

Egypt. - Civilized people lived in Egypt and had a strong kingdom for thousands of years before the time of Christ. Much of their ancient history has been learned in recent years because scholars have been able to read the old inscriptions and other writings that have been discovered. Most of the inscriptions and other records that scholars have found in Egypt would have been destroyed in a land with a moist climate and severe changes of temperature. They have been preserved in Egypt because it is an arid country. The Egyptians took great care in embalming and wrapping the bodies of their dead, which are known as mummies.

The mummies of some of the ancient kings have been discovered, and many beautiful and interesting articles used by them during their lifetime have been found in their tombs. 

The pyramids of Egypt, made of blocks of stone, were built as burial places for some of the kings. The building of such pyramids required the work of thousands of men for many years. The largest of them are about 

450 feet high. Temples with many huge columns were built in the same way. Single blocks of stone of great size were quarried, carved with inscriptions, and set up as monuments. These are known as obelisks. Some of these obelisks have been taken from Egypt and set up in foreign cities, as in Rome, in 

London, and in Central Park, New York.

The Sphinx is a giant statue carved out of rock, having the body of an animal and the head of a human being.

Egypt suffered under Turkish rule for many years. In 1883 it became a nearly independent monarchy, under British influence.

The people were justly taxed and were taught modern farming methods and the use of farm machinery. Since 1922 Egypt has been a sovereign state with its own king, but Great Britain continues to guarantee order and to protect the Suez route and neighboring colonies. 

Egypt is several times as large as the British Isles, but most of it is a desert like the Sahara. The Nile flows through it from south to north. For thousands of years the people have lifted or pumped the water over the flood plain and the great delta at its northern end. But the Egyptian ways were crude, and it was not until British engineers introduced scientific methods that the land was properly irrigated.

The floods in the lower Nile were largely due to the heavy summer rainfall of Ethiopia. 

Much of this highland area is drained by two tributaries of the Nile. As the heavy rainfall gathered in these tributaries, it hurried

AFRICA 

A. One of the locks in the Aswân Dam. On the right you can see a section of the first cataract of the Nile. on to the main stream and then flooded the lowlands, leaving a cover of fine, rich soil. 

One crop a year could be grown. 

The lower Nile began to rise in June and continued to September, reaching a height of from 30 to 50 feet above its low-water level. 

The Egyptians piled up ridges of earth to form shallow basins for holding some of the flood waters. These they built at various levels on lands that were usually flooded. 

The basins filled as the waters rose high enough to cover them. Later, when the floods went down, the water in these basins was used to irrigate the near-by fields. The basin system of irrigation is still in use in some parts of the Nile Valley, as are also some very old methods of lifting the water from the river to the fields.

In spite of the great variation in the level of the lower Nile in Egypt, it is usually navigable as far south as the first cataract at 

Aswân (A). British engineers found that they could make a large lake south of this cataract, by building a great dam across the Nile at this point. The rocks of the cataract gave an excellent foundation for such a dam, and it was built. It is one and a fourth miles in length and 164 feet in height. The lake or reservoir is 200 miles long. Water from the lake can be let out into canals, and spread over a large area of fertile fields as needed. 

As a result, more than one crop a year can now be grown in parts of the valley that formerly produced but one, and fields are now irrigated that formerly were not reached by the annual floods.

Crops of both temperate and hot climates are raised, including a large amount of wheat and other grains. Many different kinds of dates are exported, both ripe and dried. The 

Egyptian cotton, grown largely in the Nile delta, has a long, strong, fine fiber and is one of the best cottons in the world. The country stands next to the United States and India in the export of this fiber. Some Egyptian cotton is used in American mills for making special kinds of goods, but most of it goes to England. 

There are more than 14,000,000 people in Egypt, and more than nine tenths of them are

Nile delta, is the capital. It is the largest city in Africa, with a population of more than 1,000,000. In its museum is a marvelous collection of Egyptian articles, many of which have come from the tombs of Egypt's early rulers. Cairo's dry and healthful air, and its historical interest, attract people of many lands, who make it a resort for the winter months. 

Alexandria is still the chief seaport of Egypt, as it was in ancient times. 

The Suez Canal extends from Port Said, on the Mediterranean, 103 miles to Suez, at the head of the Red Sea. Of this distance, true canals cover 76 miles, and lakes 27 miles. 

The canal was completed in 1869 after ten years of work. It is 41 feet deep, and all but the very largest ocean vessels can use it. | Before it was dug, ships for the Far East sailed around the southern end of Africa or South 

America, and Mediterranean commerce was much less important than now. Now ships from London and other European ports go by the Suez route to the ports of southern and eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand.

In normal times about 5000 ships pass through the canal each year. The greatest number of the ships are British, but there are many under the French, Dutch, Japanese, Italian, and other flags. 

Libya. When you studied Spain, Italy, and Greece, you learned that the Mediterranean Sea is a vast body of water, and that long voyages are needed to go from one part of the shore to another. On a trip from 

Cairo, the great city of Egypt, to Tripoli, the traveler will go first to Alexandria and there take a ship, just as people did 2000 years ago. The ship will be much larger, safer, 'faster, and much more comfortable than in those old days. Use the scale of miles to find the distance from Alexandria to Tripoli. It

AFRICA 

is about 1000 miles. The distance looks short on our small map, but probably three days or more will, even now, be needed for the voyage; and in the old days a much longer time was necessary.

Libya is a country with a small and scattered population made up of Berbers, Arabs, Jews, and desert tribes. It is an Italian colony and is larger than Spain, France, and Germany combined. Yet, because it is mostly desert, it has fewer people than Hamburg or Glasgow. Without the Nile, Egypt would probably have as few people. 

Unfortunately, Libya has no river to moisten its desert soil.

Libya, like Egypt, was at one time a part of the Turkish Empire. The chief city is Tripoli. The sands and shoals of this part of the Mediterranean were feared by ancient seamen, and navigation is still dangerous. 

Along this shore Greek divers come every year to gather sponges from the sea bottom. 

In the deserts of Libya and in other parts of northern Africa, a plant known as esparto grass is found. It has strong fibers. The stems are gathered, bound into huge bundles, and carried by camels to the sea. There they are put on ships and sent to England, where they are used in the manufacture of paper. 

From Tripoli caravans follow desert trails across the Sahara to Lake Chad, the Niger

River, and parts of the Sudan country. 

Tunisia and Algeria. Tunisia and Al geria are the nearest and most useful colonies of France. All this region has the Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers and rainy, warm winters. Such a climate favors the growth of many crops, as you know from your earlier study of this region (pages 166 and 195). 

Tunisia and Algeria are far more progressive countries than Libya. More railroads have been built there than in most parts of Africa, and there are thousands of miles of telegraph and telephone lines. Tunis and

Algiers (A), the two capitals, are well-governed cities, and are visited every winter by many

Morocco. Morocco has been until recently an entirely independent country, ruled by a monarch called the sultan. Its resources are like those of other north African countries, but most of its people live in ignorance and barbarism, and it is not yet an orderly or safe country. France has recently gained some control over most of the country, and may in time give Morocco as good government as Algeria and Tunisia now have. 

Spain controls a small part of Morocco. 

Tangier, in a "neutral zone," is the principal city and seaport. Casablanca, the French port on the Atlantic, has an excellent natural harbor and is a very busy city (A). Fez, also in French Morocco, is an important trade center, inland from Casablanca. Here you will find well-made articles of leather. Other important cities are the capital Rabat and 

Marrakech, a trade center on the desert edge.

The Sahara. On the map, page 244, find the name Sahara. To the eastward find

Desert Plateau, Libyan Desert, and Nubian Desert. Remember, also, that Egypt is prac- 

| tically all desert except along the Nile. This vast desert area stretches east into Arabia and

Cape Blanco and Cape Verde. It is several thousand miles long, and includes nearly one third of the total area of Africa. This, you remember, is the land of the northeast trade winds. They come from over Asia and cause here the greatest desert in the world. The desert area of North Africa is greater than the entire area of the United States.

Little grows in such a desert, for much of it is too dry even for grass. There are parts that are covered with sand dunes that the winds move ever before them. Whirling storms lift dust, dirt, and sand, and drive them across the desert. Men and beasts must lie down and protect themselves as best they can when such storms overtake them.

The caravans carry ivory, ostrich feathers, and skins from central Africa or the Sudan region to the Mediterranean coast cities. They carry back to the natives various products of Europe, such as cloths of cotton and wool, beads, paper, drugs, and sugar. The chief item in this list is cotton goods from Great Britain. 

The caravan trade is not so large as it was, for short railroads that lead out to the ocean are being built in the countries south of the Sahara, and goods are being shipped in and out by rail. Also, automobiles with a special kind of wheel are being used on the desert with considerable success.

A. A native kraal in southern Africa. Fences separate the small yards about the houses. See how neatly the straw roofs are made. ground water comes out in springs. Here are oases in which are seen palm trees, gardens, villages, and people.

Between the markets on the north, and the moist and fertile regions of the south, trade has been carried on by the nomads of the desert for thousands of years. The trade routes across the desert lead from oasis to oasis, and animals must carry both goods and men, for the routes are poorly marked and there are no railroads that cross the Sahara.

Some caravans are small, and some have thousands of camels with their drivers and guards, and carry goods having a value of hundreds of thousands of dollars. A caravan journey across the Sahara may take several months, and is full of danger, for bands of robbers are common in the desert. They know where all the wells and springs are, and often demand money from passing caravans even when they do not plunder them.

Camels are the animals chiefly used to carry burdens across the desert, because they can go several days, if necessary, without drinking. Each animal carries a load of about 300 pounds, and a day's march may last sixteen hours. 

Central and Southern Africa. The cen tral and southern parts of the continent were almost as difficult for the white man to penetrate as was the desert. Along the east and west coasts, the lowlands of the rainy region are damp, unhealthful, and covered with a dense jungle growth. The coasts of the drier regions are barren and uninviting, and there are but few good harbors. Everywhere these coastal lowlands are narrow and are backed by the seaward-facing escarpments of interior plateaus. This part of the continent has always been the home of the black, or Negro, The first white men to enter it found most of the Negroes densely ignorant. For many years the few white visitors only made the condition of the natives worse. They came to Africa for little else than to buy Negro slaves from warring Negro tribes, or even to capture Negroes themselves. The captives were placed on ships and kept as prisoners during the voyage to America or to some other land where they were sold. The slave trade, however, was stopped by civilized nations more than a hundred years ago. race.

Sudan Countries and Ethiopia. The Su dan is the region south of the Sahara. It extends from the Atlantic Ocean eastward to Ethiopia and the Red Sea. On the south are the Gulf of Guinea and the watersheds between Lake Chad and the Congo River system. The Sudan is not so hot and rainy as the tropical forests, nor so hot and dry as the Sahara. Many of the Negroes of the Sudan, west of Lake Chad, belong to the Hausa tribes. These tribes are among the best and most prosperous people of the African black race.

France governs the central and much of the western part of the Sudan. In the west the chief center for trade between the Sudan and the Sahara is the ancient city of Timbuktu on the northern bend of the Niger. It is the center of many caravan trails. Natal and Cape of Good Hope. Natal is a province on the east coast, with Durban as its seaport. The principal city and seaport of 

Cape of Good Hope is Cape Town. 

Rhodesia stretches northward from the 

Transvaal to the Belgian Congo and East

Africa. It is named for Cecil Rhodes, an Englishman who did much to develop South Africa. 

Southwest Africa, a former German colony, has been placed under the control of the 

South Africa produces grain, and supports many sheep and cattle. A large amount of wool is exported, and there are many ostrich farms. Gold is mined near Johannesburg, in the Transvaal. This region is by far the greatest gold-producing area of the world.

The When 

At Kimberley in Cape of Good Hope are the largest diamond mines in the world. gems are dug in a rough state out of masses of partly decayed volcanic rock. The native laborers are watched and searched to see that they do not steal the precious stones. sold, most of the diamonds go to Antwerp or

Amsterdam to be cut and polished. After the diamonds are polished most of them are taken to the United States, which is the largest market for precious stones.

Small African Islands. - The Madeira and 

Cape Verde Islands and the island of St. 

Thomas (page 179) belong to Portugal. St.

Helena is a small island off the southwest coast of Africa. It is known as the place to which the European powers exiled Napoleon Bonaparte several years before his death. The Canary Islands belong to Spain. 

Fernando Po is part of the colony of Spanish Guinea. In the Indian Ocean the island of 

Réunion is ruled by France, and Mauritius 

Island by Great Britain. 

Madagascar. -The island of Madagascar, off the southeast coast of Africa, is the largest island of Africa, and third in size among the islands of the world. It is larger than either 

France or Germany. Madagascar is under

French rule. There is a narrow plain backed by mountains along the east coast, and the interior is largely a high plateau. There is a broad coastal plain on the west. Being in the region of the southeast trade winds, the eastern part of the island receives a heavy rainfall (maps, page 248) and has a luxuriant growth of tropical forests. Farther west there is much less rain and the forests are replaced in part by grasslands or savannas. 

Although the island belongs to France, there are but few French people living there, and most of the agriculture is in the hands of the natives. The chief crops are rice and manioc, from which a native flour and tapioca are made. Sugar cane, cacao, and coffee are raised, as they are in so many parts of Africa with a similar climate. Some vanilla beans are raised also.

Cattle raising is an important industry in the grasslands, and hides and meat are exported, chiefly to France.

Among the mineral resources is graphite, from which the lead in pencils, a mineral lubricant or grease, and stove blacking are made. Mica, a mineral that can be split into thin transparent sheets, is also found on the island. Mica is used in stoves and in the electrical industries.

The population of the island is nearly 4,000,000, mostly natives who are descended from Negro and Mongolian races. A railroad runs from Tamatave, a port on the eastern side of the island, to Tananarive, the capital. 

The French government has spent much money on roads, railroads, and in making harbor improvements.

AFRICA 

It is possible to think of Africa as a continent of the past - a continent within whose borders great civilizations rose to power and passed away. To this past belong the temples, palaces, monuments, and royal tombs of ancient Egypt. The ruins of these, scattered along the valley of the Nile, still tell us in their own voiceless way some part of the story of the great people who built them. In other ways, also, a part of the history of the days of Egypt's glory has come down to us. learning. Yet they were finally driven back across the strait into Africa, where their arts fell into decay.

It is possible, and much more reasonable, to think of Africa as a continent of the future. 

Slowly, under the leadership of Great Britain, Italy, and France, prosperity is being brought back to Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, and 

Morocco. You have already learned much about what France has done for Tunisia and Algeria and what is now being done in Morocco.

The work of Great Britain in Egypt is just as important. The building of the great dam at Aswân is only one of the ways in which Great Britain has been of help to the 

Egyptian people. 

Egyptian people. Great Britain has helped them, also, to secure a better government; and British mills make use of much of their cotton crop. Most important of all, perhaps, is the fact that Great Britain is pushing forward the building of a great railroad to connect Cape Town (A) at the southern end of the con- History tells us of other civilizations in northern Africa, not so ancient, but great in their time. Carthage, for example, was one of the splendid cities of the ancient worldyet Carthage has been but a heap of ruins for hundreds of years. The Moors, long before the time of Columbus, carried their arts and learning from their homes in northern 

Africa across the Strait of Gibraltar. There we find even today the evidence of their | tinent, with Cairo, near the mouth of the Nile.

As you have already learned, the political control of Africa is largely in the hands of 

Great Britain, France, and Belgium. The map on page 242 shows you which parts of the continent and its neighboring islands each of these countries controls. Only smaller areas are independent, or controlled by other countries. The lands controlled by 

Great Britain include (1) the whole of the southern end of the continent, (2) territories stretching from southern Egypt along the east side of Africa, to join with those at the south, (3) the entrances to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, and (4) lands along the Gulf of Guinea.

The possessions of France are even larger than those of Great Britain, but as a whole are of less value, as such large parts of them lie in the Sahara. Belgium has a central part of the continent in the basin of the 

Congo; and Portugal has two large colonies one bordering the east coast and the other the west coast of the southern part of the continent. 

Transportation. -The transportation routes in the interior of Africa are very poor and the methods of transportation are not satisfactory. Small steamboats are in use on the navigable stretches of the Nile, the Congo, the Niger, and the Zambezi, as well as on the great lakes. Short railroads lead inland from some ports, and the Union of South Africa, especially, has been active in railroad building (A). There are few roads on which wheeled vehicles can be used.

The one long railroad line planned has not yet been completed, and the carrying of burdens by the native blacks is still common.

AFRICA 

Cape-to-Cairo Railroad. - Cecil Rhodes, who was prominent in the settlement and development of South Africa, is given credit for thinking of building the Cape-to-Cairo Railroad. Parts of this route have already been built and it is being slowly but steadily extended. At the northern end of the route, a railroad has been built from Alexandria to 

Khartoum and beyond. At the southern end, the line has been constructed from 

Cape Town to the Congo. Between these two links in the route, steamships on lakes and rivers, short stretches of rail, and some overland travel by road must be used. It will probably be a long time before the railroad is completed and the whole of the trip can be made by rail. In the meantime, airplane travel has become more common, and many trips have been made into and across the continent. railroad lines connecting some of the ports with the country behind them.

Among the products that reach the Guinea coast from the interior are ivory, palm nuts, and palm oil. Peanuts from Gambia, cacao beans from the Gold Coast and from the

Portuguese islands, a small amount of wild rubber, and a little mahogany are other products. The mineral products of central and west Africa are increasing in number and value as further discoveries are made. Copper from the Belgian Congo is at present the largest in amount and the greatest in value, and enormous deposits have been located. 

There is tin in Nigeria, and some gold from the Gold Coast. 

The east African coast is divided into two regions. The one to the north is almost a desert. THARSIDE  

A. - Freight boats in the harbor at Alexandria. They are carrying baled cotton from the Sudan to the coast, where it will be put on steamers for shipment to other countries. freight. Farming is becoming important in 

Uganda, where cotton is a promising crop. 

East Africa, unfortunately for its people, is much farther from world markets than is the region around the Gulf of Guinea, and its trade will therefore be slower in developing.

South Africa gets rain enough for some crops along the coast, but the interior is chiefly a grazing region. It is largely given over to the raising of sheep and goats, and there are many millions of each. Cattle and horses are raised, but insects so annoy these animals that they are raised in much smaller numbers than in grazing countries where no such pests are found. The number of ostriches raised increases or decreases with changes in the use of their feathers.

The mineral resources of South Africa are of great value. Of these, the diamonds of the Kimberley region and the gold from the Transvaal are the most important. The market for diamonds and other precious stones used in the manufacture of jewelry is sometimes good and sometimes poor, as precious stones are not always in demand. But gold, on account of its use as money, is in constant demand. 

Cities. From what you have learned about Africa you will not expect to find many large cities. The two largest are in Egypt - 

Cairo, the capital, has a population of more than a million; and Alexandria (A), the port, has a population about half as large. These are the only cities in Africa with a population of more than half a million. 

Johannesburg, in the center of the goldmining region called the "Rand," is the largest city in the Union of South Africa. It has a population of about 380,000, most of whom make their living out of the mines or through trade. Cape Town, the chief port

AFRICA 

of South Africa, is next in size. It is a city with a beautiful and picturesque location. Another important city in the Union is 

Durban, a port which, like Cape Town, is a trading center and outlet for the mining regions of the interior. 

Algiers, with more than 250,000 people, Tunis, with more than 200,000, and Oran with about 170,000, are the chief ports on the western Mediterranean. Marrakech, with a population about as large as that of Tunis, and Casablanca, with a population a little less than that of Oran, and the smaller city of Fez are the three chief cities of Morocco. 

Ibadan in Nigeria has a population of about 250,000, while Khartoum and Omdurman in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, Port

Said on the Suez Canal, and Constantine an inland city of Algeria-each have a population of over 100,000. 

Notice that of the sixteen largest cities in

Africa, eight are ports and five others are not far from the sea. One is the center of a rich mining district and the two others are in the eastern Sudan, on the northern link of the 

Cape-to-Cairo Railroad. Making use of the tables of cities in the back of this book, compare these sixteen cities of Africa with the largest cities in our own country, in such states as New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio; or with the cities of New England, Great

Britain, France, and Germany. Such comparisons as these will help you to understand how new the settlement and development of 

Africa really is.

In encyclopedias, you can find a general survey. 

Compton's Pictured Encyclopedia, The World 

Book, The Book of Knowledge, and others are written especially for you. If you look up Egypt, the Sahara, the Congo, diamonds, cacao, elephants, or any other country, place, or product connected with Africa, you will find interesting facts that will help you.

Carpenter's Africa (American Book Company) 

takes one on a travelogue through all the interesting far-off countries. Allen's Africa, Australia, and the Islands of the Pacific (Ginn and Company) live. Pharaohs (G. P. Putnam Sons) will tell you of ancient Egypt. In Stanley's How I Found Liv ingstone (Charles Scribner's Sons) you will find a story of great adventure and historical interest set in the jungles of the Congo. Andrew's Old 

Morocco and the Forbidden Atlas (Doubleday, Doran & Co.) tells of the picturesque Spanish territories in the north of Africa. Walker's History of South Africa (Longmans, Green & Co.) discusses the Boer war and England's part in the development of southern Africa.

Macmillan Co.) there is an interesting chapter on the Nile. The great engineering feat at Suez is described in Wilbur's Egypt and the Suez Canal.

& Co.) will show you many entertaining and unsuspected facts about Africa. You can read about strange tribes in Du Chaillu's The Country of the Dwarfs (Harper and Brothers), and you can learn about the black race in McKenzie's

ASIA 

Asia is the largest continent. Its area is greater than the combined area of North and South America, or that of Europe and 

Africa. On a globe you will see that Asia is so large that by contrast Europe seems to be only one of its peninsulas. Indeed, some geographers like to think and speak of the two continents as one, called Eurasia. 

Position. On maps and on a globe, study the position of Asia in our world. At the south, one of its peninsulas reaches within a short distance of the Equator. At the north, a point on the mainland is beyond 77° north latitude; that is, within less than 

13° of the North Pole. Asia Minor, the westernmost peninsula of Asia, stretches westward between the Mediterranean and 

Black seas, and borders on the Aegean. 

Find the famous old city of Smyrna, the most western city of Asia. It is located close to 27° east longitude. In Europe this is about the same longitude as the boundary line between Poland and Russia. In Africa this longitude is over 250 miles west of Cairo, in Egypt. The most easterly point of Asia is on the shore of Bering Strait, opposite 

Alaska. It is at 170° west longitude.

Comparisons. In North and South 

America, the principal highlands have a north-south direction, and the central parts of the continents are lowlands. In Europe, the main mountain systems have an eastwest direction, and again the central part of the continent is a lowland. Africa has some scattered mountain areas, but most of it is made up of plateaus. Now study the physical map of Asia, page 278. Notice that the central part of the continent is a great highland and that the greatest lowland is the vast Siberian Plain that borders the 

Arctic Ocean.

The surface features of Asia offer some interesting contrasts. On the northern border of India are the Himalaya Mountains (A). 277

ASIA 

One great peak, Mt. Everest, is over 29,000 feet in height, and is the highest mountain peak in the world. Look westward on your map to the Caspian Sea, on the boundary between Asia and Europe. The basin in which this sea lies, and some of the land surrounding it, are below sea level. 

North of the Himalaya Mountains is the 

Plateau of Tibet. This plateau is not only the highest in the world, but is very large. 

It is more completely shut in by mountains, deserts, and the great canyons of mighty rivers than any other of the world's plateaus. 

The people who live within its boundaries know little of the rest of the world and have no desire to increase their knowledge of it. 

There are many other contrasts in Asia that are equally interesting. When you study the climate of the different parts of the continent, you will find some of the hottest and some of the coldest parts of the earth. You will find also places where no rain falls from year's end to year's end, and others where the rainfall is as much as 

500 inches in a year. To understand what such a rainfall means, find out how much the annual rainfall is in the place where you live. 

North America, South America, and Europe have great plains opening out on the world's seas, and it is not difficult to get into the central parts of these continents. Even the mountains there can be crossed, and railroads have been built across them to connect coastal lowlands with interior plains. Deserts, forests, swampy grasslands, savage peoples, and wild beasts have at times made travel in Africa difficult, but men have penetrated to remote corners of the continent, railroads are being pushed through, and steamboats are in use on rivers and lakes. 

In Asia, with a population of more than 

1,100,000,000. most of the people live in the lower lands around a great central highland. 

That highland is so large, so high, and so difficult to cross that it has kept the peoples of Asia apart.

Central Highland. The vast ranges of the Himalaya 

Mountains extend east and west, and some of its ranges and hundreds of its peaks are more than 20,000 feet high. Daring mountain climbers have more than once attempted to reach the top of Mt. Everest, but no expedition has yet succeeded. 

That mountain is nearly twice as high as Mt. Blanc in Europe, and more than twice as high as 

Mt. Whitney in the United States. 

American Museum of Natural History, N. Y. City

A. - The camels of this caravan have halted beside some sand dunes in the desert called the Gobi. Some of these camels are shedding their hair. The camel men collect this loose hair and save it to sell. It is used in making rugs, coats, and artists' brushes. 

On the slopes of the Himalayas, and among its higher valleys, there are great fields of snow and wonderful glaciers. 

These glaciers, like others that you have studied, move out of the high mountain valleys where they are formed, and down their slopes. Finally, like other mountain glaciers, they move far enough down their mountain valleys to get into lower and warmer regions where they melt as rapidly as they move forward. A number of the great rivers of Asia have their sources in the 

Himalayas, or in other high mountains of the central highlands. 

Under various names great mountain systems extend westward from the Himalayas through Afghanistan, Persia, Asia Minor, and southern Europe. Trace these ranges and learn the location of the Karakoram Mountains and the Hindu Kush. Where are the 

Elburz Mountains? You may think of these various ranges of Europe and Asia as making one great line of mountains, from the Pyrenees in western Europe to the southeastern part of Asia.

North of the Himalayas, in all of central Asia, is a region of vast plateaus and towering mountain ranges. The plateaus of Tibet, Turkistan, and Mongolia are very large. 

Tibet and the Pamirs have an altitude of more than 15,000 feet, or about three miles. 

Because the plateau of the Pamirs is so high, it is sometimes called "the roof of the world." Rising above the plateaus are many ranges of high mountains. They run in a general east-and-west direction, in about the same direction as the Himalayas. Among them are the Hindu Kush, Kunlun, Tien 

Shan, and Altai ranges. 

Turn again to the physical map. Find the Persian Gulf. Eastward find the Plateau of Iran, the Pamirs, Plateau of Turkistan, Plateau of Tibet, and the Gobi (A). The distance from the Persian Gulf to the Khinghan Mountains, at the eastern edge of the 

Gobi, is 4000 miles, with highlands all the way. This is the interior of Asia, and it covers an area as large as the United States.

ASIA Yet it has only about 5,000,000 people, while the United States has over 120,000,000. In contrast with this sparsely populated central highland of Asia, you will find that the eastern lowlands of China and the lowlands of northern India are densely inhabited. Why is there this great contrast in the number of people living in two parts of Asia so near to each other? It is because of the great differences in soils and because of even greater differences in the climate between the highlands and the lowlands.

The high mountains of southern Asia are drained by great rivers. Among these rivers are the Ganges, the Brahmaputra, and farther east the Irrawaddy and the Mekong. Although you may never have heard of the

Mekong before, it is over 2600 miles long. 

Part of the Himalayas send their waters by the Indus River to the Arabian Sea. Find all of these rivers on your map. Find also the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, which flow southward into the Persian Gulf.

On the east and on the south, the sea border of Asia is very much broken, with large lowlands and many islands, except in the far southwest. In these lowlands, except in the far northeast, and in many of the islands, the population is very dense and there are many great seaports and much trade. You will learn more about these things when you study the countries found in this part of the continent. 

In the west, Asia touches the Mediterranean, Aegean, and Black seas, and so opens out to the Atlantic Ocean. These shores, however, are not of great length, and are today of less importance in the trade of Asia than they were centuries ago. 

Asia has also an Arctic coast. You have already learned about its large rivers and its vast lowlands. Along this Arctic coast there are few people, no cities, and no ships.

Asia lies in the same zones as the continent of North America. The northern part of Siberia is intensely cold in winter. The region where the Lena River crosses the Arctic Circle is one of the coldest places known in the world. The average temperature there in January is 60° below zero. Europe and then pass for thousands of miles over the long stretches of Siberia, all the moderating effect of the Atlantic Ocean upon They The northern part of Asia is cold, and the central and western parts are dry; but the southeastern parts are wet and hot, and they contain about four fifths of the population of the continent. Southeastern Asia, including the near-by islands, has about 700,000,000 people. It is far more densely populated than any other region of equal area in the world. This is due partly to its great and fertile plains, partly to its climate, and partly to its trade with other parts of the world. In eastern China the climate is tempered by the nearness of the ocean.

Monsoons.-The climate is warm in the southern lowlands.

They are south of the Tropic of Cancer, and are but little ​above sea level. The rainfall of southern Asia is brought chiefly by winds from the ocean in summer. In summer the land of India and of other parts of southern Asia is highly heated by the almost direct rays of the sun. The air expands, rises, and flows outward at some distance above the surface of the earth, so that the air that remains presses less heavily on the surface. The cooler, heavier air from the Indian Ocean pushes in across the surface of the earth toward this area. Strong winds blow from the ocean over the land. A great amount of moisture is carried inland with them and falls as rain, especially on the windward slopes of the highlands, making part of northern

India the wettest region in the world (284 A). 

In the winter the land is cooler than the ocean, and the winds then blow southward from the land and give the country its dry season (A).

LIFE IN ASIA 

Waste Lands in Asia. There are large parts of Asia where you could travel for long distances without coming upon any settlement or even a single home. If you found any people in those lands, they would probably be nomads; that is, people who move from one place to another to find better hunting or to find fresh pastures for their herds and flocks.

You have now learned enough about Asia to know that there are large parts of it in which you would not like to live. Some are high and cold; others are covered with sand and have very little rain. On many of the mountains there are only bare rocks and snow and ice. Because of the thin air and fearful cold, you could not possibly live on them. In the far north the land is low and there is enough rain, but the soils are frozen to a depth of many feet, the rivers are often covered with ice, and there is little food to be had except reindeer meat, fish, and berries from some few low bushes. Yet there are people living in some of these regions. 

How, for example, do the people, few as they are, live in cold northern lands, and in the deserts and endless plateaus of central and western Asia? 

Certainly they cannot live by agriculture. Instead, they wander from place to place.

The nomads of northern Siberia (Russia in Asia) live in the far north only during a short summer season. At that time they gather the wild berries, and catch fish not only for summer food but to dry for winter use. In the winter they move south into the edge of the Siberian forests. There 

Arctic Circle 

Forests they may have rude huts or live in tents. 

The women stay at home and prepare the food, make clothing out of skins, and care for the herds of reindeer. The men go out in the forest to hunt for animals that have valuable furs. At all seasons the reindeer is their beast of burden and is of value because of its milk, its hide, its meat, and its bones, which are used for making tools. After the winter is over these people go back again to cold and barren northern lowlands, or tundras, where their reindeer can find food during the short summer season. are The people of the deserts and steppes also nomads. They have many horses, camels, cattle, and sheep. These animals need pasture, and as grass is thin over much of the area and the best is found in scattered patches, the people must be more or less constantly on the move to find food for their animals. Sometimes they must move every

These groups of nomads are not made up of a single family, but the sons and their families, and the servants as well, stay together, and thus the family becomes a tribe. The men of the steppe are expert horsemen from childhood, and wealth consists in owning many horses and other animals. Here, as in the tundras, the women do most of the hard work of the camp. The customs of these people make them independent and brave.

Animal Life in Asia. The animal life of 

The animal life of Asia is of great importance. Some of the animals are of help; others are dangerous and destructive. To live in far northern Asia, the people depend on their reindeer and on fish. 

In the forest belt there are fur-bearing animals otter, beaver, sable, and ermine whose pelts are shipped to the fur markets of 

Russia, to the German fur center, Leipzig, and to other countries and cities. In the 

horses are kept by the wandering tribes. In these regions the camel is one of the important beasts of burden, because it can live without water for several days when necessary. In India, elephants are found wild in the jungle. They are also trained to carry people, to haul heavy loads, and even to handle timber with their trunks. 

Lions (A), tigers (C), apes, and monkeys are found in the jungles. Crocodiles (B) are found in tropical waters, and serpents are found in the tropical forests. Insects of all kinds are numerous. Boring worms destroy timber, and the people have to take many precautions to preserve health and property.

In the East Indies, especially, there are many birds of brilliant plumage.

SOUTHWESTERN COUNTRIES 

The map of Southwestern Asia on the opposite page shows the countries west of India. The three largest of these are Persia (or Iran), Turkey, and Arabia, but the names and boundaries of others also are shown on the map.

As you study the map, notice the waters that border this part of Asia. On the north you will see the Caspian and Black seas, on the west the Aegean, Mediterranean, and Red seas, and on the south the Gulf of 

Aden and the Arabian Sea. Between the

Plateau of Arabia and the Plateau of Iran are the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf.

These two plateaus are still farther separated toward the northwest by the lowlands through which the Tigris and Euphrates rivers flow on their way to the Persian Gulf. 

Although southwestern Asia seems to include only a small part of the great continent, it is about four fifths as large as the 

United States. Yet it has only one fourth as many people as are found in our country, and ours is not one of the densely settled countries of the world.

A still greater contrast is shown between the population of southwestern Asia and that of such a densely settled region as westcentral Europe. The combined area of Great 

Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany is only a little more than one fifth that of southwestern Asia. But the combined population of these west European countries with their excellent climate, rich natural resources, many manufactures, and extensive trade, is more than three times as great as that of this part of Asia. Why should not southwestern Asia be as densely settled? Why are there so few people living in this part of Asia when there are so many living in India just to the southeast? 

Surface. The surface of much of southwestern Asia is high and rough. On the map find the two plateaus of Arabia and Iran.

The Plateau of Arabia occupies most of the Peninsula of Arabia. It is high, rugged, and barren, and only a small part of it has ever been carefully explored, most of it being known only to the nomads who wander across it. The plateau is, however, bordered by a narrow coastal lowland from the northern end of the Red Sea almost to the entrance of the Persian Gulf. There are lowlands on both sides of the Persian Gulf, and these extend northwest along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers phrates rivers the Mesopotamia (betweenthe-rivers) of ancient days.

The Plateau of Iran also is high and barren, but there is a narrow lowland along the Arabian Sea. the Arabian Sea. The mountains bordering the plateau are high and forbidding, with few passes across them to the interior. On the north of the plateau are ranges belonging to the great mountain system that extends through southern Asia and southern Europe. 

Trace the mountains at the northern edge of the plateaus of Iran and Arabia, and through Asia Minor to the Aegean Sea.

Notice especially the mountains east of the 

Caspian Sea, bordering the lowlands of 

Russia in Asia to the north.

Climate.- Study again the rainfall of southwestern Asia as shown on the maps on pages 284 and 285. You will remember that much of this region lies in the path of the trade winds that sweep out of the northeast and on toward the southwest across Arabia and into North Africa. These are drying winds, and leave but little rainfall behind except on mountain slopes, in mountain valleys, and over the irregular surface of some parts of the plateaus. This general lack of rainfall leaves much of the region a desert. Within the desert areas there may be, from time to time, some scant rainfall along the higher slopes of its irregular surface or in valleys among its highlands. This rainfall may sink into the ground and come to the surface in some lower place as a spring to form an oasis. If there is too little rain for an oasis, there may still be enough for a

ASIA 

A. Nomadic Arabs in camp on the edge of the desert. thin growth of grass. All such bits of pasture land are known by the desert nomads. 

Because of the nearness of southwestern

Asia to the Equator, its temperature ought to be high at all seasons of the year. But much of the higher land is so high above sea level that it is usually cool during the winter, and temperatures below freezing are sometimes reached.

In the summer, even in the plateaus, the direct rays of the sun, which are north of the Equator at that time, bring hot days. 

Along the narrow coastal plains the heat is intense, except when winds from the bordering seas help to cool the air. The summer heat in the Tigris-Euphrates lowland is so great that it is one of the hottest spots on earth.

In a region of so little rainfall there will be few rivers. There are only two large streams in this whole area. These are the 

Tigris and the Euphrates. Their headwaters come largely from the mountains of northern Turkey, but after leaving the mountains they flow through broad, flat plains. 

Ever since the dawn of history, water from these rivers has been used to irrigate these plains, and it is so used today. These plains were among the most fertile lands of the ancient world. Here grew up, one after another, several great civilizations; each one lasting for a time, only to be conquered finally and to give way to the next. 

The People of the Desert. The groups of nomads who live on the dry Plateau of Arabia, and in other dry regions of southwestern Asia, make a poor living and endure great hardships. They are a wild and independent people who measure their wealth by the number of animals that they own. 

Much of their life is spent in wandering with their animals from one small bit of pasture to another, where food and water for their camels, horses, sheep, and goats can be found. Occasionally some of them may visit an oasis in the desert or some small settlement on the desert edge to get food or other articles that they may need. They offer cheese, skins, wool, or camels' hair in payment for a saddle, dates, flour, or some coffee. After their trading is over they ride. back into the desert to join their flocks again. 

Towns, Farm Lands, and Crops. There are many gardens or small farms in parts of southwestern Asia, where grain, vegetables, and fruits can be grown. Most of them

Peninsula of Arabia, on the Red Sea. It is grown on the hillsides where a small amount of rain and fogs drifting in from the sea furnish the moisture needed. Here 

There are valleys among the mountains of Afghanistan and Persia, and on the margins of the Plateau of Iran, where the climate is much like that of the Mediterranean borderlands. There is a small winter rainfall, and crops of wheat and barley are raised.

Summer crops are irrigated, as they are along the Mediterranean, the water being taken from wells and streams. Figs, grapes, peaches, plums, apricots, and melons are among the fruits that are grown. Among the exports of Persia are sun-dried grapes, or raisins (A). Cotton and tobacco are grown on irrigated lands, and nut and mulberry trees are grown in protected valleys. There is a small silk industry in both Persia and 

Afghanistan, based on the use of mulberry leaves as food for silkworms.

In the more rugged parts of Persia, and in much of Afghanistan, little farming is done,
