The loom master sings the count of the different colored knots to be tied for the pattern, as a guide for the other workers. and the people give most of their attention to the raising of sheep, goats, camels, and horses. Some of the most interesting industries of this whole region are based on the use of such raw materials as hides, skins, wool, and silk. The hides and skins are used in the making of leather goods, including saddles, pouches, and book bindings. The wool and silk are used in the making of fine rugs, shawls, and cloth. 

Oriental Rugs. - The Persians, especially, are skillful in the making of fine Oriental rugs (A). These rugs are used on floors for their warmth and softness, on walls for their beauty of design and rich coloring, and as covers for great sacks of wool on which some Persians rest or sleep. Almost every district has its own patterns, colors, and methods of manufacture. Those who know about these can usually tell, by examining a rug, from what country and from what part of that country a rug came. The demand for Oriental rugs is now so great that many of them are being made in workshops instead of in the homes of the people as formerly.

Petroleum Production. It is probable that the mineral resources of southwestern Asia are not fully known. At the present time only petroleum is important. This is found in Iraq (Mesopotamia) and in Persia.

So much oil is now produced in Persia that it has become one of the most important oil regions of the Old World. 

Why the Population Is Small. Some of the things that you have learned about this southwestern part of Asia will help you to understand why so large an area has so small a population. Review these facts briefly. 

A large part of the region is a desert. Parts of this desert are unexplored and unknown, and are believed to be unproductive and uninhabited. Other parts furnish scanty pasture and a limited water supply for the

SOUTHWESTERN COUNTRIES 

295 flocks of nomadic peoples. Farm lands and towns are found in mountain valleys where there is rain or melting snow, in irrigated valleys, at the edge of deserts, and in oases where water taken from springs and wells make them possible. There are no manufacturing industries except such as are carried on in the homes of the people or in small workshops, and such as use local supplies of raw materials. Mineral resources, except oil, are almost lacking, and trade is small in amount and limited to a few articles. 

Yet explorers have found the remains of many ancient civilizations, and of great cities that were built within this region. 

Out of it have come great religions. What is the story of the rise and fall of these ancient peoples? Will that story help you further to understand why this part of Asia has today so small a number of people? 

The Story of Those Who Lived in South western Asia Long Ago. In the Old

Testament of the Bible, we find stories about the people who from time to time ruled in the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates.

Some of them also extended their power beyond the borders of Mesopotamia; to the east, as far as India; to the west, as far as the Aegean and Red seas. 

At a very early time the southern part of Mesopotamia was occupied by the Babylonians. Their royal city was at Babylon not far from the present city of Baghdad. 

The northern part of Mesopotamia was occupied at about this time by a fierce, warlike people called the Assyrians. They had their capital city at Nineveh, across the river and not far from the present city of 

Mosul. Wars between these two peoples were carried on for a long time, but finally ended when the Assyrians were conquered, and Nineveh destroyed.

Later the Babylonians were conquered by the Persians, who came out of the plateau on the east of Mesopotamia. The Persians pushed their conquests both east and west, and for a time ruled over much of this region that we have called southwestern Asia. 

The Hebrews, wandering shepherds, came from Chaldea, the region to the south of Babylon, and we find interesting stories of their wanderings in the Old Testament. 

There you can read of Abraham, going from

Ur in Chaldea westward across the desert, and finally settling in Palestine. In one of the Hebrew homes the founder of the Christian faith grew up. So both Jews and

Christians are interested in Palestine and call it the Holy Land. 

Most of the people who live in southwestern Asia are not Hebrews or Christians, but 

Mohammedans. Mohammed was a religious teacher who lived in Arabia about six hundred years after Christ; and his followers are called Mohammedans. They believe that "There is one God, and Mohammed is his prophet." Their sacred book is the Koran.

So firmly did they believe in the teachings of the prophet, that they attempted to make people accept their faith by the sword. 

Mohammed was born in Mecca, and was buried in Medina. To his followers both cities are sacred, and are visited by many thousands of pilgrims (296 A). Pilgrims from the north can make use of a railroad to

Medina, but from Medina to Mecca the journey is made by caravan. 

A Crossroad for Many Nations. This whole region has often been called a crossroad." What does that mean? From the time of the Phoenicians down to the time when the Ottoman Turks came out of central 

Asia and conquered all of southwestern Asia, it was crossed by trade routes. It was these 

Turks who blocked the trade between the 

East and the Mediterranean, and that, as you know, finally led to the discovery of the 

New World. 

During the thousands of years that trade was carried on across this southwestern part of Asia, two routes between the Mediterranean and Arabian seas were used. One

ASIA 

A. A pilgrim camp in front of a large Mohammedan mosque in a village outside Mecca (page 295). This is one of the places that must be visited by those who go on pilgrimages to Mecca. of these was by way of the Persian Gulf and the Euphrates Valley and overland to the Mediterranean. The other was by way of the Red Sea and across the Isthmus of Suez to the Mediterranean. Other trade routes crossed the plateau lands to points on the coast of Syria. Although the Turks blockaded the trade routes for a long time, they finally allowed the caravans to cross their lands again. But they ruled the nations they conquered with great harshness, and collected such heavy taxes that most of the people were always poor. Not only were the trade routes across and along the Mesopotamian valley reopened, but they are still in use.

Caravans still follow the ancient trails, and goods are still carried in and out of the hidden parts of this region on the backs of camels. Caravans no longer follow the route across the Isthmus of Suez. 

The Suez Canal was opened in 1869, and became a link in a great water route connecting the North Atlantic and Mediterranean with the Indian Ocean. As a result of the World War, Turkey was forced to give up its control of most of the people that it had once governed. Both Turkey in 

Europe and Turkey in Asia are but small remnants of the once great Ottoman Empire. 

Other methods of transportation are coming into use. Motor roads are being built and automobiles can now follow the

SOUTHWESTERN COUNTRIES 

297 old paths across the deserts, through the mountains, and on the plateaus. The motor highways connecting the larger cities are being improved. Airplanes are also in use over a few routes.

The nations of Europe have much to do with southwestern Asia. Great Britain controls the Suez Canal and Aden on the route to India and Australia. Germany before the war was building a railroad from 

Berlin to Baghdad and on to the Persian

Gulf. The Germans were seeking for a larger trade with the East, over a route that would rival Great Britain's sea route through the Suez Canal. Russia is hoping to arrange for a route across Persia to the Indian Ocean. 

The French have a "mandate" for Syria and the British have one for Palestine, lands which were under the control of the Turks before the World War. This means that the country having the mandate must keep order and insure good government for these smaller, less influential countries. 

Such a mandate is given by the League of Nations to some country strong enough to protect the dependent country, so that its people may have time to learn modern ways, with a view to taking over the control of their own affairs.

Asia is Turkey. Turkey in Asia includes all of Asia Minor, or Anatolia, the peninsula that has the Black Sea on the north, the Aegean 

Sea on the west, and the Mediterranean Sea on the south. Most of it is a rugged plateau, bordered by ranges of mountains on the north and on the south.

The interior of the peninsula is a semi-arid region, bordered on the south by the Taurus Mountains.

Some wool is exported, but much is used in the manufacture of Turkish rugs and carpets, and in the weaving of woolen cloth. The famous Angora goats that supply the fiber for mohair cloth are natives of this part of Turkey. 

Along the Mediterranean shores of Turkey there are farming regions with a Mediterranean climate. Wheat, barley, tobacco, cotton, fruits, and nuts are grown in Turkey, largely by irrigation. In the World War, Palestine, the "Holy

Land," was taken from the Turks after centuries of cruel rule. It was then placed under British protection. Most of the people of Palestine are Mohammedans, but Jews are developing there a new Zionist home land.

Palestine is a small country, but is of great interest because here the most important events of Hebrew history took place. Here 

Jesus lived, and the Christian church was founded. On the Mediterranean side is a coastal plain, the land of the ancient Philistines. Find Haifa and Jaffa, the seaports of 

Jerusalem. Back of the coastal plain is a range of low limestone mountains. On the top of this range is Jerusalem (A), the Holy City, and a few miles south is Bethlehem, the birthplace of Jesus.

East of this ridge is the deep valley of the 

Jordan River and the Dead Sea. The Jordan rises in a great spring south of Mount Hermon, flows through the Sea of Galilee and down to the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea is in so hot a region, and the rainfall is so scanty, that it has no outlet and is a salt lake. Its surface is 1292 feet below sea level, and it is so salty that no fish can live in it. The southern part of Palestine was the ancient kingdom of 

Judah, and the northern part was the kingdom of Israel, containing Nazareth, the home of Jesus.

Palestine is called in the Old Testament "a land flowing with milk and honey," but this statement is far from being true now.

Since those early days the country has been sadly neglected, its trees have been cut away, and much of the soil has been washed from the hillsides. At the present time it is beginning to prosper again under modern enterprise. 

Railroads extend from Haifa and Jaffa to 

Jerusalem. Another runs from Damascus to the sea at Beirut, and a long line extends from Smyrna to Damascus, and far southward through Trans-Jordan. Trans-Jordan is an 

Arab state under British protection. The railroad through it goes on to Medina, and may be continued to the outskirts of Mecca -the sacred cities of the Mohammedans.

Iraq and Arabia. - Iraq, also called Mesopotamia, is the region of lowland along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. It was the seat of ancient empires and of the cities of Nineveh and Babylon. Here, as in Egypt, irrigation was practiced in ancient times, and its use is again increasing with the revival of agriculture. New irrigation canals are being built and the old ones repaired. One of the chief resources is petroleum, of which large amounts are obtained. Baghdad is the principal city, with many mosques with tall, graceful minarets. Goods and passengers are carried on the rivers by rafts and steamboats. Iraq is an Arab kingdom, until recently under the protection of Great Britain. 

Arabia is about one third the size of the United States. It is widest at the south and is mainly a high plateau with a very dry climate. The only important cities are

Mecca and Medina, one the birthplace, the other the burial place of Mohammed; and 

Aden, on the southwest coast of the peninsula. This last-named city is owned by 

Great Britain and is fortified. It is an important fuel and supply station for ships using the Red Sea route. 

Oman is an independent state. Its seaport is Muscat, from which many dates are sent to the United States. In the Persian Gulf are important pearl fisheries. 

Persia. Persia, now called Iran by the

Persians, is an ancient country. Many centuries ago it was very large, reaching from the 

Mediterranean Sea to India. At that time it was the most powerful empire in the world. 

In the ancient capital of Persepolis its rulers built a magnificent palace that was burned down by Alexander the Great. Early in 

1933 the earth and sand that had so long covered the ruins of this palace were cleared away. Beautiful statues, great stairways (301 A), and other wonderful works of the ancient artists of Persia were found. They are described as the most beautiful ever found in Persia.

The Persia of today is a country nearly three times as large as France, but has less than one fourth as many people. So much of it is desert or barren mountain side that food for a large population cannot be raised. 

Much more of everything could be produced, however, if the people had the skill and the machinery that are common in 

Europe and America.

The surface of nearly all of Persia is a plateau with many mountains and valleys. 

Over much of the area the rainfall averages only about five inches a year. There are few rivers and many deserts. The streams usually disappear in the desert sands. The snow and rain of the mountains supply such streams as the country has, and the water is used in the valleys for irrigation. The northern part of the country, around the Caspian Sea, has a moister climate and considerable forest, but it is unhealthful. Silk, wool, cotton, tobacco, wheat, and barley are common products of Persia, as are fruits and gums. Many sheep and cattle are raised. 

Much of the wool is used in making rugs and shawls which are among the finest of those produced in Asia.

The cities have fine mosques and some beautiful shops. The houses are usually made of dried mud, and the windows open into an inner court, leaving the walls facing

Northern Asia. You learned much about northern Asia when you studied it as a part of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. 

Remember the three belts of country that make up this great northern lowland of Asia.

In the far north are the tundras. South of the tundra belt is the forest belt, sometimes called the Taiga. And south of the Taiga is the region where wheat is raised. 

Most of these three belts are a vast plain with a gentle slope toward the Arctic Ocean. 

Only on the south, hills and mountains begin to rise toward the central highlands of Asia. 

On the tundras there is little grass, with moss and wild flowers in the short summer,

Weary caravans arriving from Afghanistan along the Khyber Pass in India. Make an estimate of the number of beasts and men in this group. Below a foot or two, even in summer, the tundras are always frozen. Only a few nomads live in the tundra belt and in the edge of the forest belt (page 286). 

The dark forest is a shady, swampy world.

It is the home of hunters and lumbermen, with a little village or trading fort here and there. Much of it, however, has never been seen by man. Here is a vast supply of timber for which the Soviet Union and the world will sometime have use. Now it furnishes only the skins of ermine, sable, beaver, fox, mink, and marten, most of which are sent to distant lands. The great European fur markets are in London and in Leipzig. In these centers the furs are prepared for use, and then many of them are sent to the United States. Many of these Russian furs are sold in the northern cities of our country.

On the Siberian Railway, which runs through the wheat belt, are Omsk and Irkutsk, and a number of other smaller places. 

This Trans-Siberian Railroad is the only important railroad in Siberia. The building of branch lines must wait until the country is more fully settled. Some freight for shipment on the railroad is brought in over rather poor roads and by way of the rivers. The river freight comes by boat in summer, and by sledges drawn over the ice in winter. But the rivers are not very useful, for they flow from a desert wilderness in the south to a frozen wilderness in the north, and their mouths are in an icy sea.

In a limited way, they can be of service in east-and-west travel by the use of their tributaries. How can this be done? Can you trace any such routes? 

See the map, on page 278. You will find it a very zigzag journey.

Central Asia. Parts of the plateaus of central Asia are more than 15,000 feet above the level of the sea. This is in the region bordered by the Himalayas on the south, and the Hindu Kush, Tien Shan, and Altai ranges on the north. Not all of this region reaches this great height.

These lands are far from the sea. The winds blowing into, or across this region, lose their moisture on the cold slopes of the bordering mountains. It is a region of little rain. Water is scarce, the grass is sparse, few crops can be grown, and there are not many people (map, page 287). From this high central part of Asia no river reaches the sea. The streams dry up and are lost in desert sands, or they flow into salt lakes or marshes in the desert. Some few caravans cross these high and lonely plateaus and deserts between east and west, as they have done for thousands of years. Sometimes, American and European men of science go into central Asia to carry on explorations. 

But most of the vast uninhabited spaces of central Asia are little known to the modern world. 

You will learn more about these interior lands when you study the provinces of China.

So far in your study of the different parts of Asia, you have been studying regions in which the population is very sparse. On pages 305351 you are to take up those parts which are among the most densely settled regions in the world-southern and eastern Asia. It is here that 900,000,000 people live half the population of the world.

INDIA INDIA In the days when the Phoenicians were masters of the trade of the Mediterranean world the name of India was often heard in their market places. It was spoken of as a land of splendor and magnificence, and of unbelievable riches. There were stories of gorgeous temples and palaces, of great empires, and great rulers. By sea routes and by caravans there came to these Mediterranean merchants lovely silks, incense and spices, gold and precious stones from India. 

From Phoenicia to Greece, from Greece to 

Rome, from Rome to Venice, Genoa, and

Pisa, passed the control of the trade through the lands of Europe. All through the hundreds of years that this trade lasted, the stories of a gorgeous East endured. So firmly fixed 

So firmly fixed became the belief in the unlimited wealth of the Orient that when, at last, the trade with the East was shut off, Spain and Portugal | began a search for a new route. 

You know the rest of the story. A New

World was discovered. It was at first at first thought by its discoverer to be part of the "Indies" (southeastern Asia and the East Indies) for which he was searching. In that mistaken belief he named the native people of 

America" Indians"— a name their descendants bear today. A new way to the East was found by the Portuguese. The decline of the 

Mediterranean countries set in, and the rise of the countries of western Europe followed. 

Through the years of later European history there were national disputes, rivalries, and wars that have lasted down to the present day.

In the struggle for India it was the British who at last won. The story of their conquest of India has its bright and its dark pages. 

Yet neither Germany nor Russia was content to let the British enjoy the trade with the East that they had won. Just before the outbreak of the World War, both Germany and Russia were trying to get to the Indian Ocean to absorb or sidetrack some of England's trade with the East.

There is a movement in India to force the British government to give up its control. In your study of this land of many millions, try to learn whether, after all, India is a great prize for Great Britain. Try to learn also whether British control has been or has not been a good thing for the people of India. 

Position and Size. Study the map of 

India on the opposite page. At its southern end you will find Cape Comorin, about 8° north of the Equator. Southern India, therefore, is in a very warm part of the earth. 

Follow with your eye the heavy northern boundary line to the place where it bends farthest north. At that point it reaches 37° north latitude. That is nearly as far north of the Equator as Richmond, Virginia, and 

San Francisco, California. It is about 2000 miles from the northernmost to the southernmost point of India.

See how nearly midway between these two points the Tropic of Cancer crosses India. 

The part to the south lies in the Torrid Zone. 

The part to the north is in the North Temperate Zone. Yet there are parts of the temperate region which are very hot, and others which are very cold. As you study 

India, watch for the reasons for these great differences in temperature in the regions north of the Tropic of Cancer. 

Look again at the northern boundary line. 

It runs from western Baluchistan to eastern 

Burma. Notice that that this boundary is through mountains for almost all of the way.

The whole of India is three fifths as large as the United States. It is governed or controlled by Great Britain, yet in size it is equal to nineteen Great Britains, and has more than seven times as many people. 

The map colors (page 304) give a very clear idea of the surface of India. Study the colors that show elevations. South of the 

Tropic of Cancer the country is largely a plateau with an almost unbroken range of mountains along the west coast, and other but more broken ranges along the east coast. 

This is the Deccan. On the west the coastal lowland of this plateau of southern India is narrow, but on the east it is much wider, and lowlands along the rivers extend back among the highlands. Follow the entire coast line. 

From the head of the Bay of Bengal, a wide lowland reaches north to the mountains and west along the broad valley of the Ganges. 

Similar lowlands are found in the northwest along the Indus River and the Arabian Sea. 

Most of the area between the high ranges at the north and the plateau of southern India is less than 2000 feet above sea level. 

On the north of India the high wall of the Himalaya Mountains shuts out cold winds from central Asia, and also makes it difficult for enemies to attack India by land. These mountains do for India, therefore, exactly what the Alps do for northern Italy, except that the Himalayas are about twice as high as the Alps, and have fewer and much higher passes. It is interesting, also, that Mt. Blanc, the highest peak of the Alps, is only about half as high as Mt. Everest, the highest peak of the Himalayas. This last-named peak, as you know, is the highest mountain in the world - reaching almost six miles above the level of the sea.

The passes across the Himalayas are from 16,000 to 19,000 feet above the level of the In crossing these mountains it is necessea. 

would be to climb over the top of any mountain in the United States. Find the famous 

Khyber Pass between India and Afghanistan.

The British guard it carefully, and, as you have already learned, they have built a fine military highway for the use of troops and their equipment, in case of need. It would be very necessary in case of any Russian advance against India by way of Afghanistan. 

Climate of India. From what you have just read you will understand that the surface of India is divided into three well-marked regions of varying elevation. The southern part is a plateau with bordering mountains on the east and west, and with coastal lowlands and lowlands along the larger rivers. 

North of the plateau is a region of much lower elevation, especially along the Indus and Ganges rivers. North of that are the great mountains along the northern boundary. 

Such differences in elevation produce differences in temperature and rainfall. The regions of heavy and light rainfall depend, of course, mainly upon three things: (1) the direction of the prevailing winds; (2) whether these winds come from the land or from the sea; and (3) the differences in elevation of the lands over which the winds blow. 

In studying the climate of India, however, you will learn of changes in wind direction over the Indian Ocean that greatly influence the climate, especially the rainfall, of this great country. The monsoons have already been explained briefly on page 285. What causes the monsoons to change their direction as they do? 

In the summer time the plains of India and other parts of southern Asia are very hot. 

The air expands and flows outward at some distance above the level of the sea. The air that remains over these hot regions presses less heavily on the surface of the land. The cooler, heavier air over the ocean moves toward the land and pushes under the lighter air to be heated in its turn. During the

A great amount of moisture moves inland with the winds and falls as rain. There are parts of northern India where so much rain falls that they are the wettest places in the world. Along the lower Ganges, for example, several hundred inches of water fall each year.

The rainfall on the southern slopes of the Himalayas in summer is very heavy (A). 

It falls as rain on their lower parts and as snow on their upper parts. In places where the snow gathers in protected hollows it piles up in great masses and slowly changes to ice, forming large glaciers. Many rivers have their sources among these high mountains, and flow out upon and across the central plains on their way to the sea. 

On the slopes of the Himalayas there are extensive forests. extensive forests. At the foot of the mountains there are tropical forests growing for the most part in flat and swampy lands. 

Part way up the mountains, in a more temperate region, the ordinary hardwood trees are found. Higher still, are the evergreen forests, and as elevation increases these thin out and nothing is left but bare rock, snow, and glaciers. In the south edge of the Himalayas find Simla and Darjeeling (A). These places are 

These places are at an altitude high enough to be cool and restful. Here British officials, business men, teachers, and others who live in India go for vacations. It has been found that people from cooler lands cannot live for a long time in hot tropical lowlands without an occasional rest in cooler places. Instead of going back to Europe, or the United States, for a rest in a climate to which they are accustomed, they go into the mountains.

Rivers. The Himalayas do more than stop the north winds and protect India from invasion from the north. The rainfall and the water from melting snow and glaciers gather into streams that unite to form great rivers. All of these mountain-born streams carry with them rock waste to the foot of the mountains. In ages past this rock waste has been spread out to form vast plains. 

Trace the course of some of the larger rivers that flow out of the Himalayas. Find where the Indus River flows into the Arabian 

Sea. Follow it with your eye until you find the point on your map where it seems to start. It is high in the mountains. Then let your eye follow its course to Kashmir.

Here is a famous valley from which, for hundreds of years, beautifully woven shawls have come. In the days when your grandmother or her mother were young girls these 

Cashmere (or Kashmir) shawls were very highly prized. Although shawls are not now worn as much as they were in those days, they are still made in Kashmir. Follow the Indus out of the mountains, across the plain past Hyderabad to its delta on the edge of the 

Arabian Sea.

INDIA 

-A.- Devout Hindus go to Benares to bathe in the Ganges - the sacred river of India. Here you see along the bank many bathing ghats, or landing places for the convenience of bathers. 

Another great stream of northern India is the Ganges (A). You can trace its course from its source in the Himalayas, east of Simla, to the south, then southeast, and east through a great plain. At last the river bends south again and divides into several branches, each of which makes its way across the delta lands to the Bay of Bengal. Taken together these make the "Mouths of the 

Ganges." You will need to be careful in following the course of the main stream, because it is joined by a number of tributaries which flow more or less parallel to it for a long distance. Some of these tributaries flow out of the Himalayas. Others come from the plateau of Deccan to the south. 

A third great river, which finally joins one of the delta branches of the Ganges, is the Brahmaputra. It rises in the southern part of Tibet, and flows a long, long distance in an easterly direction between the Himalaya and the Trans-Himalaya Mountains. It then turns southeast for about 150 miles and flows out of the mountains to a lowland plain. Through this plain, in northern Assam, the river flows a long distance in a general westerly direction before it turns south to join the Ganges. 

These rivers have done for northern India what the river Po did for northern Italy. 

They, like the Po, have brought rock waste. out of the mountains and spread it out to

- An ox-drawn harrow in India. form broad and fertile plains. In the west there is a section of this plain through which the Indus flows that is so protected from rain-bearing winds that it is a desert. 

In that way it is like the valley of the lower Nile. The soil of these river plains is fine and fertile. Where there is enough rain, or where irrigation is possible, large crops can be raised, and on these plains you will find a very dense population. 

South of the lowlands of India is the Deccan. Much of it is a plateau over half a mile above sea level, and a large part is covered by lava from ancient volcanoes. 

This lava has decayed to form a fine, fertile soil, excellent for wheat and cotton. Along the western side is a mountain range called the Western Ghats. Along the eastern side, the Eastern Ghats are broken where the lowlands of the rivers reach a long way back into the plateau. You will notice that most of the rivers of the Deccan flow into the Bay of Bengal. In the fertile lands of their valleys, and on those of the plateau, there are thousands of villages and millions of farmers, but only a few large cities.

Wheat is one of the leading crops, as you found it to be in our own country, in Argentina, in Russia in Europe, and in many other countries. It is raised principally in the drier parts of the Indus-Ganges plain, in northern India (310 B). There it is grown as a cool-weather crop, and much of it on lands that must be irrigated. From the central part of the Indus-Ganges lowland, the wheat-producing area extends southward in a broad belt into the Deccan. Much of the wheat raised in India is exported, because it brings a higher price in world markets than other cereals, which the natives eat. That means that by selling a bushel of wheat the native farmer will be able to buy more than a bushel of some cheaper grain. It is necessary for the poor people of India to use these cheaper grains because they must work for twenty cents a day, or less. Karachi, north| of the Indus delta, is a shipping point for wheat, and at Bombay, farther south on the coast of the Arabian Sea, there are flour mills.

B. — Tea-producing regions of Asia.

Cancer Barley is grown on the Indus-Ganges plain, some of it in the same regions that produce wheat. It is also grown between the wheatraising and the rice-raising regions, in the eastern part of the lowland. 

The greatest of the cereal crops of India is rice. You have found this crop growing in some of the other parts of the world, but in no other part of the world is so much rice raised as in eastern and southeastern Asia, and in near-by islands. It is the great cereal food of the Orient. In India it is grown chiefly in the lowlands of the eastern Ganges, and along the lower Brahmaputra. The region of heaviest production is the low, hot lands of the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta (A). 

Rice is grown, also, in the Deccan and in Burma, in lowlands along the coast, and along river valleys where the fields can be flooded when necessary. Much of the rice of India is used at home, but there is usually a surplus for export. Two crops a year are common. In all the densely settled parts of Asia it is usual to raise more than a single crop each year if possible. 

Grain sorghum and millet are grown in the drier parts of the Deccan. These are used as food by the poorer people. 

One of the products of India that is raised largely for sale abroad, is tea (B).

Much fine tea is grown on the hillsides of Assam, and in the island of Ceylon. It is prepared from the leaves of a small shrub, which are picked by hand. The leaves, after withering, are rolled and dried; and the methods of preparation vary in the different countries where tea is grown. The tea plant is not a difficult shrub to raise, and the methods of preparing the leaves for market are neither elaborate nor expensive. The chief item of cost in the industry is the labor of picking and labor is cheap in India. 

Tea could be grown perfectly well in the southern part of our own country, but the cost of picking would be so great that it would not pay our farmers to raise it.

Two spices, cinnamon and pepper, are raised in India. 

Peanuts, castor beans, and flax, rape, poppy, mustard, and sesame seeds are grown and gathered for the oil that they contain. 

Some of these oils are used for food; others are used in the manufacture of various products such as ink, varnish, and paints. Both oil and oil seeds are exported.

The Indian fiber is not so long as that raised in the United States, and is somewhat more difficult to spin. One of the fibers grown in India, and almost nowhere else in the world, is jute. It is a coarse fiber used in the manufacture of burlap sacking, rope, and string. A great deal of jute is sent from India to the United States, where it is manufactured. 

Jute is raised mainly on the low, wet lands of the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta (312 A). 

Irrigation. The lower Ganges flows through a region of heavy rains. During the summer monsoons the western coast of India, from Bombay southward, is well watered. The winter monsoons give rain to Ceylon and the near-by parts of the mainland coast. But much of India is so dry during at least a part of the year that for most crops irrigation is necessary. The The natives dug irrigation canals centuries ago, but under British rule irrigation works have been greatly increased. Water for irrigation is now being supplied to more than 50,000,000 acres of land. This is over 

78,000 square miles almost equal to the combined area of England and Scotland, and larger than Missouri. Various methods of storing water are used. There are huge, government-built reservoirs, cisterns, and ponds. Yet in very dry years, when normal rainfall fails, the people of a large part of India are in danger of starvation. There has been much loss of life in this way, in spite of help from the government and gifts of private charity from other lands.

A bullock cart on a road near Delhi.

Animals of India. Some people in cold lands, such as the Eskimos in North America and the Lapps in northern Europe, live mainly on meat and fish. In India the people rarely eat meat. They live on grain, vegetables, and fruit. This is partly because the climate is hot and they do not care for meat, and partly because some of the most common of their animals are thought to be sacred. They would not think of killing a bullock or a cow. The bullock is thought to be very holy. One could walk up and eat the vegetables or fruit in front of a shop and the owner would not drive him away.

There are millions of cattle in India, but they are not kept as dairy animals. They are used to draw loads (A) and to till the fields. 

When they die their hides are sold, and hides are one of the large exports of India. The water buffalo loves the mud and is an ideal animal for use in the rice fields, just as the camel is the ideal animal for use in dry regions. There are goats and sheep also, but they too are kept largely for their hides and little of their meat is used. Horses are kept, but not in great numbers, and in the mountains there is an animal called the yak. 

The yak is like a big, shaggy ox and can

ASIA climb in the mountains where a horse cannot go.

Elephants are big and look clumsy, but they can be tamed and taught to do many kinds of work. Elephants have been trained to carry loads; to move and pile lumber in the forests and lumber yards; and to carry people either on ordinary roads or through forests where the plant growth is so dense and tangled that only an elephant could push its way through. 

There are many poisonous snakes and many insect pests, some of which are very poisonous also. They are not only out of doors, but they get into the flimsy houses and are dangerous and annoying. There are parts of the jungle in which you might meet a tiger, tiger, one of the fiercest and most dangerous of animals. Very likely you would not like to live in India, but if you had been born there you might consider it a pleasant home. — - Transportation in India. India has over 

42,000 miles of railroad. This is much more than any other country of Asia, but it is little as compared with the miles of railroad in the United States. Great Britain is only one nineteenth the size of India, but it has more than half as many miles of railroad. The railroads of India have all been built by 

British money and British skill. Naturally, the great network of railroads is in the central plains where the densest population is found and where the most goods need to be moved. 

There are, however, some railroads in the Deccan, but they are chiefly in the southern part. Trace the railroad from Calcutta far along the east coast of India almost to its southern tip. One railroad of special interest is the one that runs to Peshawar, near the Khyber Pass. Can you tell why? The chief railroad centers are Bombay, Calcutta,

Benares, and, far south along the east coast, Madras. Bombay is the most important because of its nearness to the Suez Canal. 

There are good automobile roads, and on these, and on thousands of poorer roads, many of the natives travel with their bullocks and their carts. A few ride sometimes on elephants. Many of the people of India are so poor that they must always walk. They have no money with which to pay railroad fares, and they own no automobiles or bullocks or bullock carts. locks or bullock carts. You would think it a great hardship if you always had to walk, although you may enjoy a long walk or hike once in a while.

Airplanes are coming into use for the few very wealthy people in India; they are also used by government officials and for government business. There is regular air service between the large cities, and air service between England and India has been established.

Cities. The large cities of India are few in proportion to the great population of the country. Great Britain, although much smaller and with a very much smaller population, has many more large cities than India ; and the United States, with about one third as many people, has a great many more cities of large size. India has fewer manufactures and less foreign trade than either of the other two countries, and that explains why most of the people live in the country. They cultivate little farms instead of operating machines in mills or factories. 

Bombay has been called the "Gateway of

India." It surely is the door to India for visitors who come to it from the west, and as most of the people who visit India come from Europe, the city where they land will most likely be Bombay.

On a map of the Eastern Hemisphere, trace a voyage from London to Bombay. Write down the names of all the waters over which the ship would sail. It will be a long list. 

Make also a list, in order, of all the countries which would be passed. 

Bombay is a city with a good natural harbor. The buildings look like those of a 

European city, except in the native quarters. 

Bombay is the second largest city of India.

Bombay is a city of many races. There are 

Europeans, Arab traders, Tibetans, Jews from Iraq, Japanese in a quarter of their own, and 100,000 Parsees. The Parsees are Persians who were driven out of Persia ages ago. 

They are a strong race whose religion includes the worship of fire, and they keep a sacred fire which they never allow to go out.

Bombay has many factories and is the textile center of India. It has more than three million cotton spindles. Look on the map for the railway connections of Bombay, north, south, and east. Calcutta is the great city of eastern India. 

It is 80 miles from the sea, on the Hooghly River, one of the mouths of the Ganges which flows across the delta to the Bay of Bengal. 

Calcutta has no fine harbor as Bombay has, but the river is dredged to receive large ships. 

It has a larger native population than Bombay, and many British people live there also. 

It is the chief center for the manufacture of jute. The raw material comes from near-by lowlands. lowlands. It is the center of the tea trade in northern India. Tea, burlap, and hides and skins are exported from Calcutta to 

Europe and America.

Madras is a port on the eastern coast. It has built fine sea walls out into the bay to form a harbor. From this city hides and skins are sent to the United States, and cotton to Japan.

ASIA 

Calcutta was long the capital of India, but in 1911 the government was moved to Delhi, which had been the capital centuries ago; and in 1931 it was housed in the addition to the old city called New Delhi. There were good reasons for making the change from Calcutta to Delhi. Some of these are: (1) The people in that region like the British rule better than do the people of Calcutta. (2) Delhi is much more central and easier to reach from most parts of India. (3) Its climate is better; and that, perhaps, was the chief reason for making the change. The summers are hot, but the officials then move up to Simla, farther north, which is a kind of summer capital. 

South of Delhi is Agra. In it is the Taj 

Mahal, a tomb built long ago by an emperor, to the memory of a beloved wife. It is of white marble, and many people think it is the most beautiful building in the world. 

In the Ganges Valley is Benares, a sacred city of the Hindus. It has many temples, and hundreds of thousands visit it on religious 

pilgrimages. The river is considered sacred and the pilgrims wish to bathe in it (309 A), drink some of the water, and carry more away in bottles. The water is very dirty, but these poor people believe they will be thought of much more highly if they use it. 

The chief city of the Deccan is the old walled city of Hyderabad, ruled by a native prince. 

It is larger than another city of the same name on the Indus. Hyderabad in the Deccan is a trading center far from the sea, with railroad connections to both coasts and the south. 

People of India. -No other great country, except China and Japan, has so dense a population as India. Most of the people live in many little villages in the Ganges Valley and along the lowlands of the coast. Study the distribution of population on the population map of Asia (287 A). There are many peoples, and some of them are dark-skinned even though they belong to the white race.

There are more than a hundred languages in use, and there are such differences in religion that at times those who have different faiths quarrel with each other. A. One of the ornate and beautiful temples in India. 

About 70,000,000, or one fifth of all the people, are Mohammedans. 

Brahmanism is the religion of the Hindus, who make up most of the population of India. 

Their name for God, or the 

Universal Spirit, is Brahma; but they worship many gods. 

The people are divided into classes or castes, and the members of one caste will have nothing to do with the members of another caste. People of the lowest caste are considered outcasts. Modern government and schools and the teachings of missionaries are slowly breaking down the cruel caste system.

Buddhism was founded on the teachings of an ancient prince in northern India, who was given the title of Buddha. He did not believe in castes and taught a life of purity and kindness. His followers are Buddhists. 

There are not many of them in his native country, but there are hundreds of millions in other countries, mainly in China, Japan, and Indo-China. 

The English have done much for India. 

They have kept order and have prevented wild tribes from invading the country. 

They have improved the highways and built railroads. They have very greatly increased the area irrigated. They have made a market for cotton, wheat, jute, tea, and other products. They have helped in education, prevented famine, and improved the care Government. In the government of of the health. They have stopped some

There are native Indian leaders, most of whom have been educated abroad, who are trying to secure home rule for India. The great mass of people, however, know little and care little, if only they have enough to eat and clothes to wear.

Burma and Baluchistan. Burma is a large province with about 15,000,000 people of different races. Only a small part of the country is under cultivation. Mineral products include some petroleum (A). Rangoon is the largest city and chief seaport. It

ASIA Man- exports much teakwood and rice. dalay is the chief city of the interior. On what river is it? This province of Burma is on the east side of the Bay of Bengal, but it is governed as a part of British India. 

Baluchistan, in the northwest, borders the Arabian Sea, and is west of the Indus

Valley. It is a wild, mountainous country with few people, whose main industry is grazing goats, sheep, and camels. 

Ceylon. Ceylon has been for a hundred years under British rule. It is not quite half as large as Alabama or Illinois. The The government is separate from that of India, although the island is so near. Both the summer and the winter monsoons bring rain to Ceylon. The winds of the winter monsoons are wet because they blow for hundreds of miles across the Bay of Bengal.

Much of the land is in large plantations owned by foreigners, for whom the natives work. There are few small farms. Tea is the leading crop. It is raised mostly in the southwest, where there is plenty of rain. 

Ceylon is one of the three most productive tea-growing regions of the world. Another large crop is plantation rubber. This industry got its start when seedlings were brought to Ceylon from Brazil. Now the cultivated rubber is raised not only in Ceylon, but also in other parts of the Far East. Much of the rubber of Ceylon is sent to the United States. 

Rice is an important food crop (311 A), but not enough is grown to supply the people, and much must be imported. Other products are spices, cacao, copra or dried coconut meat, and coconut oil. 

Sapphires, amethysts, rubies, and pearls are among the gems found in Ceylon, and there is a large amount of graphite, a mineral long used in making lead pencils.

The main port of Ceylon is Colombo (319A). 

It has a harbor protected by a breakwater, and is an important refueling station for many ships. It is on the route from Europe and the Suez Canal to eastern Asia.

Problems to Think About. of statements about India, with a question following each statement. Get clearly in mind in each case the facts upon which the statement is based, and then try to answer the question. 

1. Tea could be grown quite as well in the southern part of the United States as it can in India and other parts of Asia. It is not raised in our country, because it would almost certainly not be a profitable money crop. Why wouldn't it? 

2. The amount of land cultivated by an individual farmer in India seems very small indeed in comparison with what we would call a small farm in the United States. It seems small even in comparison with the small farms of the more thickly settled farming regions of Europe. How do you explain the need of such careful cultivation and the further fact that modern farm machinery is very little used in India? 

3. The United States has about 250,000 miles of railroad. India has about 42,000 miles. If India had as many miles of railroad in proportion to its area (three fifths that of the United States) it would have about 150,000 miles. If it had a mileage in proportion to its population as compared to the United States, India would have more than twice as many miles of railroad. What reasons can you think of to account for the fact that India's railroad mileage is so much less than that of the United States in proportion either to area or to population? 

4. India produces nearly all the jute raised in the world. The value of the jute exports ranks next to that of cotton, India's greatest export crop. 

Why is jute of such importance as a textile fiber? 

5. India's leading export is raw cotton and its leading import is manufactured cotton goods. 

Since India raises much cotton and has many cotton mills, and since, also, there is a great deal of spinning and weaving done by hand throughout India, what reasons can you find to explain the large amounts of manufactured cotton goods that are imported? 

6. India is one of the great wheat-producing countries of the world. Much of this wheat is sold for export and the people of India use cheaper grains, such as millet and sorghum, for food. 

Why do they not export the cheaper grains and use their wheat for food? 

7. India produces immense crops of rice and large crops of sugar cane. Why are these two crops of great importance to its people?

It stretches far southward from Burma and at its southern end is occupied by the Straits Settlements. It is there bordered by the

The Settlements area is a British colony, and connected with it are a number of Malay states that are under the protection of the British government. The work that is being done by some of the European countries in developing the resources of this part of the world is of the greatest value to its native peoples. This region produces a great variety of tropical gums, spices, fruits, and grains, but the bestknown exports are rubber and tin. 

Here, as in other parts of Indo-China, and in Ceylon and islands of the East Indies, great rubber plantations have been developed (321 A). Their combined output is more than nine tenths of the world's supply. You will remember that tin was mined in western

Bolivia in South America. The tin mines of 

Europe are nearly exhausted, and most of the world's tin supply now comes from

Some people think that the people of the United States could get along without any of the products that come from other countries. 

Would you like to try to do so? Could we do without tin, for example, or without rubber, tea, coffee, spices, and bananas?

And could we get along well with no more sugar, furs, and hides than we produce?

Singapore, on an island at the end of the Malay Peninsula, is a large city founded by the English. It is a very important port because it is on the route of all ships sailing around the south shore of Asia.

Siam is not quite so large as Texas, but has nearly twice as many people. As in India, rice and millet are important crops, and tin, gold, and gems are among the minerals found. 

Here, also, teakwood is one of the most valuable products. The government is a monarchy- one of the few still existing.

Equator - Rubber-producing regions of Asia. of Cancer The capital is Bangkok, a city crossed by the Menam River and by many canals. On these waters thousands of people live in floating homes or houseboats. 

French Indo-China has already been studied briefly as one of the possessions of France (page 138). It has an area about as large as that of Texas, with nearly four times as many people. It is chiefly an agricultural country with an area of very rich soil in the southwest. Its products are like those of the other parts of southern Asia that you have already studied. 

Rice is the chief crop (320 A), and the rich lowlands produce so much of this cereal that there is a large surplus for export. French 

Indo-China exports more rice than any other country in this part of the world except 

Burma. Sugar, cotton, and fruits also are grown on the lowlands, and tea and some coffee in lands that are somewhat higher. 

Large rubber plantations have been developed and much teakwood timber is taken from the forests. This wood, which is very hard and durable, is used in shipbuilding, in house construction, and in the manufacture of furniture. 

An oil having medicinal value is extracted from the wood, and a dye from teak leaves. 

Saïgon is the chief port, and because of the nearness of the rice fields it has many rice mills. Hanoï, in the northeastern part of the country, is the capital. The chief railroad in the country extends northward from Hanoï across the border into China, and will sometime be connected with the railroad system of southern China. Airplanes are in use to some extent, but by far the most important transportation route of the whole country is the Mekong River, which forms a part of the boundary line between French 

Indo-China and Burma and Siam. In its lower course it crosses the southern lowlands, and it is there that it is most crowded with native boats.

East Indies. The East Indies (or Malay 

Archipelago) are the islands lying between 

Asia and Australia. All except a few islands that are close to Australia are considered as belonging to Asia. The waters about them are not so deep as in most parts of the ocean. Looking on the map on page 356, you can imagine that all these islands make a sort of bridge between Asia and Australia. 

Notice that Sumatra, Borneo, and Celebes are crossed by the Equator. This means that each is partly in the Northern and partly in the Southern Hemisphere. Java and New 

Guinea are wholly in the Southern Hemisphere. All the East Indies are hot lands surrounded by warm seas. In the group are the Moluccas, or Spice Islands. These are the lands Columbus tried so hard to find; the lands which Magellan's men did find. Then, as now, men hunted for places. where they could get the things they wanted. 

The East Indies are largely of volcanic origin. Active volcanoes are numerous and earthquakes occur frequently. The vegetable and mineral products are like those of the neighboring parts of the mainland.

More of these islands belong to the Netherlands than to any other country. They are known as the Dutch East Indies. All together, they have a surface almost one fourth as large as the United States, and contain over 60,000,000 people. The most important of the Dutch possessions, though not the largest, is the island of Java, which has over 40,000,000 people, and exports tea, rubber, tobacco, tin, copra, coffee, sugar, and cinchona (quinine). The Philippine Islands. - Northeast of 

Borneo (map, page 276) are the Philippine 

Islands. They have belonged to the United

States ever since 1898, when they were taken from Spain during the Spanish-American 

War. Like the other islands of the East

Indies, they are in the Torrid Zone. There are many hundreds of islands in the group, whose total area is about 115,000 square miles. Luzon is the largest and Mindanao is nearly as large, their combined area being about two thirds that of the whole group. 

The surface of the Philippine Islands is mountainous, with many volcanic peaks, and the islands are frequently disturbed by

323 earthquakes. The whole island group is really | stations of the Pacific. It is a beautiful city only the higher parts of a mountain region, most of which is covered by the sea. 

The climate of the islands is like that of the other island groups in this part of the world. 

The temperature varies from warm to hot, and the rainfall is heavy nearly everywhere in the group. The seasonal variation in the rainfall is shown on the maps, pages 284, 285. 

A rather dry season comes in the winter, but rainfall is distributed so that the islands are largely covered with a dense plant and forest growth. Because of the dampness of the ground many of the native homes are raised on poles, to keep the floor of the hut dry. 

The houses of the poorer people and of the savage tribes are built of poles and thatched with grass or boughs.

Many kinds of trees are found in the forests, including a great variety of hardwoods. Since the United States took over the government of the islands, the forests have been divided into districts, which have been placed in the charge of expert foresters. 

The soils are deep and rich. In places they have been formed in part out of volcanic rock, and made richer by the decaying plant growth of ages past. many 

Copra, coconut oil used in the preparation of food products, and fresh coconuts are exported. From the abaca plant a fiber called manila hemp is obtained. It is used in the manufacture of ropes, and much of it is exported to the United States. Cane sugar and tobacco are other exports to our country. 

Other crops include rice, the chief food of the people, and corn, bananas, coffee, and spices. There are some deposits of soft coal, and other minerals have been found, but there is very little mining. 

During the time the islands have belonged to the United States, good roads, railroads, and thousands of miles of telegraph lines have been built.

The chief city is Manila, one of the great trading centers and refueling and supply with a wonderfully soft and pleasant winter climate; and it is becoming popular as a winter resort. Iloilo, on the island of Panay, is the second city in size. ence.

CHINA 

On the map facing this page study the area on the mainland named "Chinese Republic" and included within the heavy black boundary line. There is much confusion at the present time as to the size of the area to which the name may correctly be given.

This question is tied up with the question as to how much of the total area is actually controlled by the central Chinese government. 

For many years a large eastern part of this area has been called China proper meaning, of course, that it is the real China.

The rest of this area is divided into the great provinces of Tibet, Sinkiang, and Mongolia.

China proper has long been, and is today, the real heart of the country. It is the part where most of the people live, where agriculture and the arts have reached their highest development, and where the chief cities have grown up.

The control of the central government over the three outlying provinces varies greatly. 

In Tibet it is very slight, and that province is practically independent. Sinkiang (or 

Chinese Turkistan) is largely desert, and the control of the central government there is very limited. In Mongolia, the Russians have been pushing in from the north, and in their presence is a threat of future trouble. 

Manchuria, with a population largely Chinese, was formerly another outlying province of China. In recent years, however, there has been much trouble over its control, because of the conflicting claims of Chinese, Russians, and Japanese. In 1932 and 1933

Japan sent troops to take possession of the province, gave it a new government, and proclaimed its independence under a new name - Manchukuo. Also they enlarged it by the seizure of a neighboring area on the southwest. The new government is under 

Japanese influence.

The Chinese People and Their History. 

Until the middle of the nineteenth century the people of China proper lived almost by themselves. The mountains and deserts of the western provinces shut them away from western Asia and eastern Europe. There was a wilderness to the north until the Russians built a railroad through Siberia to the Pacific. The Himalayas and other mountains separated the Chinese people from India and Indo-China. On the ocean, it took months for a European sailing vessel to reach them, and, besides, the Chinese did not allow foreigners to trade in their coast cities. They were satisfied with their customs, learning, and arts, and they did not want to have anything to do with other nations. 

Confucius, born 550 years before Christ, was their great teacher and philosopher. 

He taught the Chinese the best ways of life as he saw them. He said that people should not do to others things they would not like done to themselves. He thought the people should know their poetry and history, and so for centuries Chinese scholars have memorized the teachings of Confucius and the works of their poets and historians. The result of his teaching was that the Chinese liked to keep their old customs and to follow their old ways of living.

For ages the Chinese have known how to make exquisite silk goods and fine chinaware.

They made paper and published books long before Europeans invented printing. Instead of using type, however, they printed from blocks of hard wood, on each of which the words for a whole page had been cut. 

It is said by some that the Chinese invented the mariner's compass and made gunpowder before these things were known in Europe. 

But there are good scholars who do not think that these last two statements are true. 

Twelve hundred years ago, the Chinese built a canal 700 miles long which is still used. 

Two hundred years before Christ they began to build the Great Wall (A), most of which

CHINA still stands to show their skill and industry. It extends more than 1200 miles from east to west, winds its way across hills and valleys, and has many watchtowers. It was built as a protection against Mongolian invaders from the north. It served its purpose, for at that time those wild enemies were horsemen, and they could not ride over or around the wall. A small Chinese army could defend the wall against them. 

This brief story of the Chinese people shows that for many centuries they have been an able and intelligent people, but they have been slow to adopt new customs. They have great respect for the past, and do not readily change from the habits and mode of life of their forefathers. Because of this, as well as for other reasons, they worship their ancestors. They like to think that old ways are best, and for a long time they opposed the building of railroads and the use of machines because they were afraid they would lose their work when railroads took the place of porters and junks, and when machines took the place of labor by hand. Yet the 

Chinese people are coming gradually to appreciate the modern ways of the western world.

The homes of most of the people are poor, being made of bamboo or dried mud. Little fuel is used, although China has much coal, and mines are in operation. Many of the people try to keep warm in garments padded with cotton (A).

Climate. The climate of China and its outlying provinces varies greatly in different sections. This is partly because the land extends across so many degrees of latitude. 

Most of it is in the North Temperate Zone, although its more southern parts are south of the Tropic of Cancer. If the United States extended through as many degrees of latitude, it would reach from Yucatan or Cuba north to Hudson Bay. Part of China is low and near the ocean, while the interior is high and far removed from the influence of the sea. 

Little moisture can reach the high interior provinces, because most of their area is in the course of the westerly winds. These winds have moved across Europe and western Asia

ASIA and have lost their moisture before they reach Sinkiang, Tibet, or Mongolia. The high wall of the Himalayas also shuts out moisture from the south. 

Much of China proper has a great deal more rain. All the southern parts are in the path of the monsoon winds that bring so much rain to India. The south coasts often have as much as 100 inches of rainfall a year. 

The rainfall is much less in the north, where it amounts to about 24 inches. In the regions of heavier rainfall, farming is very successful, partly because there is plenty of rain during most of the growing season and partly because full streams and canals supply water for irrigation whenever that is necessary. 

Violent storms called typhoons sometimes start in the East Indies and sweep the Chinese coasts, doing great damage. They are like the West Indian hurricanes.

In the following pages the words China and Chinese are used to mean China proper and its people. The outlying provinces (Tibet, Sinkiang, and Mongolia) will be described separately, later on. 

China proper is only about half as large as the United States, but it has over three times as many people. It is divided into eighteen provinces, somewhat as our country is divided into states. A complete census of 

China is not taken, and the population is not known accurately. The country is mountainous in the west, where it joins Tibet, and in the south, where it borders Indo-China and Burma. The main lowlands are in the east, especially along the great rivers. 

Northern China. Northern China is in about the same latitude as northern United 

States. Compare the latitude of Peiping with the latitude of the city of New York.

The summers and winters are similar to those in northeastern United States. If you lived in that part of China during the winter time, you might find it a very cold country indeed, because there is very little fuel to burn and the houses are not kept warm. The Chinese people use clothing which is heavily padded to keep them warm. Perhaps you have seen pictures of the men's coats, with long sleeves into which they can slip their hands, as they hold their arms across their bodies. They use these long sleeves as a sort of muff. The people of this part of China are taller and much more vigorous than those who live farther south.

Middle China. The largest of the rivers of China is the Yangtze, which to the Chinese is "the great river." It rises in Tibet, is 

3100 miles long, and is the main commercial river of China. Ocean steamers can go up this stream as far as Hankow, 600 miles from the sea. River steamers can go 400 miles farther. Native boats reach a point 1500 miles from the ocean. In some places men use ropes to pull the boats, and it is a common sight to see men with these ropes walking or running along the river banks. There are several large cities on the Yangtze, and the near-by country has a dense population.

ASIA of the dense population of this region, with its many large cities. Here are great lowlands with fine and fertile soils. There are many, many days of warmth each year. 

There are abundant rains so well distributed that on most of the land two or three crops a year can be grown.

As most of the larger cities are on navigable waterways, ships can reach them. Some of these cities have factories, and all of them carry on much trade. From Ichang toward the west the lowlands narrow, but they still border the Yangtze as far as Chungking and beyond.

Not far from the mouth of the Yangtze is the city of Shanghai. This is the greatest of the Chinese seaports, and through it goes the trade of the southern part of the Plains of China. There are docks on both sides of the river, but not enough to take care of all the ships that come to this port. The commerce that must be handled is so great that the harbor is always crowded and many ships anchor in midstream, unloading and loading with the help of small boats that carry the cargo to and from the shore. More goods from our country enter China through Shanghai than through any other Chinese port; and from Shanghai, Chinese products are shipped to the United States. 

River boats are used to carry imported articles up the Yangtze to cities in the interior, but many of the imported products are for use in Shanghai. There are cotton and silk mills, flour mills, oil refineries, and plants for the repair and building of ships. 

Shanghai has become the largest cottonmanufacturing center of China, largely because it is near the chief cotton-growing region.

Hankow also can be reached by ocean ships. 

It is the center of trade for a large region and is the most important business center in the interior of China. Here and in the neighboring cities of Hanyang and Wuchang are iron and steel, cotton and silk, and flour mills. 

Southern China.- South of the region that you have just been studying is a somewhat mountainous district. An island-like portion of it is cut off to the east by lowlands along a tributary of the Yangtze River. The northern border of the western part is indented by other lowlands. This highland rises toward the west and southwest, and in so doing cuts off to the east the fine farming and industrial region of South China. It is a region of heavy summer rainfall because of the summer monsoons which blow inland from the sea.

Southern China is drained by the Si River, which rises in the highlands farther west and has its outlet in the South China Sea. The lowlands through which it flows, and much of the higher land which surrounds it, are warm enough to grow two crops a year. In much of this area, rice is grown on lowland fields and on terraces that can be flooded. Tea shrubs are grown on the hillsides, and mulberry trees are grown for the raising of silkworms. 

Most of the tea and silk go to Europe and the United States. The population is so large that rice must be imported most of it from Indo-China. 

The island of Hong Kong off the coast, not far from the mouth of the Si River, and a part of the near-by mainland, are under the control of Great Britain. A great city, named 

Victoria, has been built on a fine harbor in Hong Kong and has become the center of British trade in this part of the Far East. It is one of the world's busiest ports and of the greatest importance to Great Britain (325A). 

Canton, on the Si River, is the largest city of southern China. Much of the city is like other Chinese cities that you have studied. The streets are narrow and the houses and shops are small and crowded close together. It is in this district that you will find the carvers of wood, stone, and ivory; and the makers of toys, fans, lanterns, and jewelry. All of this work is done by hand, as is also some weaving and embroidery. There

Thousands of years ago the Chinese began to cut away their forests, dig canals, and build terraces on which to grow rice and other crops. 

China was a densely populated and a great agricultural country long before the New 

World was discovered.

Most of the Chinese roads are very bad, and only recently have attempts been made to pave city streets, or to build sewers to carry off the filth of the cities. Goods are still carried on the backs of men and animals, or pulled along the streams and canals in boats. Both goods and men are transported on a kind of wheelbarrow with a large wheel in the center. Sometimes people are carried in chairs supported on poles resting on the shoulders of two men. 

In recent years, however, there has been some improvement in means of transportation. Important railroads have been built and others are under construction. Automobiles and trucks are in use in the newer parts of the cities, and nearly 35,000 miles of automobile highways have been built. 

Some use is being made of the airplane, and you can go by airplane between some of the great cities.

Agriculture. -The rich lowland region of eastern China proper is one of the very densely populated parts of our earth. As most of the people are farmers (A) you can understand why farms are small, and why each farmer tries to raise all he possibly can on his little patch of land. In the United 

States a farm of a hundred acres is not considered a large one for a small family. 

China, the man with five acres has a large farm, and the average is less than two acres. In All of the work on these small farms must be done by hand (B). A few simple tools and perhaps a water buffalo, or oxen, are about all that the Chinese farmer has to help him in his work. He tries to raise as many crops a year on his land as he can. While one crop is growing he is starting the plants in a small seed bed for the next crop. If he is raising a crop that is planted in hills and climbs poles or trellises, he will plant still other seeds between the hills of the pole crop, or in the ground underneath the trellises.

The Chinese farmers have long known that it is necessary to change, or rotate, the crops. They save everything that can possibly be useful as a fertilizer; otherwise they could not have raised crops on the same ground for thousands of years. On the

335 steep slopes they have made many terraces to prevent the washing away of the soil, and to give them more farm land, as the farmers do in Italy and Germany. On the lower courses of the Chinese rivers rafts are built and covered with soil for making gardens. 

Thousands of people have their little homes on such rafts, for every foot of space is precious where so many millions of people must be housed and fed. 

The natural rainfall does not always provide moisture enough for the crops. In the plains, especially in central and southern China, water is raised from the rivers for irrigation, and for flooding the fields on which the immense crops of rice are grown. Rice makes up a large part of the people's food. 

Two crops a year of rice and other products are commonly grown. The Chinese raise fish in the irrigating ditches and plant mulberry trees along the banks, to furnish food for silkworms. China is one of the leading countries of the world in the production of raw silk (A). This is largely because it has the cheap labor necessary for feeding the worms and unwinding the silk fibers from the cocoons. Cotton is raised and is used in home and factory manufactures.

China supplies a large part of the world's tea. The tea plant or bush needs a warm climate, but will endure some frost. It requires plenty of moisture, but the water must not stand around the roots. Hence warm, well-watered but well-drained hillsides are good ground for the crop. Three times a year the leaves are picked, dried in the sun, heated, rolled in the hand, and then baked over charcoal fires. This process, which causes fermentation, makes "black tea." 

For "green tea," the leaves are roasted without being fermented. Some of the tea is pressed into "bricks," for convenience in packing in small spaces. Much of this brick tea is carried for great distances on pack animals. The cheaper bricks are made from the poorer leaves and small twigs.

The main crops raised in the different parts of China vary because of the differences in climate. Soy beans, wheat, and millet are raised in the north; and tea, rice, cane sugar, and bananas in the south. In the north, the farmers can raise but one crop in the short summer season. 

In the south, where it is warm during most of the year, they are able to raise two or three crops each 

Four fifths of the Chinese are farmers, and they are good farmers. For fertilizer they use everything that will make the soil rich and restore plant food taken out of the soil by the crops. They use muck, sewage, the waste from the house, and the muddy slime from the rivers. Because each family must get a living from a very small patch of ground, they must use every foot of it. 

They have no room for orchards, pastures, meadows, or wide roads. They do not keep cattle because they need all of their land to raise food for human beings. As a result they have very little milk to use. They do keep hogs and fowls, for these will eat things which might otherwise go to waste.

Manufacturing. -There is much fine handwork done in China. There are skillful workers who make beautiful articles out of a small amount of raw materials. Among these are silk weavers, carvers of ivory, and workers in metals. The Chinese are not only skillful, they are artistic, patient, and painstaking. They have learned how to do their work well, and they refuse to spoil it by being in a hurry.

The coal and iron deposits of China are among the largest in the world. These minerals are not yet mined in large quantities, nor will they be until methods of transportation are much improved. Remember how in our country it has been necessary to transport iron ore from Minnesota and northern Michigan to the lower lake ports and Pittsburgh for manufacture. Spain is taken to Great Britain, where there is coal for blast furnaces and rolling mills.

China was made a republic in 1912. The country, however, is so very large, and communication and travel are so difficult, that the people in different parts do not know each other very well. 

Because of this they do not always work well together, and so the government is not very strongly organized. Some of the eighteen provinces of China proper have been at times almost independent. 

Although the Chinese find it hard to work for a common purpose, they usually unite to protect themselves from foreigners. 

Some foreign nations forced the Chinese government to grant them spheres of influence" in China. This was a polite way of making the Chinese do as they wished and give them their trade. The Chinese government does not want the government of Japan, Great Britain, or any other foreign country to tell it what to do. It wants to get rid of foreign control. If a foreigner commits a crime in China, for example, the 

Chinese want to try him in their courts; they do not want him tried by foreigners. 

China is friendly to the United States.

Our government has never tried to force the Chinese to lease land to the United States or to grant rights to citizens of the United States that are not granted to the citizens of other countries. Our country wants the open door" in China. This means equal rights for all to trade there.

Chinese education

Chinese education meant studying the Chinese classics and poetry and committing to memory the works of Confucius and other 

Chinese philosophers and poets. Now the young Chinese want to study the sciences and industries of the western world instead.

Schools, colleges, and hospitals were founded by missionaries and others who wished to help the Chinese. Now, the Chinese having learned how to do so, want to manage these themselves.
