ASIA Tibet. 

A. Yaks, although strange to us, are ordinary and useful beasts of burden in Tibet.

OUTLYING PROVINCES 

Tibet is a high and mountainous plateau. The western part is from 14,000 to 16,000 feet above sea level and is very cold. The surrounding mountains rise much higher. As a whole the region is dry, but streams fed by mountain snows drain toward the interior of the country and end in swamps or lakes. The dryness of the air is so great that evaporation is rapid and the lakes have no outlet, and are therefore salt. The eastern parts of Tibet, however, are much lower, and many streams flow out of the highlands toward the sea. The people and the cultivated lands are mainly in the drainage basin of the Brahmaputra River. Barley thrives there, and it is the chief grain and the most important food crop. The herdsmen keep sheep, goats, and yaks-animals which can live where the grass supply is scanty. 

Yaks (A) are much like cattle, but they have coats of long, soft hair, and most of them are either black or white. Yak's milk is rich, and is made into curds, which are a favorite food of the Tibetans. Ropes and tent coverings are made of the hair, the flesh is good for food, and the animals are used to carry loads, but not to draw wagons or plows. Thus the yak is as useful in this high, cold region as the reindeer is on the 

Arctic plains. 

Cashmere wool, clipped from goats, is an important export, and brick tea from China proper is one of the chief imports. 

The Tibetans are so isolated by mountains, and so far from China proper, that they are but little controlled by the central government. Lhasa, the capital, is regarded by the Tibetans as a sacred city. They try to shut out all foreigners, and only a few have ever succeeded in entering it.

MANCHURIA 

Manchuria, or Manchukuo, is east of Mongolia. It has extensive plains in the central part, with mountains and forests in the east. 

It is well watered, and has good soil and a favorable climate. 

The forests are useful as a source of lumber, and in them, as in those of Siberia (page 302), fur-bearing animals are hunted and trapped. 

Cattle are raised on the plains, and fishing has become an important industry along the coast. Deposits of coal, iron, and gold have been found. Most of the people of Manchuria, however, are farmers, and agriculture is the chief industry. Among the crops grown are wheat, millet, corn, and barley.

But in most parts of Manchuria the largest single crop is the soy bean, raised largely for food and for the oil it contains. The cake (A) remaining after the oil is pressed out is used as a fertilizer and as a cattle food. 

Courtesy South Manchuria Railway Co. 

A. 

Bean cakes in a warehouse on a wharf in Dairen, the chief port of Manchuria. These cakes are made from the pulp left after pressing the oil from soy beans. Many are exported to our country and other lands. The men in the picture are loading the cakes on a steamer.

ASIA 

Much of the oil is shipped across the ocean to our Pacific ports for use in the soap factories of our country.

Manchuria has more people than all the three outlying provinces of China already described. China proper is much warmer than Manchuria is, and the Chinese people love their home land and cling to the place where they were born and where their ancestors lie buried. Yet, in recent years, millions of Chinese left their old homes and sought new ones in this land of cold and snowy winters, where only one crop a year can be raised. They were forced to migrate because China proper is overpopulated and famine faces them every year or so; or else they migrated because of floods or because of civil wars.

In Manchuria the Chinese settlers found good soils and plenty of rain for crops, and in most parts of the country there is little danger from floods. But they did not escape from warfare. In 1932 and 1933 Japan, as you know, sent troops into this region and took its control away from the old Chinese government (page 325). The Japanese claimed that this was necessary in order to protect property owned by their countrymen. 

Since this was done, more and more natives of Japan have settled in this old province of China, and the Japanese have invested large sums in industries there.

Many years ago, the Russians laid a railroad across Manchuria from Siberia to Port Arthur, where they built a great fortress on ground leased from China. Japan captured the fortress in a war with Russia in 1905, and gained control of Port Arthur, Dairen, and the Manchurian Railroad. Russia and 

Japan, one after the other, thus gained great influence in the control of Manchuria. 

When Japan set up the new government of Manchukuo (page 325), it made Changchun (renamed Hsinking) the capital. 

Mukden, in southern Manchuria, was the former capital of the province, and is still its largest city. It is a railroad center and a fur market. It has tanneries and manufactures flour, soy-bean oil, cotton goods, carpets, and rugs. Mukden is partly a 

Chinese and partly a Japanese city. High walls, pierced by narrow gateways, surround the old Chinese section. Many of the streets are narrow, and the plaster-covered stone or brick buildings are low and closely crowded. 

There are many little shops where articles are still made by hand, with the painstaking care of Chinese artists. Other parts of the old Chinese city have been cleared, and broad streets laid out, along which modern buildings have been put up. The Japanese part of the city is much newer and is laid out with wide, paved streets and large, modern buildings. 

There are coal mines near Mukden, and iron mines between Mukden and Dairen. 

Iron and steel plants have been built near the iron mines. Some of the mines and steel plants were developed by the Chinese, and others by the Japanese.

Dairen (339 A), in the region governed directly by Japan, is the chief port of Manchuria.

Some of the words that we use to give the idea of distance or direction are used in a very exact way. Others are used in a loose or inexact way. In the exact use of the words north and south, for example, we mean the direction along a meridian line, as shown on a map or globe. East and west are, in their exact meaning, directions along a parallel of latitude. Yet in this book the terms East, Near East, and Far East are used in a different way. When the people of western 

Europe were first trading with the people of Asia, they thought and spoke of the goods that came from Asia as coming from the "East." Later, the parts of Europe and

Asia around the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea were spoken of as the "Near

East," and the lands of eastern Asia as the 

That is the way we use the "Far East." terms today.

China and Japan, therefore, are in the Far East. But we can actually reach these lands by traveling either east or west.

China, Japan, and other lands of the Far East are often spoken of as Oriental countries and their people as Orientals. The word 

Orient means East; and Oriental lands and people are the lands and people of the East. 

Japan is also called the "Land of the Rising 

Sun" because the sun rises in the east. 

Japan is today the most progressive country of the Orient. This means that the people and government of Japan have adopted the ways and methods of the most highly civilized governments and people of what we call the Western World; that is,

ASIA 

Europe and America. They have learned about Western inventions, and they have bought Western machinery. They have also adopted Western educational methods. 

They have sent some of their young people to be educated in Europe and in the United States. They have founded modern universities, built railroads and many warships, and created and trained a strong army and navy. They have established a great merchant marine and extended their trade all over the world.

These changes have come rapidly, as they began only a little more than seventy-five years ago. Nobody knows when the ancestors of the Japanese came over from the continent of Asia and settled on the Japan 

Islands. It was a long time ago. They❘ were of the Mongolian or yellow race, like most of the other people of eastern Asia. 

The Japanese are different from the Chinese, partly because they have lived so long in a different land.

In 1853 the United States sent Commodore Perry to Japan in command of some of our warships. Our countrymen wanted to trade with Japan. But Japan had shut the doors of its country in the faces of all other nations and because of this had earned the name of the "Hermit Nation." Just what did this mean? Perry tried to arrange with the

Japanese government some way so our people could trade with the Japanese people. 

The fleet called again in 1854, and that time a treaty was made which allowed our people certain trading privileges. Then Japan opened its doors to the world. These doors are open still, but Japan, like other countries, looks carefully after its own safety and commercial welfare. 

Physical Features of Japan. On the maps, pages 278 and 324, study the chain of islands off the eastern coast of Asia, reaching from the south end of the peninsula of 

Kamchatka, almost to the Philippine Islands.

Notice the seas that lie between the islands and the mainland. They are: Sea of 

Okhotsk, Sea of Japan, Yellow Sea, and East 

China Sea. 

You will find on the map four islands which taken together have been part of Japan for thousands of years. They are called the 

Japan Islands, and sometimes Japan proper. 

Their names are Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu. Of these Honshu is much the largest, and has the most people and most of the great cities. The Japan Islands are not the whole of the Empire of Japan. 

That empire includes also several other groups of islands and a part of the mainland of Asia. To the northeast are the Kurile 

Islands, a small barren group of volcanic islands that contain several active volcanoes. 

The south half of the large island of Sakhalin has belonged to Japan since the close of its war with Russia in 1905. To the southwest is another chain of small islands, the Nansei group; and southwest of these is the island of Taiwan, or Formosa. The ancient country of Korea, occupying a peninsula of Asia, has been made a part of the Japanese Empire, and is now called Chosen. At the close of the World War, Japan took over some small islands in the Pacific Ocean which had belonged to Germany.

The area of the present Japanese Empire is more than 265,000 square miles. This is equal in size to the state of Texas or to more than five New Yorks. The British Isles are less than half as large.

Notice that the island of Taiwan at its south end is at about 22° and therefore south of the Tropic of Cancer. The chain of islands is about 2000 miles long. This alone would give great differences in climate between the north and the south. In North America this distance would take us from Cuba to the northern part of Newfoundland. That is from a land of palm trees and sugar cane to a land of almost constant ice and snow.

Snow-capped Fujiyama is the most famous of the Japanese mountains. It is an old volcanic cone, but it is not lost among other mountains or dwarfed by higher peaks. but lovely form. At its base are beautiful lakes. 

The main islands are mountainous, and many are volcanic in origin. Some of the volcanoes are active, but many more of them have been dormant, or quiet, for a long time. 

Fujiyama (A) has had no eruption for many years, and always has a cloak of snow on its summit. It is over 12,000 feet high, and is one of the most symmetrical, or regular, in shape of the volcanic cones of the world. 

It is beautiful whether seen from the sea or from the land. To the Japanese it is a sacred mountain. They admire its beauty and they make pilgrimages to its summit.

Earthquakes are frequent. Most of them are slight and do no harm. Some would not be known unless instruments were used From whatever direction it is seen it has the same simple On one of these you see a native boat called a sampan. which make a record of slight earth quivers. 

Sometimes, however, there are earthquakes that are destructive. Large parts of Tokyo and other cities have at times been so shaken that they were left in ruins. Yet whenever such a thing has happened, the enterprising 

Japanese have quickly rebuilt, using steel in any high buildings to guard, so far as possible, against their falling in future earthquakes. Most of the dwellings, however, are low and made of wood. This is wise. in an earthquake region, for although the houses may often sway they seldom fall.

The Japan Islands rise from a continental shelf, as do the British Isles off the west coast of Europe (map, page 278). It is

ASIA believed that they have been slowly sinking for a long, long time. The result is that the ocean ocean waters have flowed into, or "drowned," many valleys, and given the islands a very irregular coast line and fine harbors. 

Climate. Since Japan extends over a wide range of latitude, the average temperature of its northern part is much lower than that of its southern part. Differences in elevation also bring about a range of temperature between lowlands and mountain peaks that is almost equal to that caused by difference in latitude. But these facts are equally true of any country that stretches through many degrees of latitude across the North Temperate Zone, and that has high mountains. There are two other influences that are felt in Japan, however, that are not felt in all other regions of the kind just mentioned. One of these is that the Japan Islands are long north and south, narrow east and west, and are on their eastern shores washed by a warm ocean current (78 A). The other is that winds, very much like the monsoons of India, blow across the islands from the east and southeast in summer, toward the interior of Asia; and other winds blow from the west and northwest across the islands in winter, coming from Asia.

The summer monsoon picks up much moisture as it crosses the ocean before reaching Japan, and its temperature is still further increased by crossing the Japan Current. 

When this wind reaches the islands there is a heavy rainfall over the eastern lowlands and on the eastern slopes of the mountains. 

The influence of the ocean current upon the climate of Japan is much greater than that of the Gulf Stream along the eastern coast of the United States, because of the monsoon character of the summer wind over Japan. There is no such steady summer monsoon blowing across the Gulf Stream into eastern United States. The influence of the Japan Current is more like the influence of the Gulf Stream Drift off the northwest coast of the British Isles. 

The winter winds are cold and dry. They blow out of the cold lands of interior Asia, but they do grow somewhat warmer as they move toward the southeast and over the seas that separate Japan from the mainland. 

They pick up some moisture, some of which falls as snow at the north and on the higher mountain slopes. You have learned of the fierce storms, called typhoons, that sometimes sweep northward in the region of these islands, and along the Chinese coast (page 328). 

These destructive winds frequently come at the time when rice is ripening and do great damage to that crop. In a country where there is never a large return to the farmer for his hard work, it is very discouraging to have crops destroyed in this way. 

People of Japan. When you were studying some of the countries of western Europe, you were asked to find the density of population (as on page 114). Using the Tables in the back of this book, make some comparisons between the population of Japan proper and that of the British Isles. Which of these island groups has the greater area? 

Which one has the larger population?

Which one has the greater density of population? You know, of course, that in both countries there is much waste land and some forested areas. So there are regions where the density of population is much greater than the figures show. Some farming districts of the island of Honshu have more than 1000 people for each square mile. 

As in other countries with modern industries, many of the people are gathered into cities, and most of these are in Japan proper. 

At present there are about 65,000,000 people in these islands. The population is growing rapidly, and Japan does not know where to settle her growing population. The problem is made more difficult because the Japanese are not allowed to enter as settlers into the United States, Canada, or Australia.

JAPAN A. 

Stone lanterns, dwarfed trees, and rock formations are typical of Japanese gardens.

They have added Chosen and Taiwan to their empire and they are pushing into 

Manchuria (pages 339-340).

Although the Japanese are of the Mongolian race, as are the Chinese, they are smaller and more keen and active. They are pleasant, gentle in their manner, soft of voice, and polite. They are quick and eager to learn new things and have rapidly adopted the use of modern machines and modern inventions. 

The Japanese are fond of lovely things. 

They like the mountains, the forests, the shrubs, and the flowers (A). Their cherry trees are famous for beauty. Some that were given to our government have been planted in Washington, D. C., and every spring thousands of people visit that city to see the Japanese cherry blossoms.

There is little furniture in the homes of the Japanese except the thick mats on which they sit. They like one picture instead of many, and one stalk with blossoms if properly placed seems to them more beautiful than a large bouquet of gorgeous blossoms. 

They think our homes have too many things in them. They are neat in appearance, and few people in the world are as clean as they. 

Because Japan is so crowded with people, labor is very cheap, and only by great care is enough food secured to go around. One reason why the Japanese are not allowed to settle in Canada, Australia, and the United States, is that they are willing to work longer hours and for smaller wages than are the peoples of those countries. 

Government. -The head of the Japanese nation is the Emperor (sometimes called the 

Mikado by Western people). There are two lawmaking bodies, one consisting of the nobility and the other chosen by the people. The Japanese are proud of their country, their government, and their people, and are very patriotic.

Agriculture. The problem of supplying enough food for all the people of Japan is very serious. 

As in China, the people eat little meat. They do eat fish, which are abundant in the surrounding waters. There is only a little pasture land in Japan. This is partly because the land cannot be spared for this use, and partly because grass does not grow well in many parts. Grass does grow well in the north of Japan, and some cattle are raised there, but not many. The people depend chiefly on grain, vegetables, and fruit for their food, in addition to fish. 

Most of their farms are very small and are cultivated as carefully as gardens. The main crop is rice, and yet Japan proper has to import some rice to provide enough for its people. Other grains raised are millet, bar- | ley, rye, and wheat. Much tea is raised (A), both for home use and for export.

The rice crop (347 A) of Japan is raised as in China and India, on wet lowlands which can be flooded. It is planted on terraced hillsides, also, where the plants can be flooded in the growing season. The rice is reaped by hand, and threshed by treading on it or by the use of a simple machine. The rice straw is used to cover roofs, or to make hats, mats, and baskets. If any is left it goes back to enrich the soil. 

Silk, as you know, is an animal product, but the silkworm eats mulberry leaves, and many mulberry trees are grown in Japan. 

Much labor is needed to pick the leaves, and to feed the worms. It is even more work to unwind the small cocoons of silk

Tea especially is an important crop in the great island of Taiwan. 

Another product that comes from Taiwan is camphor. It is made from the chips or twigs or leaves of camphor trees. The 

Japanese are now careful to replace with young trees all camphor trees that die or are cut down.

Japan raises cotton, but there is not room for large fields, and most of the cotton for mills in Japan comes from the United States, India, and China.

Minerals and Forest Resources. - Coal and some iron are among the important minerals of Japan, and this is fortunate for the people, because modern Japan is building railroads, ships, and modern steel business and factory buildings. To keep all of these industries going, it is necessary to import much iron. The deposits of copper are large, and this metal also is of great value in the modern electrical industries now being developed in Japan. Petroleum is found on the island of Honshu, and Chosen yields copper, gold, and silver.

The Japanese are very skillful in the art of lacquering. From the sap of a kind of sumac tree they make lac, which is a varnish. 

They inlay woods in beautiful patterns, and then apply the lac, which when dried is given a high polish. As in India and China, many useful objects are made from bamboo. 

Bamboo is light, strong, and hollow, and the Japanese use it in making mats, hats, sails, paper, and furniture. They also use it for house frames, poles, and water pipes, and they use the young bamboo shoots for food.

Manufactures and Trade. You know that most of the Japanese are farmers as most of the Chinese are, but manufacturing is being carried on in Japan much more than in China. Small articles of rare beauty are made in the workshops of the people (A), and the artist who can do fine wood, stone, or ivory carving does not need to work in a mill or factory.

Large factories are being built, however, to take over the manufacture of silk and cotton fabrics, paper, and to some extent chinaware. The Japanese also make many toys, lanterns, fans, and a great variety of small articles for trade with the Western world. Iron and steel mills and shipbuilding yards have been established, and give employment to many workers.

Most of the raw cotton for the mills making cloth and cotton yarn is imported, and the finished goods are exported. In this way Japan sells the labor of her people, both the labor in the factories and the labor of all those who handle the raw materials or finished goods on any one of the transportation lines.

The raw material needed in the silk industry, the paper industry, and in the iron and steel industries, comes in part from Japanese fields, and forests, and mines. 

Japanese ports are now open to the trade of all the trading nations of the world, and much of this trade is carried by the ships of the Japanese merchant marine. Yokohama, which is almost as large as Pittsburgh or San Francisco, is the port of Tokyo, the capital; and to this port go most of the goods and passengers from the United States. 

This trade is handled by large ocean-going ships, most of which are too large to be able to get up the bay to Tokyo. Where in the interior of Great Britain, France, and China are there large cities whose trade is largely carried on through near-by, but better-located, ports? Tokyo (341 A), with a population of about 5,000,000, is a modern city with fine public buildings, many lovely gardens, and thousands of simple, modest, but clean and pleasant homes. Yokohama (349 A) has a fine harbor with docks, piers, and all the equipment of a good port. In

Japan Proper and the British Isles Com pared. In some ways the Japan Islands and the British Isles are much alike; in 

other ways very different. Each group rises from the continental shelf of the near-by continent. Japan proper is somewhat larger than the British Isles and has a somewhat larger population. But the difference in each case is not so very great. Both Great 

Britain and Japan have become great manufacturing and trading countries. In their race for world trade, the British people have three advantages: (1) an earlier start, (2) a great colonial empire, and (3) established markets.

Japan has cheap, abundant, and easily trained labor, a sense of the artistic and beautiful, and a tireless energy.

Both countries must import raw materials, but Great Britain gets many of hers from various parts of her own empire. Japan seeks to extend its empire, so that it also may be placed in the same favorable position. 

There are mountains and lowlands in both regions, but in Japan the mountains are higher and much more extensive than those in the British Isles. Both island groups are in the North Temperate Zone, yet northern Japan has much colder winters than the British Isles have in any of their parts. This is because the British Isles are in the region of the westerly winds which come over the ocean and give them an oceanic climate. In Japan the winter winds are from the cold, frozen, barren lands of Asia, and the temperature contrasts between summer and winter are greater.

Both countries have the sea all around them. Both are lands that long ago sank to a lower level and therefore have many bays and inlets. Long before men lived upon the islands, the British Isles had many volcanoes and were disturbed by earthquakes. 

Japan has volcanoes and earthquakes now. 

Great Britain has more pastures and more live stock, and imports meat and dairy products for its people, and wheat for white bread. 

In Japan most of the people live largely upon rice and vegetables. In both Great Britain. and Japan proper, fish is an important food

Japan now does, but in Great Britain the iron and steel industries seem to be declining at the present time, while in Japan they are increasing. 

Drawing on Your Stores of Knowledge. 

After reading the account of Japan in the preceding pages, you should be able to talk clearly about the facts upon which the following statements are based and to give good answers to the questions raised in connection with them. 

1. The entire Japanese Empire has an area of more than 265,000 square miles, almost exactly the same as the area of the state of Texas. Texas has a population of about 6,000,000. The Japanese Empire has a population of about 92,000,000, more than fifteen times the population of Texas and more than two thirds as many people as there are in the entire United States. What very difficult problem for the Japanese nation do these facts suggest? 

2. The chief islands of Japan, like those of the 

British Isles, have many fine harbors. What explains this similarity? 

3. Earthquakes, often destructive of both life and property, are of frequent occurrence in Japan. In what way are the Japanese able to guard against some of these destructive results? 

4. Japan is favorably located for taking a large part in the commerce of the Pacific Ocean. What facts show that Japan is using this favorable position to good advantage? 

5. The waters around Japan make one of the three fine deep-sea fishing grounds of the world. 

Where are the other two? 

6. The chief industry of the people of Japan is agriculture. They are almost exclusively grain farmers. What grains do they raise? Why do they not carry on mixed farming as extensively as farmers do in the United States? Why do they not have any large grazing industry? The

Japanese produce nearly all the food which their nation needs. How can they do this in such a limited area? 

7. Japan produces large amounts of tea and silk for use at home and for export. What is one reason for the success of the Japanese with these two products? 

8. Manufacturing industries are developing rapidly in Japan. What conditions are especially favorable for this rapid growth? 

9. In less than a century Japan has become by far the most progressive and powerful country in Asia. How has this change been brought about? Tell what part the United States played in bringing about trade relations between Japan and the outside world. 

10. Japan is like Great Britain in some respects and unlike in others. Make this clear.

ASIA A. Floating houses on the Menam River. In parts of Asia the population is so dense and the land is so valuable that many people live the year round in house boats. 

ASIA AS A WHOLE 

To most of us Asia is a story-book continent. It is the home of strange peoples whose ways of living are very different from those in our own country. It is a land of vast highlands and high mountains. Within its borders are the highest mountain ranges and the highest mountain peak in the world. 

On its frozen northern plains, in its vast and lonely forests, on its steppes, its high plateaus, and its arid wastes small populations, mostly nomads, find a poor living. In contrast, some of its river valleys and lowland plains support a population of great density (A). 

Here you find lands that have been cultivated for thousands of years, and during much of that time they have been forced to yield two or more crops a year. Yet so carefully have these lands been tended that they are probably more fertile today than they were ages ago. 

Asia is a land of ancient civilizations whose days of glory and power belong to a great past. 

Yet off its eastern shores is an island group whose people today take high rank among the progressive nations of modern times. In southwestern Asia we find the records of several great civilizations. Although most of them long ago perished from the earth, we have learned and are still learning about them. them. The ruins of their temples, palaces, and great cities have been located, and many have been uncovered. Enough has been found to show that there were great artists and builders among all these ancient peoples. 

Out of Asia came the great religions of the world, and there the greatest of religious leaders lived and taught. It was in Asia that Jesus was born, and there he lived and taught his disciples. From the little area where his life was spent, Christianity has spread through a large part of the world.

ASIA AS A WHOLE 

353 Both in ancient and in modern times there have been some men in Asia who have enjoyed great wealth and have surrounded themselves with magnificence and luxury.

Most of those who were able to live such lives have belonged to the ruling class. They have been able to command the work of the people. The great majority of the people of 

Asia have for centuries lived in poverty and ignorance. They are so poor that famine is never far away. The failure of a single crop in the Ganges Valley, or in most parts of China, means that many must go hungry, and that hundreds will starve to death.

There are parts of Asia where vast deposits of coal and iron, large reserves of petroleum, and various other minerals are known to exist. 

It is upon such resources, little used by the ancient peoples, that the modern industries of the Western world have been built up. 

In the Western world, along with the mining, smelting, and working of metals, have gone the invention and use of machinery for great mills and factories, and the development of new means of transportation.

Until very recently nearly all of the mineral resources of Asia remained practically untouched. Japan is the only one of the 

Asiatic nations that has actively entered into modern industry. Among the vast majority of the peoples of the East, old methods of hand work are still being used. In some regions, generally where coal and iron are found close together, and where railroads have been built, foreign capital has been invested and native labor has been trained in modern methods of work. The clang and roar of machinery is now heard in many cities of the East. But all that has been done is very, very little compared with what can be done when more of these natural resources are used. This will come when more railroads have been built so that metals, fuels, and the raw materials of manufacture can be brought together in regions where labor is plentiful and markets can be reached.

1. Asia includes nearly one third of the land surface of the world. The oasis of Siwa in northern Africa has a section that is 440 feet below sea level. The lowest point in North 

America is Death Valley in California, 276 feet below sea level. Lake Eyre in southern Australia is 39 feet below sea level. None of the surface of South America is below sea level. How much lower is the level of the Dead Sea than the

5. Asia includes the wettest as well as the driest regions in the world. There are places in

Asia averages under 10 inches a year, and more than two thirds of the continent averages less than 20 inches. Name three countries with some of the wettest regions. Name three countries with some of the driest regions. 

6. The most densely populated large regions of the world are in Asia. Since more than half of Asia can support only a sparse population, it is clear that the richer regions must be very densely populated in order to take care of the many millions who must find enough food for their use. 

Use the map on page 287 to find out what three countries and what island have the most densely populated sections. Java is about the size of the state of New York and has a population of about 42 millions, or an average of more than 800 to the square mile. No other area of the same extent has anything like so dense a population. Suppose the farm lands of the densely peopled lowlands of southern and eastern Asia could produce only one crop a year as do most of the farms in our country, what would happen to the people?

Additional Reading. Any encyclopedia will give you much additional information on points connected with Asia. The general article on that continent will tell you about its physical features, its climate, its peoples, its history, and its products. 

If you want to know more about special countries, cities, rivers, animals, or products, turn to the article on whatever topic you wish to investigate. 

You may, for instance, want to learn about the great religions that have arisen in Asia. In that case turn to the articles on Brahmanism, Buddhism, Christianity, and Mohammedanism.

Carpenter's Asia (American Book Company) 

will take you on sight-seeing tours all over the continent. Huntington's Asia (Rand McNally & Co.) is full of interesting accounts of the peoples. 

There are many travel books about different parts of Asia. Among those that you might especially enjoy are Franck's China and The Japanese Empire in the Travels in Many Lands series (Owen Publishing Co.), Johnston's China and

Finnemore's Japan in the Peeps at Many Lands series (The Macmillan Co.), and Tietjens's Japan, 

Korea, and Formosa in the Burton Holmes Travel

Stories (Wheeler Publishing Co.). 

Many books tell about child life among the peoples of Asia. Among these are Roy's When I 

Was a Boy in India (Lothrop, Lee and Shepard 

Co.), Price's The Middle Country, a Chinese Lad's

Adventures in His Own Land (World Book Co.), and Mirza's When I Was a Boy in Persia (Lothrop, Lee and Shepard Co.).

In connection with India, there are Mukerji's many splendid stories, such as Ghond, the Hunter; 

Kari, the Elephant; and Hari, the Jungle Lad (E. P. Dutton and Co.). And no one who reads 

Kipling's books will ever forget such wonder stories as his The Jungle Book (in two series); 

Kim; and Plain Tales from the Hills (Doubleday, Doran and Co.) all dealing with scenes and incidents in India. Among Kipling's short tales that you will enjoy are "Moti Guj― Mutineer," the story of an elephant, and "Wee Willie Winkie," the story of the colonel's son at an army post.

Early Settlers. - Captain James Cook, a noted English explorer, landed on the southeastern coast of this lonely continent in 1770, while on a trip around the world. He claimed the eastern coast for Great Britain. 

Eighteen years later the British made their first settlement, which later grew into Sydney. Men who had been put in British jails because they did not pay their debts, or for other reasons, were sent to this distant continent as a punishment. Soon other settlers founded colonies on the eastern and southeastern coasts. These parts of Australia have a mild climate attractive to white people of the Temperate Zone. 357

THE COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA 

359 

When the first British settlers arrived, they | is land for many times that number of people, found Australia sparsely populated by black- but the Australians prefer to build up their skinned, curly-haired savages whom they country slowly. They believe in a white called "black fellows." As the colonists Australia," and have passed immigration pushed their settlements farther and farther laws that shut out members of the black and inland, the black fellows were forced back yellow races. from the coast into the interior of the country. It is there that they are living today. 

Some of them are still wild, untamed savages, but each year their number becomes less. 

The discovery of gold on the eastern coast in 1851 brought many more white settlers to the continent. It is interesting to know that although much gold was found and gold mines are still being worked, the majority of the gold seekers finally turned to farming and stock raising as surer ways of making a living.

The Commonwealth. In 1901 the colonies which the settlers had founded united to form the Commonwealth of Australia. The sev eral colonies became states under a federal government. Like Canada, Australia governs itself, although it is a member of the 

British Commonwealth of Nations, as you have already learned (page 83). 

There are now six states and three territories. Look at the map on the opposite page. On the mainland you will find the states of Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, and Western Australia.

To the south of the mainland, separated from it by Bass Strait, lies the island state of Tasmania. Two of the territories, Federal Capital Territory and Northern Territory, are on the mainland; the third, Territory of Papua, is situated on the island of New Guinea to the north.

The Australian parliament meets at the national capital, Canberra, in Federal Capital Territory, as our Congress meets at Washington, and makes the laws under which the country is governed. 

Population. Nearly all the Australians are of British descent. The total population of the country is now nearly 7,000,000, or less than that of the city of London. There There 

Size. — Australia is nearly 2000 miles across from east to west, and it averages more than 1000 miles in width from north to south. Its total area, including Tasmania and Papua, is over 3,000,000 square miles.

It is about the size of the mainland of the United States, and nearly as large as Europe. 

You see that although Australia is the smallest continent, it is nevertheless a vast country. 

Follow the coastline of Australia on the map on page 358 and notice how regular it is, and how little broken by bays. There are few natural harbors. Thirty miles or more off the northeast coast, a coral formation called the Great Barrier Reef extends about 

1000 miles from northwest to southeast.

Surface. Australia is made up of a central plain bordered by mountains on the east, north, and west. Turn to the map on page 

358. It shows that on the east the broad plain slopes upward into a range of mountains called the Great Dividing Range.

None of the mountains are very high. The highest parts are toward the south, where the range is sometimes called the Australian Alps. Here there are a few peaks, all of which are less than 7400 feet high. The mountains of the northern and western borders of the continent are lower. In the south-central section, the land slopes toward the Great Australian Bight and there are no mountains. How much of the map is colored green? Yellow? What does each color mean?

Rivers. The longest rivers, the Murray and its chief tributary the Darling, flow westward and southwestward from from the Great Dividing Range to the ocean on the south. The Murray-Darling is the only important river system in Australia. Other smaller rivers flow from the mountains to the sea on the east, north, and west coasts. 

The central plain has no rivers, as the small streams in the interior dry up or enter lakes

Climate. Study the wind and rainfall maps on this page. You will see that the winds bring a great deal of rain to the eastern parts of Australia. They rise in crossing the slopes of the Great Dividing Range and are cooled as they rise. In the Australian summer, the equatorial calms move southward over northern Australia, and as in other continents rain falls in this zone of calms. 

During this period northern and northeastern Australia have an average rainfall of over 40 inches (A). In the Australian winter, when the equatorial calm belt and the wind belts move northward, southwestern Australia gets some moisture from the prevailing westerlies of the Southern Hemisphere (B).

In the summer, the westerly winds are too far south to touch the mainland, although they bring some rain to the island of Tasmania at that time.

The interior and the south-central coast are dry, and much of the land is a desert. 

Much of the interior has as little as 5 inches of rainfall a year. Parts of the eastern and northern coasts have more than 50 inches.

A. — Distribution of population in Australia. 

The climate of much of Australia is continental, hot in summer and cold in winter. 

Remember that Australia has its winter during our summer, and its summer during our winter. Explain why this is so. June, July, and August are the coldest months. 

January and February are the warmest. It is never very cold on the continent, although in the south there are frosts, and the temperature is at times as low as 30°. Snow falls only in the mountainous regions. The north is much warmer, for it lies in the Tropics. 

Distribution of People. Since the eastern coast of Australia has plenty of rain, you will find that section of the country most densely populated. It is a region of forests and cleared lands where the people can grow crops, raise live stock, and engage in lumbering. By using the rivers, they can get their products to market.

The population map (A) shows a large number of people on the eastern and southeastern slopes of the Great Dividing Range, in Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria. Most of the large cities are found there. Few people live in the northeast because that part of the country is very hot. 

In most of the interior of the country there is little or no population because the rainfall is too scanty for agriculture or even for stock raising (maps, pages 364, 367). The southwest coast has a small population, but the number of people is increasing. As you have learned, this part of the continent gets some moisture from the prevailing westerlies, enough for farming and ranching. 

Cities. Sydney, the capital of New South 

Wales, is the oldest and largest city, with more than 1,200,000 inhabitants (357 A). It is the eastern terminal of the Trans-Australia 

Railroad, the only important railroad system. 

Perth is the western terminal. Because

Sydney is a seaport, much foreign commerce passes through it. Melbourne, the capital of Victoria, is the second city in size, with about 1,000,000 inhabitants. Adelaide and

Brisbane are other important centers of population. Hobart is the chief city in Tasmania. Of what states are these cities the capitals? Locate them on a map. Which are seaports? In a straight line how far is it from Sydney to Perth? From Melbourne to Hobart? 

Plant Life. The plants of Australia differ greatly from those of other continents.

Among the most curious of the trees are the bottle tree and the eucalyptus. The bottle tree, as the name implies, is shaped like a huge bottle with branches growing out of the top. The eucalyptus is tall, rising from two to four hundred feet in the air. It has leaves more gray than green. Instead of shedding its leaves, it sheds its bark every year. The wood is hard and durable, and is used for shipbuilding, paving blocks, railroad ties, and telegraph poles. The leaves are pressed for the eucalyptus oil used in medicines.

In the tropical north there are palms and bamboos, as well as ferns and grasses that grow to the size of trees. On the northeast coast bananas, oranges, pineapples, and sugar cane are grown. In the southeastern and the

A. Kangaroos. Notice the short front legs and the well-developed hind legs and tail. southwestern parts of the continent and in Tasmania, there are many vineyards and orchards. Seeds for the cultivated crops and the fruit trees were brought to Australia by the settlers. 

as Animals. The native animals are peculiar as the native plants. The kangaroo (A) is one of the most curious. Some of the kangaroos are as small as large cats; others are as tall as men. The front legs are short and weak, but the hind legs and tail are long and strong. Instead of running when chased, kangaroos leap over the ground, standing nearly upright and using the tail as well as the hind legs in jumping. 

A mother kangaroo carries her young in a pouch or fold of the skin on the under side of her body. Such animals are called marsupials. A marsupial found in the United 

States is the opossum. 

The platypus (B), an animal the size of a large rabbit, has webbed feet like a duck, fur like a seal, and a broad beak like a duck's bill. It is at home both on the land and in B. 

A platypus. Notice the dark fur, webbed foot, and broad bill. the water. It hatches its young from eggs and, like the kangaroo, carries them in a pouch. 

Emus, which resemble ostriches, and lyre birds are native to Australia. In the hot north, gayly colored parrots and other tropical birds are numerous. Many kinds of song birds are found along the eastern coast, and in the interior hawks and eagles fly over the desert. The common domestic animals have been introduced from other countries, and in the interior camels are used on the deserts. 

The Pacific Slope. The Pacific Slope is the plain extending along the eastern coast, sloping east from the Great Dividing Range to the Pacific Ocean. Find it on the map on page 358, and notice how it curves eastward into the ocean. The Pacific Slope is long from north to south, but it is only from 70 to 

200 miles wide.

The rainfall on the Pacific Slope is plentiful and the soil is fertile. In Victoria, New

ern Australia, is the Central Plain. This is a region of light or little rainfall, and the interior is a desert. The outer regions which slope up to the mountains, however, have a rainfall of from 10 to 30 inches yearly.

Here are wheat farms and large areas covered with grass and shrubs which furnish pastures for beef cattle and sheep. These regions are called the grasslands or "the bush." Sheep and Wool. - Grazing is the chief occupation of the continent. Over 100,000,000 sheep pasture on the grasslands, and each wheat is stored in sacks out of doors, and sheep averages nearly 10 pounds of wool a there are very few grain elevators.

Some of the wheat is ground into flour in mills in the cities, but much is exported, especially to Great Britain (363 A). Australia is the fourth largest wheat-exporting country in the world. Only Canada, Argentina, and the United States export more.

Dairying. There are many dairy farms in New South Wales and Victoria. With the help of the government, dairying has made great progress in recent years. Butter, cheese, and dried or condensed milk are important exports, sent chiefly to Great Britain. 

Other Products of Eastern Australia. - 

In the tropical northern part of the Pacific Slope, sugar cane, some cotton, tobacco, bananas, oranges, and pineapples are grown for the home markets. On the higher slopes of the range, lumbering is carried on. Most of the forests are of hardwoods, especially eucalyptus. Some of the timber is exported, although Australia has so few evergreen forests that pine and other soft woods for building purposes must be imported.

SHEEP AND WOOL

Australia leads the world in wool exports, furnishing more than one third of the world total. Although the sheep are raised for both meat and wool, and mutton is shipped abroad, wool is the most valuable single product of the continent. The greater part of the wool goes to Great Britain, where it is made into cloth of fine quality (page 91).

Much Australian wool, however, goes to 

France, Germany, the United States, and other wool-manufacturing countries. 

Sheep Stations. - Sheep ranches, called sheep stations in Australia, are very large. 

Some of them have an area of over one hundred square miles. This is because in regions of poor pasture it takes several acres of land to keep one sheep for a year. However, this land is not costly to buy. Many of the station owners got their lands in the first place as gifts from the government; or they bought the ground for a small price per acre. 

Each of the great sheep stations employs many men. The buildings are usually many miles from any settlement where supplies can be purchased or work done. As a result, you will usually find at each station some one who knows how to do whatever needs to be done to carry on the work without help from the outside. You will find homes for the men, a store, a carpenter shop, a blacksmith shop, and other buildings, as well as an office where the business of the ranch is looked after. 

When Australia was first settled, sheep were allowed to graze over the open range, but later the ranches were fenced in to keep out the dingoes, or wild dogs, which killed the sheep. Now, if you travel through Australia, you see thousands of miles of wire fences.

There is another reason for the fences. 

Rabbits, brought into the country as pets,

AUSTRALIA 

escaped and so increased in number that they began to destroy the pastures and caused great damage. They not only ate the grass of the pastures, but they destroyed the young trees by eating their bark. The government is trying to get rid of them, and offers a sum of money for each animal killed. Many thousands have been killed, but thousands still infest the grazing lands, as they have no natural enemies among the animals of Australia. 

Wire fences are now sunk deep in the ground, so that the rabbits cannot burrow under them. As the fence net is so small that the rabbits cannot get through, it is usually possible to keep them out of regions that have been cleared.

The most valuable and most common of the different breeds of sheep is the merino, brought to Australia from Spain. The merino is small, but its wool is fine and heavy. 

The event of the year on a sheep station is shearing time. Shearing gangs travel from station to station, and clip the wool with mechanical clippers, run by electricity, steam, or compressed air. The stations have large sheds built especially for shearing (365 A).

Here the shearers work steadily for many hours each day until all of the sheep have been shorn.

Wool Shipping. -The wool from each sheep is separated into different parts, because of differences in its length or fineness. 

It is sorted and baled, usually in 400-pound sacks. It is then ready for its long trip to market. Since the sheep stations are far from the railroads and steamships, it is difficult to transport the wool to shipping centers. Some ranchers, who live near good roads, use motor trucks. The majority, however, use wagons drawn by horses or oxen. Near the desert, camel caravans are sometimes employed. In the chief markets, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Brisbane, wool is sold to buyers from many parts of the world, and shipped over the various ocean routes. 

Ocean Routes. The most important ocean route to Europe from Australia is by way of Aden and the Suez Canal. Some of the ships on this route stop at Batavia, Singapore, and Colombo on the way. Another route is through the Panama Canal. Wool for the United States is usually shipped to 

San Francisco, or through the Panama Canal to the eastern seaports. Other sea routes pass around the Cape of Good Hope and 

Cape Horn. Trace all these routes on a globe, so that you will have a clear picture of them in mind.

Beef Cattle.

Cattle droving in New South Wales. A part of the herd is being driven to pasture. 

Second in importance to sheep raising in Australia, is cattle raising. 

Both beef cattle and dairy cattle are raised. 

Much frozen or chilled beef, hides, and leather are exported, as well as the dairy products that you read about on page 364. Most of these exports go to Great Britain, which in return sends manufactured articles. 

Compare the cattle map (B) with the sheep map (364 A). You will find many cattle ranches, as well as sheep stations, in the grasslands of the Central Plain. But most of the cattle ranches are nearer the bordering slopes of the mountains, where there is more water and better grass. 

Australia pastures over 10,000,000 cattle. 

Most of them are beef animals, the profit coming from the meat and from the hides of the animals. The beef cattle are generally driven to market in herds, grazing as they walk the many miles to the cities. They travel over routes that are supplied with water. When the city to which they are being driven is reached, they are slaughtered. 

The meat is either sold to the home markets or chilled or frozen for export. The hides may be shipped as raw hides or made into leather before they are shipped.

It has few inhabitants except in the city of Perth. In the north it is too hot for farming. In the central region the rainfall is too scanty for crops, although there is some pasture on the slopes where cattle and sheep are grazed. 

The principal occupation is ranching, but gold has been found in several places, and there are a number of gold-mining towns. 

Farther south, where the rainfall is moderate and the temperature is mild, there are wheat farms and orchards. Some mixed farming also is carried on. Wool, hides, meat, and wheat are shipped from Fremantle, the seaport suburb of the city of Perth. But the

Western Coast of Australia has not been developed, for there is still much land in the east and southeast on which it is easier to make a living. 

Mines and Minerals. Australia is rich in mineral deposits. Formerly gold was the chief mineral, and in the early days many adventurers went to Australia hoping to make their fortunes. Some gold is still mined in the southwestern and southeastern parts, but coal is now the leading mineral product. It is mined largely on the eastern, southeastern, and southwestern coasts. Some of it is sold abroad, and to steamships which stop for fuel. Copper, lead, silver, zinc, and tin mines also are worked. Tasmania has especially valuable mineral deposits.

Rubies and sapphires are found in the northeast near the Gulf of Carpentaria, and opals are mined in the eastern part of the 

Central Plain. Pearls are taken from the waters of the Indian Ocean on the Western Coast. 

New Guinea. The island of New Guinea lies to the north of Australia. Find it on the map on page 356. The eastern half is divided between the Territory of Papua and the Territory of New Guinea. These two 

New Guinea is part of the East Indies, which are generally considered as belonging with Asia, as you have already learned elsewhere. But it lies near Australia and is somewhat like it in plant and animal life. It is a large island, with an area of more than 

300,000 square miles. It has lowlands and highlands, some of the mountains rising more than 15,000 feet above sea level. 

In the lowlands of Papua rubber and coconut plantations are being developed by the labor of natives who are being taught by white men. There are very few white men on the island, however, for the rainfall is heavy and the climate is tropical. The chief settlement is Port Moresby, where ships call to bring in supplies and to take on cargoes of rubber and copra, which, as you know, is the dried meat of coconuts.

Australia is the smallest continent.. It is far from other continents, and lies entirely south of the Equator in the Torrid and South Temperate Zones. It is all one country and inhabited largely by the white race. is self-governing, and part of the British 

Commonwealth of Nations.

A great part of it is desert. On the grasslands millions of sheep and cattle graze. 

Grazing and agriculture are the main occupations. Wool, mutton, beef, hides, leather, wheat, butter, cheese, dried or condensed milk, and fruit are the chief exports.

NEW ZEALAND 

New Zealand lies about 1200 miles to the southeast of Australia. Like Australia, it is part of the British Commonwealth of Nations (page 83), and self-governing. Find New

Zealand on a globe. Notice that it is half way round the world from the mother country, England.

New Zealand consists of two large islands, separated by Cook Strait, and many small islands. It is about the size of Colorado, more than 100,000 square miles in area. 

1,500,000. Most of the New Zealanders are

Population. The population is more than of British descent. The original natives, called Maoris, number about 69,000. They are a strong, intelligent race, and quickly adopted the ways of white men. They have a share in the government and elect members of their own race to the parliament.

NEW ZEALAND 

Photo from New Zealand government printer. Courtesy Matson Line 

A. The Tasman, the largest glacier in New Zealand. The snow-capped peak in the center background is the

The New Zealanders are very progressive, and have passed many laws that make the country a pleasant place for people who must work. Old-age insurance protects the worker when he becomes old. Sickness funds take care of him when he is unable to work. The law fixes the number of hours a day or a week he works. It also sets up the wages he must get for his labor.

Surface and Climate. - Mountain ranges form the backbone of both North and South Islands. Turn to the map on page 358, and see how much of the islands is over 2000 feet above sea level. The highest peak is Mt. 

Cook, named for the explorer James Cook. 

How high is it?

In the mountains the scenery is magnificent. Some of the peaks are at all times covered with snow. In the higher ranges, there are great glaciers. There are many picturesque waterfalls, active volcanoes, geysers, and other hot springs. In the mountains are also fertile valleys and plateaus, where crops are raised. Most of the rivers. are short mountain torrents. Bordering the coast are many fertile lowland plains. 

The climate is mild, except in the high mountains. There are no great extremes of heat or cold. The rainfall is heaviest on the western side, because the prevailing winds are westerlies. On the eastern side the rainfall is sometimes so light that irrigation is necessary for farming. 

Animals. New Zealand has animals as odd as those of Australia. There are various kinds of marsupials, black swans, and gaylycolored birds. The native kea parrot has caused much damage to the sheep herders. 

It alights on the backs of sheep and kills them with its sharp beak, to eat the fat surrounding the kidneys. Rabbits destroy pastures, as they do in Australia. In the mountains red and fallow deer and wapiti supply game for sportsmen.

ISLANDS OF THE PACIFIC 

Thousands of islands are scattered over the Pacific Ocean, but only the larger groups are important. Turn to the map on page 

356, where you will see these larger groups. 

The smaller ones are not shown. You learned about the East Indies when you studied Asia and New Guinea when you studied Australia (page 368). 

The Larger Islands. East of New 

Guinea is the Bismarck Archipelago, belonging to the Commonwealth of Australia. Southeast of these are the Solomon 

Islands under British control. Also under 

British control are Santa Cruz, the Fiji 

Islands, Tonga Islands, and Cook Islands.

The New Hebrides are governed jointly by Great Britain and France. New Cale 

Formation. Some of the Pacific Islands are the tops of volcanic mountains. Most of the volcanoes are dead, but a few are still active. These high islands are mountainous, and therefore usually have a heavy rainfall. 

They are often covered with dense forests. 

Other islands are coral formations, and are rather flat, or low. The scenery on some of them, especially Tahiti, is beautiful, and many artists have visited them. 

Their Importance. - Coconut, banana, and breadfruit trees grow in abundance on most of the islands. Food is so plentiful, and the climate is so warm that life is easy. The natives are therefore not very industrious, but they are certainly a very happy people. 

Copra is the chief export. But the principal value of the islands is their use as coaling stations and harbors for the ships that must pass their way.

TEMPERATURE AND TIME ZONES AND HEAT BELTS 

Zones. You will find it interesting to compare the two maps on the opposite page. 

The upper one shows the surface of the earth divided into five zones. The names given to these five zones are "heat " or temperature names. The boundaries of these five zones, however, are fixed by the way in which the rays of the sun meet the earth's surface at certain times each year. 

The Torrid Zone is bounded on the north by the Tropic of Cancer, which is 231° north of the Equator. This is the line that marks the northern limit reached by the direct rays of the sun on June 21 each year. The Torrid

Zone is bounded on the south by the Tropic of Capricorn, which is 231° south of the Equator, and marks the southern limit reached by the direct rays of the sun on 

December 21 each year. Zone. When you learn that a country is in one of these five zones, you have learned something about its position on the surface of the earth, and much about the direction of the sun's rays there. You have also learned something - but not all about its climate, especially its temperature. 

Heat Belts. The heat belts, shown on the lower map on the opposite page, are divided in another way. The hot belt is that part of the earth where the average temperature at the earth's surface at sea level is more than 68°. The cold caps are regions where the average annual temperature at sea level is less than 50°. In the temperate belts, therefore, the average annual temperature at sea level is more than 50° and less than 68°. To get sea-level temperature for a place that is above sea level, 1° of temperature is added for each 300 feet of elevation. For example, in the hot-belt part of South America, the northern Andes are included. Of course the actual annual average temperature of the mountains is much less than 68°. But if the average is taken for any point in the mountains and to that elevation above sea level, the temperature as it would be at sea level is found. 

The North Frigid Zone is a cap around the North Pole, reaching as far south as the Arctic Circle. The South Frigid Zone is a cap around the South Pole, reaching as far north as the Antarctic Circle. These circles are 

231° from the poles and are fixed in the follow-temperature 1° is added for each 300 feet of ing ways: when the direct rays of the sun, on June 21, are on the Tropic of Cancer, horizontal rays of the sun touch the earth's surface 231 beyond the North Pole, or at the Arctic Circle. At the same time, other horizontal rays of the sun touch the earth 

2340 short of the South Pole, or at the Antarctic Circle. Six months later, when the direct rays of the sun are on the Tropic of Capricorn, the sun's rays reach beyond the South 

Pole and fall short of the North Pole 2310, again fixing the position of the Antarctic and 

Arctic circles.

Between the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer is the North Temperate Zone, and between the Antarctic Circle and the Tropic of Capricorn is the South Temperate You will see that each heat belt varies in width although the zones shown in the map above do not. This is chiefly because of the way land temperatures are affected by the prevailing winds blowing across the sea to the land in different parts of the earth. 

You will notice that the hot belt is on both sides of the Equator, but more in the Northern Hemisphere than in the Southern 

Hemisphere. The North Temperate belt is much broader than the South Temperate belt, more irregular in outline, and includes nearly half the land surface of the earth. It is in these temperate belts that the most pro- |gressive peoples of the earth live. 373 N6.22

TIME

Measurement of Time. -The rotation of the earth through one full turn gives a length of time called a day. Each day is divided into twenty-four hours, each hour into sixty minutes, and each minute into sixty seconds.

One full revolution of the earth about the sun gives a period of time called a year. Vancouver Portland

Seattl 120° and clocks are now used instead of sundials and hourglasses. 

In our country twelve o'clock comes both at noon and at midnight, and so we have all the hours from one to twelve before noon (A.M.) and after noon (P.M.). In some countries, however, watches and clocks are made to show twenty-four hours. In those countries the time we call one o'clock in the afternoon becomes thirteen o'clock, our two o'clock in the afternoon becomes fourteen o'clock, and our midnight becomes twenty-four o'clock. 

Standard Time. Local time varies from place to place, because noon varies from place to place. Because it is often necessary that people in a large area should be able to do things at the same time, the United States has been divided into standard time belts.

Within each of these belts, the same time is used for all places, instead of the local time for each place. The standard time chosen for each belt is the local time of a selected meridian. Map C shows you the standard time belts of our country. Learn their names.

In passing from one time belt to another when you travel west, you need to set your watch back one hour; but when traveling east, you must set it ahead one hour. • Paradise Through the centuries men have invented ways to measure time. One of the early ways was to use the sundial (A). This instrument is placed so that the sun causes its upright part to cast a shadow on the level | surface on which it stands. The position of this shadow is marked for noon and for the hours of sunlight before and after noon. 

One way of measuring units of time, such as an hour, was by using an hourglass (B). In such a glass, sand runs from one half of the glass to the other through a narrow opening. 

Just enough sand is put in the glass to take an hour in flowing from the upper part to the lower. The glass can then be turned over to measure the next hour. Other such glasses have been made to measure longer or shorter periods of time. Watches Huntington
